char.manlius: Marcus Manlius, guardian of the Capitol

level.actium.fact: On September 2, 31 BC, off Actium, Octavian and Agrippa trapped Antony's fleet in the bay. Cleopatra's presence divided his staff: Roman commanders were unwilling to fight under the Egyptian queen, and some defected to the enemy even before the battle. In the midst of the battle, her squadron of sixty ships hoisted sails and headed south — Antony abandoned his flagship and, on a swift quinquereme, followed suit. His fleet surrendered, and his army defected to Octavian without a fight.
level.actium.goal: The fleet is defeated, and the general follows the foreign sails
level.actium.hint: A queen in the battle line costs Antony the trust of his captains, and his army loses strength. Then he is beaten at sea, and when her sails turn south, he will abandon his fleet and follow: the shame is not in defeat, but in this.
level.actium.intro: Two fleets converged off Cape Actium. Antony's ships are heavier, but his men are deserting to his rival, and an Egyptian squadron stands in his line.
level.actium.title: Actium
level.agincourt.fact: On October 25, 1415, St. Crispin's Day, English archers, protected by stakes driven into the ground, decimated French knights bogged down in the mud of a ploughed field; dismounted and pressed together, they fell upon each other and suffocated under the weight of their armor. The Constable d'Albret, three dukes, and up to a thousand noble knights perished – against a few hundred Englishmen. In the heat of battle, Henry, fearing an attack from the rear, ordered the prisoners to be killed – an order that shocked even his own knights. Shakespeare gave this day a speech about the «band of brothers»; France received Troyes and a child English king on its throne.
level.agincourt.goal: A handful of sick archers destroy the flower of French chivalry in the mud.
level.agincourt.hint: Stakes before the line – that's the preparation. Don't advance yourself: wait for the knights to cross the ploughed field – in the mud, their armor ceases to be a strength. Don't kill prisoners: the goal is victory, not a massacre.
level.agincourt.intro: Henry V leads six thousand weary, dysentery-stricken Englishmen towards Calais. Thirty thousand Frenchmen under Constable d'Albret block their path. Between them lies a freshly ploughed field, and it has been raining all night.
level.agincourt.source: Gesta Henrici Quinti (The Deeds of Henry V); Enguerrand de Monstrelet
level.agincourt.title: Agincourt
level.alaric.fact: In 408, Honorius, swayed by court slanders, executed Stilicho—the Vandal general who had held the border for twenty years and twice repelled Alaric. At the same time, the families of Gothic federates were massacred, and thirty thousand warriors defected to Alaric. On August 24, 410, the Goths entered through the Salarian Gate and plundered the city for three days, the first time it had been taken by an enemy since 390 BC. Procopius recounts that when Honorius was informed 'Roma has perished,' he believed they spoke of his favorite rooster named Roma, and was relieved to learn it was merely the city.
level.alaric.goal: Rome taken by an enemy for the first time in eight hundred years
level.alaric.hint: As long as the old general holds the border, the Goths will not approach the walls — first, the court will get rid of him. Then the Goths will bargain at the walls, and the emperor will refuse. He will go to the birds — there will be no one to answer, and the city will stand.
level.alaric.intro: The Goths stand before Rome for the third time. The Emperor sits in Ravenna beyond the marshes, unresponsive to their terms—and the only general who knew how to fight them is no longer at court.
level.alaric.source: Procopius, 'History of the Wars,' Book III (Vandalic War), 2; Jordanes, 'Getica'
level.alaric.title: Goths at the Gates
level.alesia.fact: In 52 BC, Caesar surrounded Alesia with an eighteen-kilometer inner circumvallation and a twenty-kilometer outer contravallation, against Commius' Gallic army coming to the rescue. The besieged expelled women and children from the city — Caesar did not let them through the ramparts, and they died between the walls. After the failed attack from outside, Vercingetorix, according to Plutarch, rode around Caesar on horseback in his finest armor, dismounted, and threw his weapons at Caesar's feet. He was held in prison for six years, paraded in a triumph, and strangled. Gaul became Roman for five hundred years.
level.alesia.goal: The besieger himself becomes besieged — and still takes the chief by starvation
level.alesia.hint: To storm the hill is to repeat Gergovia; without ramparts, outside relief will crush the besiegers. Encircle both the city and yourself with walls — then hunger will do its work, and the chieftain will cast his weapons at the feet of one who holds sway.
level.alesia.intro: All Gaul has risen under Vercingetorix. At Gergovia, he already repelled Caesar. Now he has barricaded himself with eighty thousand men in Alesia on a hill, and all Gaul is coming to his aid.
level.alesia.source: Caesar, 'Commentarii de Bello Gallico', VII, 68–89; Plutarch, 'Caesar', 27
level.alesia.title: Weapons at His Feet
level.alexandria.fact: In August 30 BC, Antony, receiving false news of Cleopatra's death, fell on his sword; the dying man was hoisted by ropes into the mausoleum, and he died in her arms. Octavian kept the queen under guard, intending to parade her in his triumph — and after meeting him, she understood there would be no negotiation. Plutarch writes of a snake in a basket of figs, immediately adding that no one knows the truth; only two barely visible pricks were found on her body. With her death, the Ptolemaic dynasty ended, and Egypt became the personal possession of the victor.
level.alexandria.goal: Both depart on their own — the victor has no one to lead in triumph.
level.alexandria.hint: The general falls on his sword due to a false report; the queen remains a widow. The serpent does not come immediately: first, one must hear what the victor offers — and he offers a path behind his chariot.
level.alexandria.intro: After Actium, Egypt is doomed. Octavian is at the gates of Alexandria, and he needs not so much the country as a living queen — for his triumph in Rome.
level.alexandria.title: Cleopatra's Asp
level.alexei.fact: In 1718, Tsarevich Alexei, who had fled abroad and was accused of treason against his reformist father, was returned, condemned to death, and died in the Peter and Paul Fortress under unclear circumstances.
level.alexei.goal: The reformist Tsar judges his own son
level.alexei.hint: No revolt here – the court decides the heir's fate.
level.alexei.title: The Case of Tsarevich Alexei
level.alps.fact: In 1799, Suvorov defeated French armies in Italy at the Adda, Trebbia, and Novi. Paul I had promoted him to field marshal even earlier, and now granted him the title of Prince of Italy. According to the allies' plan, he moved through St. Gotthard into Switzerland; the Austrians did not send the promised mules and withdrew their troops, while Masséna defeated Rimsky-Korsakov's Russian corps near Zurich. On September 14 (25), at the Devil's Bridge over the Reuss, the French blew up a span; soldiers tied logs with officers' scarves and crossed under fire. The army, without bread or ammunition, broke out of encirclement via Panix, losing a quarter of its strength but bringing fifteen hundred prisoners. Paul bestowed upon Suvorov the rank of Generalissimo, the fourth in Russian history — but a month later, he fell into disgrace again; the commander died in St. Petersburg in May 1800.
level.alps.goal: The commander defeats the French, abandoned by allies, starves in the mountains — and leads the army across tied logs.
level.alps.hint: First, the Italian Campaign — the mighty Suvorov defeats the French. The victor is abandoned by the Austrians — he is hungry and no longer a force. Then, the Devil's Bridge: the hungry commander passes through — a legend, once again with weight and power. The Emperor bestows a rank upon the legend. Lay down arms — the end.
level.alps.intro: Seventy-year-old Suvorov, recalled from disgrace by Paul I, drives the French out of Italy in four months. He is then sent across the Alps to Switzerland, where Masséna awaits, but the Austrian allies depart and fail to send the promised mules.
level.alps.source: D. Milyutin, 'History of the 1799 War'; A. Petrushevsky
level.alps.title: Devil's Bridge
level.anagni.fact: In 1296 the bull Clericis laicos forbade taxing the clergy without Rome's consent; in 1302 Unam Sanctam declared that there is no salvation outside submission to the pope. In June 1303, at an assembly in the Louvre, Guillaume de Nogaret accused Boniface VIII of heresy, simony and the murder of his predecessor, and demanded a general council. On 7 September 1303 Nogaret and Sciarra Colonna burst into Anagni with an armed band and held the nearly seventy-year-old pope for three days; the famous slap is most likely a legend, but the humiliation was real. The townspeople freed him, he returned to Rome and died on 11 October of the same year. The next pope was Benedict XI, who reigned less than a year; in 1305 the Frenchman Clement V was elected, and from 1309 the curia sat at Avignon — the Avignon captivity lasted until 1377. In 1311 Clement lifted Nogaret's excommunication, declaring that he had acted out of pious zeal.
level.anagni.goal: The lawyer declares the pope a heretic and puts him under guard — and the next pope takes his seat beyond the Rhône, under the king's hand
level.anagni.hint: First the Louvre: a lawyer whom no one has bought accuses the pope before the Estates. The accused man is seized in his own summer residence. Only after that does the king move the curia to France — and he needs the man who did the deed beside him. The Mint is a trap: a bought lawyer will accuse no one.
level.anagni.intro: The king taxed the lands of the Church, the pope forbade payment — and declared that every earthly creature is subject to the Roman pontiff. So the king needed not a sword but a lawyer. Guillaume de Nogaret can dress any wish of the king in the form of a lawful accusation.
level.anagni.source: J. Favier, 'Philip the Fair'; Dante, 'Purgatorio', Canto XX
level.anagni.title: The Slap at Anagni
level.anne_boleyn.fact: Anne Boleyn, for whom Henry broke with Rome, bore a daughter, Elizabeth, but no son. Losing interest in her, the king allowed Thomas Cromwell to fabricate charges of treason, incest, and witchcraft. On May 19, 1536, Anne was beheaded in the Tower. The accusations were almost certainly false.
level.anne_boleyn.goal: For her, Rome fell — and on the block, she too.
level.anne_boleyn.hint: A wedding, then an accusation: Cromwell, with his authority, condemns the queen in a tribunal speech. The condemned is executed by the king.
level.anne_boleyn.source: E. Ives, 'The Life and Death of Anne Boleyn'
level.anne_boleyn.title: Anne Boleyn
level.anne_cleves.fact: The marriage to Anne of Cleves (1540) was arranged by Cromwell based on a flattering portrait by Holbein. In person, Anne did not please the king (the myth of the 'Flanders mare' was malicious gossip); the marriage was annulled after six months as unconsummated. Anne agreed and became the 'King's good sister,' outliving all of Henry's wives. Cromwell, however, paid with his head for this marriage.
level.anne_cleves.goal: An unwanted marriage quietly annulled — Anne remains whole.
level.anne_cleves.hint: A foreign bride must first be presented to court by a counselor — otherwise the door remains shut. A wedding, then the king's speech in the tribunal dissolves the marriage. Do not send her to the Tower: she will survive.
level.anne_cleves.intro: Cromwell proposes a bride from overseas to the king, one he has not seen.
level.anne_cleves.source: A. Weir, 'The Six Wives of Henry VIII'
level.anne_cleves.title: Anne of Cleves
level.antoinette.fact: On October 16, 1793, Marie Antoinette, the 'Widow Capet,' was guillotined nine months after her husband. The Revolutionary Tribunal accused her of treason and conspiracy with foreign powers.
level.antoinette.goal: The former queen is tried and executed
level.antoinette.hint: The Jacobin Club has no part in this — lead her through trial and to the scaffold.
level.antoinette.title: The Widow Capet
level.aquae_sextiae.fact: In 102 BC, Gaius Marius kept his legions behind the camp's rampart for six days while the Teutons marched past, shouting to the Romans: 'What shall we tell your wives? We'll be in Rome soon.' Plutarch writes that he deliberately let the soldiers watch the enemy until fear turned into anger. Then, at Aquae Sextiae, he engaged in battle on a slope, while Legate Marcellus, with three thousand men, struck from ambush in the rear. The Teutons were annihilated; their women fought from their wagons and killed their children and themselves to avoid slavery. A year later, Marius similarly dealt with the Cimbri at Vercellae.
level.aquae_sextiae.goal: Legions accustomed to fear cease to fear — and the Teutons are no more
level.aquae_sextiae.hint: To engage in open battle immediately is to lose, as five armies did before. To let the enemies pass by, so the soldiers grow accustomed to their sight — that is strength. The legate with his cohorts must be hidden in the hills beforehand.
level.aquae_sextiae.intro: The Teutons are marching on Italy — hundreds of thousands, with wagons, wives, and children. They have already destroyed five Roman armies. Marius has barricaded himself in his camp near the Rhône and will not sally forth.
level.aquae_sextiae.title: See You in Rome
level.aragon_divorce.fact: Pope Clement VII refused to annul Henry's marriage to Catherine of Aragon. In 1533–34, Henry broke with Rome: by the 'Act of Supremacy,' he declared himself Supreme Head of the Church of England, personally declared the marriage invalid, and married Anne Boleyn. Thus began the English Reformation.
level.aragon_divorce.goal: Henry breaks with Rome and divorces Catherine.
level.aragon_divorce.hint: No agreement with the Pope — the Emperor stands behind him. The King declares himself head of the Church and gains authority, then condemns the queen in a tribunal speech — the marriage is dissolved.
level.aragon_divorce.intro: Henry is married to Catherine, but yearns for a divorce — and the Pope is against it.
level.aragon_divorce.title: The Divorce from Rome
level.archimedes_l.fact: From 214–212 BC, Marcellus besieged Syracuse. According to Polybius and Plutarch, Archimedes' machines — cranes with hooks, catapults, possibly mirrors — made the assault impossible; the Romans fled at the mere sight of a rope above the wall. The city was taken at night during a festival of Artemis, when the guards were drunk. Marcellus ordered Archimedes' life to be spared, but a legionary slew the old man, who allegedly asked not to disturb his drawing in the sand: «Noli turbare circulos meos». Marcellus, it is said, mourned him and buried him with honors; a century and a half later, Cicero found the neglected tomb by the sphere and cylinder carved into the stone.
level.archimedes_l.goal: An impregnable city is taken when its defenders are drunk — and he who defended it is slain.
level.archimedes_l.hint: While the machines stand, the assault will break against the walls. You must await a festival, when the garrison is drunk and the city is no longer strong — then battle. And the scholar will be killed not by the general, but by a common legionary.
level.archimedes_l.intro: Syracuse has defected from Rome, and Marcellus has brought his fleet to its walls. The city is defended not so much by Epicydes' garrison as by one old man — Archimedes: his machines lift ships from the water and cast them down.
level.archimedes_l.title: Circles in the Sand
level.arcole.fact: From November 15–17, 1796, at Arcole, Bonaparte stormed the bridge over the Alpone for three days; on the first day, he seized a standard and led the grenadiers under grapeshot, was thrown into a swamp, and pulled out by his aides-de-camp — Gros's painting with this standard is known throughout France. Alvinczi retreated, Mantua fell two months later, and Italy was conquered. All this time, Napoleon wrote letters to Josephine that set paper ablaze ('I kiss your heart, then lower, then much lower') — while she was having an affair with a Hussar lieutenant in Paris.
level.arcole.goal: The general with the standard advances onto the bridge under grapeshot — and Italy is his
level.arcole.hint: First, letters to Josephine — the love that drives him forward. On the bridge, the general himself takes the standard — this is his strength and weight. Then, a battle with the strong Austrian — and he is defeated. Waiting for reinforcements is not for him.
level.arcole.intro: Twenty-seven-year-old General Bonaparte, with a ragged army, defeats the Austrians in Italy — and every evening writes to Josephine in Paris, who replies sporadically. Field Marshal Alvinczi marches to relieve the siege of Mantua; the bridge over the Alpone at Arcole is swept by fire.
level.arcole.title: The Bridge of Arcole
level.armada.fact: In 1588, Philip II of Spain launched the "Invincible Armada" of 130 ships against England. The English fleet, where Francis Drake distinguished himself, scattered the Spanish with fireships off Gravelines, and a storm completed their rout. The victory saved Protestant England and elevated Elizabeth to the pinnacle of glory.
level.armada.goal: Drake's fireships scatter the Armada — Elizabeth triumphs
level.armada.hint: Two forces at sea — a draw. Drake's fireships in the harbor at night break the Armada's formation — and then the Battle of Gravelines is won by Drake himself. The Queen watches from the shore.
level.armada.intro: Philip II sends the "Invincible Armada" to punish the heretic Elizabeth. Francis Drake awaits off the coast.
level.armada.title: The Invincible Armada
level.aspromonte.fact: On August 24, 1862, Garibaldi sailed from Catania to Calabria with two thousand volunteers, without artillery or a plan—only with the slogan 'Roma o morte'. As early as August 3, the king had declared the expedition illegal, and on August 29, on the Aspromonte plateau, Colonel Pallavicini and his Bersaglieri opened fire; Garibaldi forbade his men to return fire—'do not shoot Italian soldiers'—and was wounded by two bullets, in the thigh and right ankle. He was taken to Varignano fortress near La Spezia; doctors from all over Europe debated where the bullet was lodged, and only in November did the Florentine Zanetti extract it with a probe sent from Paris by surgeon Nélaton. On October 5, the king granted amnesty to all; the Rattazzi government, which had itself encouraged the expedition, fell. Rome was taken only in 1870, when Napoleon III lost his army at Sedan—without Garibaldi. He kept the bullet from Aspromonte until his death.
level.aspromonte.goal: The Hero of the Thousand once again gathers volunteers with the cry 'Rome or Death!'—and the king, to whom he gave half a country, stops him with a bullet in the leg.
level.aspromonte.hint: First, 'Rome or Death': the general raises volunteers—strong and on the march. The king disavows the expedition—now they are enemies. The disavowing king meets the marching general at Aspromonte: he orders his men not to shoot—wounded and captured. Storming Rome from the French and fighting the Bersaglieri—that is not what he did: 'Do not shoot!'
level.aspromonte.intro: 1862. Italy is united, but without Rome: there, the Pope is under the protection of Napoleon III's French garrison. In Palermo, Garibaldi, with the tacit connivance of the Rattazzi government, gathers volunteers—'Rome or Death!'—and crosses into Calabria. Napoleon threatens; King Victor Emmanuel, who shook his hand in Teano two years prior, issues a proclamation: this is a rebellion.
level.aspromonte.source: G. Garibaldi, 'Memoirs'; G. Trevelyan, 'Garibaldi and the Making of Italy'; D. Mack Smith, 'Garibaldi'
level.aspromonte.title: Aspromonte
level.attila.fact: In 452, Attila razed Aquileia to the ground—the survivors fled to the lagoon, from which Venice arose. At the Mincius River, an embassy led by Pope Leo I met him, and the army turned back. Christian tradition speaks of a miracle; contemporaries cited simpler reasons—famine in the ravaged valley, an epidemic in the camp, and troops approaching from the East. A year later, Attila died on his wedding night from a hemorrhage, and his empire disintegrated within two years.
level.attila.goal: The chieftain is turned back without a single battle
level.attila.hint: He cannot be stopped in open battle — there, the last army is lost. A general of standing must wear him down with hunger in a ravaged valley — and only then does an embassy make sense.
level.attila.intro: Aquileia is razed, the Po Valley lies open, there is nothing and no one to march on Rome: the last army of the West is exhausted from last year's battle.
level.attila.title: Meeting at the Mincius
level.augustus.fact: On January 13, 27 BC, Octavian announced in the Senate that he was relinquishing all extraordinary powers and restoring the Republic. The Senate, for whom this meant a new civil war, immediately begged him to stay — and three days later, at the suggestion of Munatius Plancus, gave him the name Augustus, 'the revered one'. He refused to be called king or dictator his entire life, preferring princeps — 'first among the senators'. Formally, the Republic continued for another five hundred years.
level.augustus.goal: All power goes to him who publicly renounced it.
level.augustus.hint: Rome kills kings, but fears anarchy. Relinquish your powers in such a way that the Senate yields on its own — and then it will proclaim you, and even invent an unprecedented name. Do not take the crown from the tray.
level.augustus.intro: The civil wars are over, and there is but one victor. Yet Rome kills kings — and Octavian remembers this. In the Senate sits Munatius Plancus, a master of offering the right word at the opportune moment, and beside Octavian — the loyal Agrippa.
level.augustus.source: Suetonius, 'The Divine Augustus', 28; Dio Cassius, LIII
level.augustus.title: First Citizen
level.aurelian.fact: Aurelian ruled for five years, and in that time he recovered both Zenobia's Palmyrene Empire and Tetricus' Gallic Empire—both rulers marched in his triumph but remained alive: the queen was given a villa near Rome, the usurper a governorship. Coins called him restitutor orbis, 'restorer of the world.' In 275, he was murdered by his own officers: his secretary Eros, fearing punishment for a minor offense, forged a list of those the emperor supposedly intended to execute. The deceived commanders cut him down on the road to Thrace.
level.aurelian.goal: Three fragments once again one empire, and its unifier lives
level.aurelian.hint: Begin with the East: only the conqueror of the queen has the authority to negotiate with Gaul. And 'Restorer of the World' he will be proclaimed by the one who yielded. Fear the man with the pen beside you more than an army.
level.aurelian.intro: The Empire has fractured into three parts: Gaul has seceded, the East has been seized by the Palmyrene queen, and in the middle lies what remains. Legions raise a new emperor every year.
level.aurelian.title: Restorer of the World
level.austerlitz.fact: On December 2, 1805, on the anniversary of his coronation, Napoleon crushed the armies of Alexander I and Francis II at Austerlitz. He deliberately abandoned the Pratzen Heights and weakened his right flank; when the Allies moved to outflank, the French struck the vacated center. Kutuzov, who had opposed the battle, was dismissed by the Tsar and wounded. The sun, breaking through the morning fog, became a proverb — 'the Sun of Austerlitz.' Tolstoy placed the wounded Prince Andrei on this field under a high sky; Austria withdrew from the war, and the Holy Roman Empire ceased to exist eight months later.
level.austerlitz.goal: The Emperor feigns weakness — and the Russians hand him victory
level.austerlitz.hint: Abandoning the heights is not weakness, but strength: the enemy will overextend. The Tsar will not accept Kutuzov's advice to wait. And then Alexander attacks — and is defeated.
level.austerlitz.intro: The Russo-Austrian army, with two emperors, outnumbers the French. Kutuzov advises waiting; young Alexander I wants battle. Napoleon deliberately abandons the Pratzen Heights — let them think he is weak.
level.austerlitz.source: Bulletins of the Grande Armée; L. Tolstoy, 'War and Peace', Vol. 1
level.austerlitz.title: The Sun of Austerlitz
level.avignon_plague.fact: The plague reached Marseille in November 1347 and Avignon in January 1348; by contemporary count, eleven thousand people were buried in the new church cemetery within six weeks. The pope's personal surgeon Guy de Chauliac stayed in the city, caught the disease, survived, and left the best medical description of it in his Chirurgia Magna; it was he who ordered Clement VI to sit in a room between two braziers kept constantly burning — and the pope never fell ill. When the graveyards overflowed, Clement consecrated the Rhône so that bodies could be committed to the river. By bulls of 4 July and 26 September 1348 he forbade the killing of Jews on pain of excommunication, pointing out that they were dying of the plague like everyone else and that those who accused them had been seduced by the devil, the father of lies; pogroms swept Germany, but in the papal lands Jews were given refuge. In 1349 a separate bull condemned the flagellants. Europe lost between a third and a half of its people.
level.avignon_plague.goal: The physician shuts the pope in between two braziers, the pope stops the pogroms with a bull — and consecrates the river, because there is nowhere left to bury the dead
level.avignon_plague.hint: First the braziers: the physician guards the pope, and he outlives the pestilence. The surviving pope silences the preacher of pogroms with a bull. And only a shepherd who has taken the city upon himself dares to consecrate the Rhône. The square before the palace is a trap: let the preacher speak first, and it is the pope who will be condemned.
level.avignon_plague.intro: In January 1348 the plague enters Avignon — the most crowded city in Christendom, where three times more people live under the pope than the walls can hold. The graveyards fill up in weeks. Flagellants march through the streets, whipping themselves bloody and shouting that the Jews have sent the plague.
level.avignon_plague.source: Guy de Chauliac, 'Chirurgia Magna'; R. Horrox, 'The Black Death: Sources'
level.avignon_plague.title: The Pope Between Two Fires
level.babington.fact: In 1586, Walsingham, through double agent Gilbert Gifford, arranged secret correspondence between Mary, Queen of Scots, and the conspirators via beer barrels delivered to Chartley Castle — and read every letter. On July 17, Mary replied to Babington, approving the plan; the decipherer Thomas Phelippes drew a gallows on the copy. Babington and thirteen others were executed in September with such cruelty that Elizabeth ordered the second group simply to be hanged. Mary was tried in October and beheaded in February 1587 — you have already seen how.
level.babington.goal: A spy leads the conspiracy from the start — and the conspirator writes his own sentence.
level.babington.hint: A conspiracy in correspondence. A double agent carries barrels to Walsingham — upon reading them, he condemns the conspirator by his own hand. The condemned is executed by an influential spy. The Queen's reply letter — that's another story.
level.babington.intro: Mary, Queen of Scots, is in her nineteenth year of English captivity. Young Catholic Anthony Babington proposes a conspiracy: to kill Elizabeth and free Mary. Letters travel in beer barrels — and each one is first read by Walsingham.
level.babington.source: Conyers Read, 'Mr. Secretary Walsingham and the Policy of Queen Elizabeth'; Fotheringhay trial records
level.babington.title: Letters in a Beer Barrel
level.barbara_secret.fact: Sigismund Augustus secretly married Barbara in Vilnius in the summer of 1547. When he became king in 1548, Queen Bona and the Sejm demanded a divorce; the king replied that he would sooner give up the crown. On 7 December 1550 Barbara was crowned in Kraków, and on 8 May 1551 she died — rumour blamed Bona for poisoning her, though there is no proof. The king followed the coffin on foot all the way to Vilnius. According to legend, the magician Pan Twardowski later summoned Barbara's spirit for him in a magic mirror.
level.barbara_secret.goal: The king secretly marries a Lithuanian widow, weathers the fury of his mother and the Sejm — and crowns her
level.barbara_secret.hint: First the wedding — a secret one. Then the storm: his mother and the Sejm demand a divorce. If the king gives in, Barbara will never wear a crown.
level.barbara_secret.intro: 1547. Young Sigismund Augustus, heir to the throne, is in love with Barbara Radziwiłł — the widow of a Lithuanian magnate, a beauty who is the subject of gossip. His mother, Queen Bona, hates the Radziwiłłs. The nobility considers the match beneath him.
level.barbara_secret.source: Letters of Sigismund Augustus; Łukasz Górnicki, The History of the Polish Crown
level.barbara_secret.title: The King's Secret Marriage
level.basil_bulgar.fact: On July 29, 1014, at the Kleidion Pass (Key) in Belasitsa, strategos Nikephoros Xiphias outflanked the Bulgarian barricade through the mountains, and Tsar Samuel's army was defeated; the tsar himself fled. According to Skylitzes, Basil ordered about fifteen thousand prisoners to be blinded, leaving one one-eyed guide for every hundred, and sent them to the tsar; Samuel, seeing them on October 4, collapsed and died two days later. For this, the emperor was nicknamed the Bulgar-Slayer; by 1018, Bulgaria was fully annexed – for the first time since the 7th century, the empire's border once again ran along the Danube. Basil died in 1025, unmarried, leaving a treasury of two hundred thousand pounds of gold; half a century later, the empire would lose at Manzikert.
level.basil_bulgar.goal: The Emperor takes the gorge by outflanking, defeats the Bulgarians — and sends fifteen thousand blind prisoners to the tsar.
level.basil_bulgar.hint: First, outflank the gorge — the emperor is ready, strength. Kleidion: a strong emperor strikes the tsar. The victor blinds the defeated tsar's prisoners — the Bulgar-Slayer, and the tsar will not survive this sight. Accepting tribute means yielding; a yielding tsar will not see the blind.
level.basil_bulgar.intro: For forty years, Basil II has waged war against Tsar Samuel's Bulgaria. He does not marry, does not celebrate, does not read — he only fights. The Bulgarians await him in the mountain pass of Kleidion (Key), having blocked the gorge with a wall.
level.basil_bulgar.source: John Skylitzes, 'Synopsis of Histories'; P. Stephenson, 'The Legend of Basil the Bulgar-Slayer'
level.basil_bulgar.title: The Bulgar-Slayer
level.bastille.fact: On July 14, 1789, after several hours of skirmishing, the crowd from the Faubourg Saint-Antoine took the Bastille: Commander de Launay surrendered under the promise of his life, but he was led to the Hôtel de Ville and torn apart, his head paraded on a pike. Inside the fortress, seven prisoners were found — four counterfeiters, two madmen, and one aristocratic libertine. Louis XVI, who had hunted without success that day, wrote 'Rien' — 'nothing' — in his diary; to the words of the Duke of La Rochefoucauld-Liancourt, 'Sire, it is a revolt,' he reportedly replied, 'No, sir, it is a revolution.' The fortress was dismantled within a year, its stones sold as souvenirs.
level.bastille.goal: The faubourg takes the fortress with seven prisoners — and the king writes 'Nothing' in his diary
level.bastille.hint: The faubourg must gather and become a force — then the assault: the commander is defeated. Negotiations at the moat lead nowhere: the crowd has no weight. And the king in Versailles hunted that day — and wrote 'Rien'.
level.bastille.intro: Paris is hungry and frightened by troops at its gates. At Les Invalides, the crowd seized thirty thousand muskets — but without gunpowder. The gunpowder is in the Bastille, beyond the moat and drawbridge, with Commandant de Launay, a hundred invalids, and thirty Swiss guards.
level.bastille.source: J. Michelet, 'History of the French Revolution'; S. Schama, 'Citizens'
level.bastille.title: July 14th
level.becket.fact: In 1162, Henry II secured the election of his chancellor, Thomas Becket, as Archbishop of Canterbury. Becket unexpectedly transformed into an unyielding defender of church rights, fled to France, returned in 1170, and excommunicated the bishops who had crowned the heir without him. The King, in Normandy, exclaimed in anger something like, «Who will rid me of this troublesome priest?» – and four knights, including Reginald FitzUrse, hacked Becket to death by the cathedral altar during vespers on December 29, 1170. Three years later, he was canonized; Henry walked barefoot to his tomb and allowed the monks to scourge him. Canterbury became England's foremost pilgrimage – the destination of Chaucer's heroes.
level.becket.goal: The King receives a martyr, not a servant, from his archbishop-friend.
level.becket.hint: First, your friend must be elevated to the see. Then, the king merely needs to flare up in front of his knights – and four will interpret his words as an order. Reconciliation negates everything.
level.becket.intro: Henry II made his friend and chancellor, Thomas Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, hoping to subjugate the Church through him. Becket donned his cassock – and began defending the Church from the King more fiercely than the previous archbishop.
level.becket.source: Edward Grim, 'The Life of St. Thomas'; William FitzStephen
level.becket.title: Who will rid me of this priest
level.belisarius_blind.fact: At the end of 562 Belisarius's name was spoken at a trial over a conspiracy against Justinian; the general was removed from affairs and held under house arrest. In July 563 the emperor restored his ranks and property; Belisarius died in March 565, a few months before Justinian himself, wealthy and restored to honour. He was turned into a blind beggar with a bowl much later: the first hint of it comes from the twelfth-century Byzantine scholar John Tzetzes, citing an unknown source, and three centuries afterwards historians were repeating the story as fact. The image owed its worldwide fame to Marmontel's novel 'Belisarius' (1767) and Jacques-Louis David's canvas 'Belisarius Begging for Alms' (1781): that is where the phrase 'Date obolum Belisario' comes from. Not one of Belisarius's contemporaries wrote of his blinding.
level.belisarius_blind.goal: The empire's finest general is broken not by a battle but by a denunciation — and legend carries him all the way to a beggar's bowl
level.belisarius_blind.hint: First the denunciation: the emperor believes the paper, and the general loses his standing. A man under suspicion is stripped of everything. And only to a man in disgrace will legend add blindness and a bowl — beside the woman who followed him through every campaign. The Hippodrome is a proclamation: a man showered with honours cannot be toppled by a denunciation.
level.belisarius_blind.intro: The general who won Africa and Italy back for the empire is old, and still dangerous — dangerous because the army loves him. The court whispers that he is aiming higher. And one day his name comes up in testimony at a trial over a conspiracy against the emperor.
level.belisarius_blind.source: Theophanes the Confessor, 'Chronographia'; John Tzetzes, 'Chiliades', III (on the legend)
level.belisarius_blind.title: An Obol for Belisarius
level.bellarmine_1616.fact: On February 24, 1616, the theologians of the Holy Office declared the thesis of a stationary Sun 'formally heretical', and that of the Earth's motion 'at least erroneous in faith'. On February 26, Cardinal Bellarmine, by order of Paul V, summoned Galileo and admonished him to abandon this opinion; Galileo complied. On March 5, the Congregation of the Index prohibited Copernicus's book 'until corrected'. When rumors spread throughout Rome that Galileo had recanted and been punished, he asked Bellarmine for a certificate: on May 26, the cardinal confirmed in writing that there had been no recantation or penance—he had merely been informed of the decision. However, another, unsigned notary's note remained in the file: Galileo was instructed 'not to hold, teach, or defend in any way'. In 1633, this very note was presented at his trial, and Bellarmine's certificate, which Galileo brought as justification, became proof that he knew of the prohibition. Bellarmine had been dead for twelve years by then, and Cardinal Barberini was Pope Urban VIII.
level.bellarmine_1616.goal: The Holy Office declares the Earth's motion heresy, the cardinal gently warns the astronomer, and he asks for a document stating he did not recant—and seventeen years later, this document will be laid before his judges.
level.bellarmine_1616.hint: First, the Holy Office: the inquisitor receives a decree. With the decree in hand, the cardinal warns the astronomer—he is warned and remains silent. The warned man asks the cardinal for a certificate. Formally recanting is not allowed—there was no recantation in 1616; fleeing to Venice either—he himself left its protection. Barberini is, for now, merely a friend and poet.
level.bellarmine_1616.intro: Winter 1616. Galileo arrives in Rome to prove that the Earth moves, and debates it in salons; friends write to him: be silent. The theologians of the Holy Office gather to evaluate two theses: the Sun is stationary at the center of the world, the Earth rotates. Cardinal Bellarmine—the one who judged Bruno—receives a papal commission. Cardinal Maffeo Barberini, a friend and admirer of Galileo, is for now still only a cardinal.
level.bellarmine_1616.source: Documents of the Galileo trial (Vatican Secret Archives); Bellarmine's certificate of 26.05.1616; A. Fantoli, 'Galileo: For Copernicanism and for the Church'
level.bellarmine_1616.title: The Warning of 1616
level.belweder_1830.fact: On the evening of 29 November 1830, Second Lieutenant Piotr Wysocki roused the cadets of the Officer Cadet School; the signal was to be a fire at a brewery in Solec. The conspirators burst into the Belweder, but Grand Duke Constantine hid and then left Warsaw. The townspeople seized the Arsenal. On 25 January 1831 the Sejm declared Nicholas I dethroned from the Polish throne; a war began that lasted until the autumn. After the defeat the Kingdom of Poland lost its constitution and its army, and thousands of participants went into exile.
level.belweder_1830.goal: At the signal of a fire, cadets storm the Belweder, the grand duke flees — and the Sejm dethrones the emperor from the Polish throne
level.belweder_1830.hint: Without a signal no one will move. The grand duke did not die that night — he hid and fled. And the dethronement was done not with a dagger, but with words.
level.belweder_1830.intro: 1830. The Kingdom of Poland has a constitution, an army and a Sejm, but its king is the Russian emperor Nicholas I, and in Warsaw everything is run by his brother, Grand Duke Constantine. A conspiracy is brewing in the Officer Cadet School.
level.belweder_1830.source: Act of Dethronement, 25 January 1831; Maurycy Mochnacki, The Uprising of the Polish Nation in 1830–1831
level.belweder_1830.title: The November Night
level.biron.fact: In 1730 the Supreme Privy Council invited the widowed duchess of Courland, Anna Ioannovna, to the throne, obliging her to sign the "conditions": no war, no promotions, no execution of nobles and no spending of the treasury without the Council. On 25 February 1730, backed by the gentry and the guards, Anna tore the paper up in public. From Mitau she brought Ernst Johann Biron, her chief chamberlain and from 1737 Duke of Courland; the decade of his influence would be called the Bironovshchina. In February 1740 a house of ice was built on the Neva between the Admiralty and the Winter Palace — some seventeen metres long, with an ice bed, ice trees and cannon that fired real powder. The whim was Anna's own, and it was managed by cabinet minister Artemy Volynsky — the same man executed a few months later on Biron's denunciation. In the ice house they held the jester's wedding of Prince Mikhail Golitsyn, demoted to fool for marrying an Italian and turning Catholic, and the Kalmyk Avdotya Buzheninova; the couple were locked in the ice bedroom overnight under guard. Anna died on 17 October 1740, leaving Biron regent for the infant emperor; three weeks later Field Marshal Münnich arrested him at night in his bedroom, and the Duke of Courland went to Pelym in Siberia.
level.biron.goal: The Courlander receives the key and a decade of power, while the empress amuses herself with a jester's wedding in a house of ice
level.biron.hint: The key first: the empress hands power to the Courlander — and the country begins to hate him. She is also the one who demotes the prince to jester. And then the empress holds the jester's wedding on the ice. The Council's conditions are the trap: an empress bound by them hands over no key.
level.biron.intro: The widowed Duchess of Courland was called to the Russian throne on one condition: sign the 'Conditions' and rule with an eye on the eight men of the Supreme Council. She signed — and tore the paper up a month later. With her from Mitau came a Grand Chamberlain whose name would be given to an entire decade.
level.biron.source: G. W. Kraft, 'A True and Detailed Description of the Ice House'; E. Anisimov, 'Anna Ioannovna'
level.biron.title: The Ice House
level.black_death.fact: The plague reached Europe in the autumn of 1347 aboard Genoese galleys from Caffa and within three years killed between a third and a half of the population — as many as 25 million people. In 1348 Venice was the first to set up a health board and hold suspect ships at distant islands; at Ragusa (Dubrovnik) in 1377 the term was fixed — first thirty days (trentino), then forty, quaranta giorni, which is where the word quarantine comes from. Boccaccio lived through the plague in Florence, losing his father and stepmother, and built The Decameron on it: seven ladies and three young men leave the dead city for a villa above Fiesole and tell one tale each per day. The processions and flagellant marches with which cities met the infection only spread it further.
level.black_death.goal: The plague arrives with the galleys; Venice locks ships away on distant islands, while a storyteller who fled Florence writes The Decameron
level.black_death.hint: The galleys first: the master brings the plague ashore. The doge locks the infected ship away on a far island. Meanwhile the storyteller leaves plague-struck Florence — and only outside the city does he compose his book. A procession is the worst thing you can do in a plague.
level.black_death.intro: In the autumn of 1347 Genoese galleys from Caffa in the Crimea put in at Messina in Sicily. Their oarsmen are dead or dying. Within three years the plague will kill one European in three — and leave behind two things that last: quarantine and The Decameron.
level.black_death.source: G. Boccaccio, The Decameron (introduction); P. Ziegler, The Black Death
level.black_death.title: The Black Death
level.blenheim.fact: Sarah Churchill, Marlborough's wife, was Queen Anne's closest friend – in letters, they called each other «Mrs. Freeman» and «Mrs. Morley,» without titles. This gave the Duke power no minister possessed. In the summer of 1704, he secretly marched his army four hundred kilometers from Flanders to the Danube – Paris learned of it when it was too late – and on August 13 at Blenheim, together with Prince Eugene, he routed the French; Marshal Tallard was captured. The grateful Queen gifted Marlborough the Woodstock estate and a palace named Blenheim – where Winston Churchill would be born a century and a half later. The friendship with Sarah ended in a quarrel six years later, and the Duke lost everything.
level.blenheim.goal: The friendship of two women gives a commander free rein – and he breaks the French army on the Danube.
level.blenheim.hint: The Duke's friendship with the Queen (through his wife Sarah) makes Marlborough indispensable to the Crown — otherwise, they won't let him go. The march to the Danube is preparation; without it, standing in Flanders resolves nothing. And only then, the battle.
level.blenheim.intro: Louis XIV marches on Vienna; if it falls, France will dominate Europe. The English army is in Flanders and, by all rules, should remain there. Marlborough decides otherwise – and everything depends on whether the Queen trusts him.
level.blenheim.source: W. Churchill, 'Marlborough: His Life and Times'; Sarah Churchill's correspondence
level.blenheim.title: Blenheim
level.blois.fact: On 12 May 1588, the Day of the Barricades, Paris was blocked with barrels and chains and Henry III fled his own capital — the city's master was Henri de Guise, called Le Balafré. On 23 December 1588 at Blois the king summoned the duke to his cabinet, where eight men of his personal guard, the Forty-Five, stabbed him with daggers; the next day they killed his brother, the Cardinal de Guise. Looking at the body, the king said that now at last he was king; Catherine de' Medici, dying downstairs, answered the news: "You cut well, my son — will you know how to sew?" She died on 5 January 1589. The Sorbonne released his subjects from their oath, the pope excommunicated him, and he allied with the Huguenot Henry of Navarre to besiege Paris. On 1 August 1589 the Dominican Jacques Clément asked for a private audience to deliver a letter and stabbed the king in the belly; the assassin was cut down on the spot, the king died the next day naming the Navarrese as his heir. So ended the house of Valois.
level.blois.goal: The king kills the man who drove him out of Paris — and eight months later dies by a monk's knife
level.blois.hint: First the barricades: the city rises for the duke, and the king flees his capital. The banished man calls the strong one into his cabinet and locks the doors. A king cursed by the Church has eight months left — and a fanatic monk will count them off. The table at Nancy is a trap: a duke who has been given his way will not raise the city.
level.blois.intro: Paris loves not the king but the duke with the scar across his face — the leader of the Catholic League. In his own capital the king is no master: he is left with a title, debts, and forty-five noble bodyguards he feeds out of his own pocket. In the winter of 1588 the court gathers at Blois for the Estates General, and the Estates listen to the duke.
level.blois.source: Pierre de L'Estoile, 'Journal of Henry III'; J.-M. Constant, 'The Guises'
level.blois.title: Now I Am King
level.bloody_mary.fact: Mary I (1553–1558) returned England to the authority of Rome and married Philip II of Spain. Her reign was dubbed "Bloody": about 280 Protestants were burned at the stake, including Archbishop Thomas Cranmer (1556), author of the English prayer book. She never bore an heir.
level.bloody_mary.goal: The Queen is crowned, wed to Spain — and burns the archbishop.
level.bloody_mary.hint: First a coronation — with it comes authority. Then a wedding with a Spaniard, and the already condemned archbishop awaits the pyre.
level.bloody_mary.intro: Mary I is Queen. She will return England to Rome, marry Philip of Spain — and deal with the heretics.
level.bloody_mary.title: Bloody Mary
level.bohemond_antioch.fact: The Siege of Antioch lasted from October 1097 to June 3, 1098. Bohemond bribed Firuz, an Armenian apostate who commanded the Tower of the Two Sisters, and had already secured the other leaders' agreement: the city would go to whoever took it, provided Alexios did not appear. On the night of June 3, his men scaled ladders—Antioch fell. Two days later, Kerbogha of Mosul approached the city and besieged the besiegers. The deserter Stephen of Blois met Alexios in Philomelium and assured him that the Crusaders were doomed; the emperor turned back. On June 28, the Crusaders, having found the Holy Lance, defeated Kerbogha—and Bohemond declared the Oath of Vlachernae null and void: the emperor had not come. Raymond of Toulouse argued, but was outvoted. In 1108, by the Treaty of Devol, Bohemond recognized himself as Alexios's vassal for Antioch—and never returned to it; he died in 1111 in Apulia.
level.bohemond_antioch.goal: A Norman buys a tower, the emperor turns back—and the oath given at Blachernae is broken: Antioch remains Bohemond's.
level.bohemond_antioch.hint: The Tower of the Two Sisters is bought by one who is not bought, has yielded to no one, and is not defeated. The emperor must turn back at Philomelium—to leave. And only then does the Norman, having entered the city, declare himself prince before the one who did not come. Persuading him to return the city is a path to another story; in this one, he did not return.
level.bohemond_antioch.intro: For eight months, the Crusaders stand before Antioch, starving and eating their horses. Bohemond secretly conspired with Firuz, an Armenian tower commander—and demands from the leaders: the city will go to whoever takes it, if the emperor does not come to their aid. Alexios Komnenos marches with his army through Anatolia.
level.bohemond_antioch.source: Anna Komnene, 'The Alexiad', Book XI; 'Gesta Francorum'; Raymond of Aguilers, 'History of the Franks Who Took Jerusalem'
level.bohemond_antioch.title: Prince of Antioch
level.bolingbroke.fact: In 1398, Richard II exiled Henry Bolingbroke for ten years, and after the death of his father John of Gaunt in 1399, confiscated the Lancastrian inheritance. Bolingbroke landed at Ravenspur 'to claim only his own'; the king's army dispersed, and Richard surrendered in Wales. Parliament deposed him, and Bolingbroke became Henry IV — the first king whose title came not by birth, but by Parliament. Richard died in Pontefract Castle in February 1400 — most likely from starvation; Shakespeare gave him axe-wielding murderers. Thus began the usurpation, from which the Wars of the Roses would grow half a century later.
level.bolingbroke.goal: The king takes his cousin's inheritance — and loses his crown, and then his life in a castle.
level.bolingbroke.hint: First, the king exiles his cousin — the exile leaves with influence and returns strong. A landing — and the king is defeated. The deposed is not executed: he is starved in Pontefract. The king will not forgive his cousin.
level.bolingbroke.intro: Richard II banished his cousin Bolingbroke for ten years, and when his father died, he seized the inheritance. While the king was fighting in Ireland, the exile landed in Yorkshire with three ships.
level.bolingbroke.source: Thomas Walsingham, 'Historia Anglicana'; Jean Froissart, Vol. IV
level.bolingbroke.title: Pontefract
level.bolotnikov.fact: Ivan Bolotnikov was a fighting bondsman of Prince Telyatevsky; he fled to the Cossacks, was taken prisoner and spent several years as a rower on a Turkish galley. In the summer of 1606 he turned up at Putivl as the voivode of a 'Tsar Dmitry' he had never laid eyes on, and his 'seductive letters' called on bondsmen to strike down their masters and take their property. By October 1606 his army was camped at Kolomenskoye, right outside Moscow. But noble detachments were marching alongside the serfs: in November Prokopy Lyapunov's men of Ryazan went over to Vasily Shuisky, and on 2 December, in the battle by the village of Kotly, Istoma Pashkov left as well — the rising fell apart. Bolotnikov withdrew to Kaluga, then to Tula; in the summer of 1607 the tsar's troops dammed the river Upa and flooded the town. On 10 October 1607 he surrendered on an oath sworn upon the cross that his life would be spared: he was exiled to Kargopol, blinded and drowned.
level.bolotnikov.goal: The ataman raises the whole Russian south — and loses his army the day the gentry understand whom he is calling them to butcher
level.bolotnikov.hint: First the letters: the ataman becomes a force. Then the camp at Kolomenskoye — a nobleman leads his hundreds away, and the force drains out. Only now the fight at Kotly: a strong tsar strikes the man who has been deserted. The beaten man is finished off at the dam on the Upa. The Pomestny Prikaz is a trap: a bought nobleman will lead no one away.
level.bolotnikov.intro: In the summer of 1606 a former fighting bondsman who had been a galley slave in Turkey turned up as the voivode of a 'Tsar Dmitry' he had never seen. His letters called on bondsmen to strike down the boyars and take their estates. Under those letters not only peasants but noble hundreds marched on Moscow — and it was they who read what was written with care.
level.bolotnikov.source: 'The New Chronicler'; I. Smirnov, 'The Bolotnikov Revolt'
level.bolotnikov.title: The Seductive Letters
level.bona_sums.fact: In February 1556 Bona left for Bari, taking with her, so it was said, a treasury on twenty-four wagons. She lent Philip II 430,000 ducats. In November 1557 she was poisoned by her trusted courtier Gian Lorenzo Pappacoda — bribed, as contemporaries believed, by the Spanish — who then produced a will in Philip's favour. For two hundred years Poland demanded the return of the "Neapolitan sums" and received nothing. Bona left behind Italian vegetables: Poles still call the soup bundle of carrot, parsley and celery "włoszczyzna" — "Italian stuff".
level.bona_sums.goal: The queen leaves for Italy with the treasury, lends money to the King of Spain — and is poisoned, and the debt is never repaid to Poland
level.bona_sums.hint: You can only lend money you have with you. A courtier bought by the queen herself would not poison her — but that is not how it happened.
level.bona_sums.intro: 1556. The dowager queen Bona Sforza, an Italian who wielded power at her husband's court for forty years, has fallen out with her son. She decides to return to her Duchy of Bari, taking a huge treasury with her. The King of Spain, Philip II, who rules Naples, needs money.
level.bona_sums.source: W. Pociecha, Queen Bona (1949–1958); Łukasz Górnicki, The History of the Polish Crown
level.bona_sums.title: The Neapolitan Sums
level.bonfire.fact: On May 23, 1498, Girolamo Savonarola was hanged and burned in the Piazza della Signoria in Florence, his ashes cast into the Arno River to prevent any relics from remaining. Thus, the Pope dealt with his accuser.
level.bonfire.goal: The excommunicated preacher faces the pyre
level.bonfire.hint: First, excommunication; then, the pyre in the piazza.
level.bonfire.intro: The pyre awaits the excommunicated Savonarola.
level.bonfire.title: Savonarola's Pyre
level.bordeaux_duel.fact: On the morning of June 1, 1283, Peter of Aragon, having traveled across Spain disguised as a horse merchant's servant, entered the lists in Bordeaux with three companions, declared to Edward's seneschal that he had appeared, demanded written proof—and rode off before noon. At the appointed hour, Charles of Anjou arrived with his hundred knights, rode around the empty field, and declared his opponent a perjurer; Peter made the same declaration about Charles. Edward I, forbidden by Pope Martin IV, refused to preside, and the combat did not take place: the duel was merely a pretext for both to avoid war at an inconvenient moment. While the kings measured honor, Peter's admiral Roger of Lauria defeated the Angevin fleet off Malta on June 8, and in 1284 captured Charles's son in the Bay of Naples; Charles himself died in January 1285, never having recovered Sicily.
level.bordeaux_duel.goal: Two kings challenge each other to a battle of a hundred knights against a hundred—and both arrive at the lists at different times to declare the other a coward.
level.bordeaux_duel.hint: First, the challenge: the Angevin throws down the gauntlet to his enemy. Then the lists—but there is only one place on it: each king enters the field alone, at his own hour. Edward was supposed to be the judge—and refused; and crossing swords means doing what did not happen.
level.bordeaux_duel.intro: After the Sicilian Vespers, Charles of Anjou lost the island, and Peter of Aragon donned its crown. Instead of war, Charles proposes to settle the dispute chivalrously: a hundred knights against a hundred, in Bordeaux, on the lands of the English King Edward, on June 1, 1283. The Pope forbids Edward to preside. Both kings swear to appear.
level.bordeaux_duel.source: Bernat Desclot, 'Chronicle'; Bartolomeo da Neocastro, 'Historia Sicula'; S. Runciman, 'The Sicilian Vespers'
level.bordeaux_duel.title: The Duel of Bordeaux
level.bosworth.fact: On 22 August 1485 the Battle of Bosworth was decided by betrayal: Lord Thomas Stanley held back to the last moment, then threw his forces onto Henry Tudor's side. Richard III fell in battle — the last English king to die on the field. His crown, by tradition, was found in a hawthorn bush and placed on Henry right there on the field. So ended the Wars of the Roses and began the Tudor dynasty.
level.bosworth.goal: Stanley's betrayal decides Bosworth — the crown passes to Henry Tudor
level.bosworth.hint: Richard is stronger — until Lord Stanley defects: with his men, the claimant gains strength. Then battle, and an influential ally will proclaim the victor king right on the field.
level.bosworth.intro: Richard III reigns. Henry Tudor marches for the crown — but all will hinge on whose side Lord Stanley takes.
level.bosworth.title: Bosworth
level.bouvines.fact: On Sunday, July 27, 1214, at Bouvines, Philip II Augustus defeated the coalition of Emperor Otto IV, the Count of Flanders, and the English gold of John Lackland. For the first time, infantry from urban communes stood in battle — Paris welcomed the king with a seven-day celebration. John, having lost his allies, concluded a truce at Chinon and returned to England to the barons, who a year later would force him to sign the Magna Carta. French historians call Bouvines 'the first national day': from it, France became the strongest kingdom in Europe for a century and a half.
level.bouvines.goal: The King and the townspeople defeat the coalition — and John asks for a truce
level.bouvines.hint: Philip's strength is the communal militia; gather it. It's not customary to fight on Sunday — but the battle will be on Sunday. The defeated John, swayed by the weight of victory, is persuaded to a truce.
level.bouvines.intro: John Lackland assembled a coalition against the French king: the Emperor, the Count of Flanders, and English gold. Philip Augustus, for the first time, calls the militia of the cities — the communes, to whom he himself granted liberties — under his banners.
level.bouvines.source: William the Breton, 'Philippide'; G. Duby, 'The Sunday of Bouvines'
level.bouvines.title: Bouvines
level.brennus.fact: Around 390 BC, Brennus' Gauls defeated the Romans near the Allia river and occupied the city; the survivors barricaded themselves on the Capitoline Hill. A night assault was thwarted by Juno's sacred geese, which had not been eaten even during the famine. When the ransom gold was weighed with false weights and the Romans protested, Brennus threw his sword onto the scales with the words «Vae victis» — «Woe to the vanquished». According to Livy, Camillus then appeared: «Rome is redeemed by iron, not by gold». Historians consider this last-minute rescue a patriotic embellishment — the Gauls, it seems, did carry off the gold after all.
level.brennus.goal: The Gauls are expelled, and Rome has not paid an ounce of gold.
level.brennus.hint: The assault will be foiled not by warriors, but by geese. Afterwards, the army must be gathered – and no attempt to fight made prematurely. Do not put gold on the scales.
level.brennus.intro: Brennus's Gauls defeated the Romans and entered the city. Everything burns, except the Capitol, where the survivors are holed up; Rome's best general, Camillus, is in exile in Veii.
level.brennus.title: The Geese of the Capitoline
level.brumaire.fact: On November 9–10, 1799 (18–19 Brumaire, Year VIII), Napoleon staged a coup, dissolving the Directory and establishing the Consulate. He appointed himself First Consul — the de facto dictator of France.
level.brumaire.goal: The General seizes power and becomes First Consul
level.brumaire.hint: First — glory at Toulon, then — a coup d'état.
level.brumaire.title: 18 Brumaire
level.bruno.fact: In May 1592, Giovanni Mocenigo denounced Bruno to the Venetian Inquisition; in 1593, he was extradited to Rome. Seven years of interrogations; he was offered to recant his teachings on the infinity of worlds and the multiplicity of suns — he agreed to retract minor points, but not the main tenets. On February 8, 1600, his sentence was read, and he, according to an eyewitness, told the judges: 'Perhaps you pronounce this sentence against me with greater fear than I receive it.' On February 17, he was burned at the stake in Campo de' Fiori with a gag, so he could not speak; his ashes were thrown into the Tiber. The same Bellarmine would warn Galileo sixteen years later. In 1889, a monument facing the Vatican was erected on the site of the pyre; John Paul II in 2000 called the execution a 'sad episode,' but did not rehabilitate him.
level.bruno.goal: The philosopher is denounced to the Inquisition, they await his recantation for eight years — and burn him in the square with a gag in his mouth.
level.bruno.hint: First, the denunciation — a weighty inquisitor accuses the philosopher, condemned. Seven years in prison — he does not recant, he persists. The weighty inquisitor burns the persistent one. To recant means to yield; then there is no pyre, but also no Bruno.
level.bruno.intro: The former monk Giordano Bruno teaches that stars are suns, and worlds are infinitely numerous. The Venetian patrician Mocenigo, who had invited him to teach mnemonics, denounces him to the Inquisition. Cardinal Bellarmine handles the case.
level.bruno.source: 'Documenti della vita di Giordano Bruno'; F. Yates, 'Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition'
level.bruno.title: Campo de' Fiori
level.byczyna_1588.fact: Maximilian besieged Kraków but could not take it and withdrew to Silesia. On 24 January 1588 at Byczyna, Zamoyski defeated his army and took the archduke prisoner; he spent thirteen months in Krasnystaw and in 1589 renounced the Polish crown. Zamoyski was chancellor, hetman and founder of Zamość, the Renaissance "ideal city" now on the UNESCO list. He is credited with the words: "Such will be the Commonwealths as the upbringing of their youth."
level.byczyna_1588.goal: The nobility elects two kings at once — and Hetman Zamoyski settles the dispute on the battlefield, capturing an Austrian archduke
level.byczyna_1588.hint: You can only fight once the pretender has been elected. The prisoner abdicates in favour of whoever stayed in the country — if Vasa leaves for Sweden, the throne will stand empty.
level.byczyna_1588.intro: 1587. King Stephen Báthory is dead. At the election the nobility split: Chancellor and Hetman Jan Zamoyski backed the Swedish prince Sigismund Vasa, while his enemies the Zborowskis backed the Austrian archduke Maximilian of Habsburg. Both were proclaimed king.
level.byczyna_1588.source: Reinhold Heidenstein, History of Poland from the Death of Sigismund Augustus
level.byczyna_1588.title: Byczyna
level.caesar_assassination.fact: On March 15, 44 BC (the Ides of March), Julius Caesar was assassinated in the Senate by a group of conspirators — over 60 senators led by Brutus and Cassius. The phrase 'Et tu, Brute?' is Shakespeare's literary version; Suetonius reports the words 'And you, child?' in Greek.
level.caesar_assassination.goal: Friend Brutus joins the conspiracy and kills Caesar.
level.caesar_assassination.hint: Brutus weaves the conspiracy with Cassius — not with Caesar himself. Antony must not be part of the conspiracy.
level.caesar_assassination.intro: There are over sixty conspirators, and their plot is worthless: the Senate will not follow a handful of the aggrieved. They need one man — the one Caesar loves and trusts.
level.caesar_assassination.source: Suetonius, 'The Lives of the Twelve Caesars'
level.caesar_assassination.title: Et tu, Brute?
level.caesar_crown.fact: At Lupercalia in February 44 BC, Mark Antony thrice offered Caesar a royal diadem — and Caesar thrice publicly refused it to the approving roar of the crowd. He never became King of Rome, but persistent rumors of royal ambitions (not least due to Cleopatra's presence in Rome) spurred the conspirators to action.
level.caesar_crown.goal: The people love Caesar — but he will not be king
level.caesar_crown.hint: First, love in private, then friendship with an ally — and only then, at the Lupercalia, will a loyal hand offer the crown, which Caesar will gracefully refuse. Keep Cleopatra away from the crown.
level.caesar_crown.intro: Caesar is dictator for life, but the word 'king' has been cursed in Rome for five centuries. At the festival of Lupercalia, Antony holds a royal diadem, and in the Forum, a crowd gathers.
level.caesar_crown.title: King of Rome?
level.caligula.fact: Suetonius writes that Caligula built Incitatus, his horse, a marble stable, gave him slaves and a house, and intended to make him consul. He mocked the Praetorian tribune Cassius Chaerea for his thin voice: when assigning him a password, he would use words like 'Priapus' or 'Venus,' and for a kiss, he would form his hand into an obscene gesture. On January 24, 41 AD, Chaerea stabbed him in an underground passage of the palace — with the first blow, 'as if in a theater.' The Guard, finding no other Julio-Claudians, pulled Caligula's stammering uncle, Claudius, from behind a curtain — and proclaimed him emperor.
level.caligula.goal: The Princeps makes a horse a consul, and an officer a murderer
level.caligula.hint: Exalt the horse, humiliate the tribune — every day, with a password. The offended officer will become an enemy; gifts will no longer buy him. He will kill the Princeps in a palace passage.
level.caligula.intro: Caligula is in his fourth year of ruling Rome and has long ceased to consider the Senate as people. Most of all, he loves his horse Incitatus, and most of all, he teases the Guard tribune Chaerea — for his squeaky voice.
level.caligula.title: A Horse for Consul
level.cannae.fact: On August 2, 216 BC, Hannibal curved his formation forward with a weak center: the Romans pushed through it, were drawn in — and the African infantry closed its wings, while the cavalry struck from the rear. According to Polybius, about 48,000 Romans perished, among them Consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus. The second consul, Gaius Terentius Varro, whom tradition blames for the defeat, escaped — and the Senate officially thanked him for «not despairing of the Republic». Maharbal urged an immediate march on Rome; Hannibal refused, and Maharbal retorted: «You know how to win, but not how to use victory».
level.cannae.goal: Eight legions vanish in the trap, but one consul leaves alive
level.cannae.hint: Victory goes to him who prepares the trap in advance. And into the trap will fall the consul whom you place there: one perished, the other returned to Rome.
level.cannae.intro: Rome has assembled the largest army in its history — eight legions — and leads it against Hannibal. Two consuls command on alternating days: the cautious Aemilius Paullus and Varro, who promised the crowd to overwhelm by numbers.
level.cannae.title: The Cauldron of Cannae
level.carrhae.fact: In 53 BC, Marcus Licinius Crassus invaded Parthia. Abgar, the king of Osroene and a secret ally of the Parthians, led him away from the Euphrates into the open steppe near Carrhae, where Surenas' horse archers decimated the legions without approaching; camels supplied arrows. Crassus' son, Publius, died, his head shown to his father on a spear. Crassus was killed during negotiations; according to legend, the Parthians poured molten gold down his throat — 'quench the thirst you never knew in life.' His head was brought to King Orodes during a performance of Euripides' 'Bacchae' — and an actor carried it onto the stage as the head of Pentheus. Around twenty thousand perished; Augustus would only reclaim the legionary eagles thirty years later.
level.carrhae.goal: The wealthiest Roman leads legions into the desert — and perishes during negotiations.
level.carrhae.hint: To stay by the river means to retain strength, but the guide has already been bought by the Parthians and will lead the army into the steppe: there, cavalry rules. The defeated general is called to negotiations — and killed.
level.carrhae.intro: Crassus is the wealthiest man in Rome, but Caesar has Gaul, Pompey has the East, and he has nothing. He leads seven legions against Parthia, about which he knows nothing. King Abgar provides him with a guide — whom the Parthians have long since bought.
level.carrhae.title: Gold Down the Throat
level.casanova.fact: On July 26, 1755, Casanova was arrested on a denunciation and imprisoned indefinitely in the Piombi — cells under the lead roof of the Doge's Palace, where it was unbearably hot in summer and cold in winter. For a year, he sharpened an iron bolt against marble, made a hole in the floor — and was transferred to another cell; with a second prisoner, the monk Balbi, on the night of November 1, 1756, he broke through the ceiling, climbed onto the roof, descended into the palace's attic halls, changed into formal attire, and in the morning exited through the main staircase — the guard mistook him for an official locked in for the night. Via Munich, he reached Paris, where he devised a royal lottery. He published the account of his escape in 1788, and it became his most famous story until his 'Memoirs' themselves.
level.casanova.goal: The libertine is imprisoned without trial under a lead roof — and he exits the Doge's Palace through the main door.
level.casanova.hint: First, the denunciation — a weighty inquisitor accuses the libertine, condemned. In the Piombi, he sharpens a bolt for a year — ready to escape. At night, he breaks through the roof and leaves — a legend. To beg the inquisitor means a yielding man will not escape.
level.casanova.intro: Giacomo Casanova — gambler, lover, kabbalist, and freethinker — is too conspicuous for Venice. A denunciation into the Lion's Mouth, and he sits without trial in the Piombi, the 'lead' prison under the roof of the Doge's Palace, from which no one has ever escaped.
level.casanova.source: G. Casanova, 'Story of My Escape from the Prisons of the Venetian Republic'
level.casanova.title: Escape from the Piombi
level.castel_escape.fact: Cellini was arrested in October 1538 on a denunciation by Perugino, a former apprentice, and imprisoned in Castel Sant'Angelo. According to his own account, he cut his sheets into strips, broke out the door's staples, descended by rope from the tower, then from the wall—and, jumping from the final height, broke his leg; he crawled to the gates, where he was picked up by Cardinal Cornaro's servants. Paul III, learning of the escape, ordered him returned to the castle, to a damp cell beneath the garden, where, he claimed, an angel appeared to him, and a halo had since stood above his head. He was freed in December 1539 at the request of Cardinal Ippolito d'Este on behalf of Francis I; in 1540, Cellini went to Paris and made the king a golden salt cellar—his only surviving piece of jewelry. Pier Luigi Farnese, who sought his execution, was stabbed to death by his own courtiers in 1547.
level.castel_escape.goal: A jeweler is imprisoned in the castle for stealing papal jewels, he descends by a rope of sheets and breaks his leg—and the King of France frees him from prison.
level.castel_escape.hint: First, the accusation: the Pope with authority condemns his enemy—the jeweler in the castle. The condemned man tears sheets and descends from the wall—an escape and a broken leg. The escapee with a broken leg is pulled from prison by the King of France. The Pope's son's gallows—death; fleeing to France before arrest—that won't work, one doesn't leave the castle that way.
level.castel_escape.intro: 1538. A former apprentice denounces Cellini to Pope Paul III: in 1527, while melting down tiaras in the besieged castle, Cellini stole eighty thousand ducats worth of jewels. The jeweler is imprisoned in that very Castel Sant'Angelo, from whose walls he had fired upon the Landsknechts eleven years prior. The commandant goes mad and believes himself a bat, the Pope's son Pier Luigi demands a gallows—and in Paris, Francis I inquires about the prisoner.
level.castel_escape.source: B. Cellini, 'The Life of Benvenuto, Son of Maestro Giovanni Cellini, Florentine, Written by Himself', Book I, Chapters CIX–CXXVIII
level.castel_escape.title: Escape from Castel Sant'Angelo
level.catilina.fact: In 63 BC, Consul Cicero denounced Lucius Sergius Catilina directly in the Senate — «How long, Catilina, will you abuse our patience?» — and that very night, he left to join his army in Etruria. Evidence came from intercepted letters of the conspirators to envoys of the Gallic Allobroges tribe. Five men, including Praetor Lentulus Sura, were strangled in the Tullianum without a verdict from the popular assembly: in the Senate, Caesar proposed life imprisonment, but Cato swayed the debate in favor of death. Cicero was proclaimed «father of the fatherland» — but five years later, he was sent into exile precisely for executing Roman citizens without trial.
level.catilina.goal: The conspiracy is crushed at the cost of execution without trial
level.catilina.hint: First, a speech – the accused flees. Then, letters – the conspirator is caught. Only one who has not been condemned himself can execute: Caesar's speech on mercy is not for the consul to heed.
level.catilina.intro: The ruined patrician Catiline has failed three times in consular elections and decided to seize power differently — an army gathers for him in Etruria. Consul Cicero has no evidence, only certainty.
level.catilina.source: Sallust, «The Conspiracy of Catiline»; Cicero, «Catilinarian Orations»
level.catilina.title: O Tempora, O Mores
level.cato_utica.fact: In April 46 BC, Caesar defeated the Pompeians at Thapsus. Cato the Younger, in Utica, sent everyone who wished to flee out of the city, dined, reread Plato's 'Phaedo' twice, and fell upon his sword. Doctors stitched the wound — he tore it open with his hands. Caesar, upon learning, said: 'Cato, I envy your death, because you envied me the chance to pardon you.' For Romans, Cato became an emblem of freedom that could not be taken away; Dante placed him as guardian at the foot of Purgatory — the only pagan in that role.
level.cato_utica.goal: The last republican refuses the victor's mercy — and life itself.
level.cato_utica.hint: First, the last army must be defeated. Cato will spend the night with Plato, contemplating the immortality of the soul — and then fall upon his sword. He will not accept Caesar's mercy: one who accepts a pardon cannot do what he did.
level.cato_utica.intro: After Pharsalus, the Pompeians flee to Africa. Their last army is with Metellus Scipio, and the last conscience of the republic is Cato, who holds Utica. Caesar follows.
level.cato_utica.title: Cato in Utica
level.caudine.fact: In 321 BC, in the Caudine Forks, the Samnites under Gaius Pontius trapped both consular armies. Pontius's father, Herennius, advised: either release everyone unharmed — and gain Rome's everlasting friendship, or kill everyone — and deprive Rome of an army for a generation. He allowed no middle ground. The Samnites chose a middle ground: they disarmed the Romans and drove them under the yoke of spears. Rome deemed the peace signed by the consuls in the gorge invalid, handed the consuls themselves over to the Samnites — and fought for another thirty years until Samnium was conquered. From then on, the Romans pronounced the word «humiliation» with a Samnite accent.
level.caudine.goal: The victor chooses a middle ground — and Rome never forgives it.
level.caudine.hint: First, a trap in the gorge. The father's advice: «either release everyone as friends, or kill everyone.» The victor will heed the advice and choose what the old man precisely did not advise: to drive them under the yoke. There should be no massacre.
level.caudine.intro: The Samnites lured both consular armies into a narrow gorge and blocked the exits. Their leader, Gaius Pontius, sent for his father, the old Herennius, for advice: what to do with eight legions captured without a fight?
level.caudine.title: The Caudine Forks
level.cavour.fact: In 1855 Cavour sent fifteen thousand Piedmontese to the Crimean War, where Sardinia had nothing at stake, purely to earn a seat at the peace congress. In July 1858 he met Napoleon III secretly at the spa town of Plombières: France would provide two hundred thousand soldiers against Austria, Piedmont would hand over Nice and Savoy and marry the king's daughter to the emperor's cousin. The war of 1859 brought Magenta and Solferino — at Solferino some forty thousand were killed or wounded in a single day; the sight of the field shook the Swiss traveller Henry Dunant, and four years later he founded the Red Cross. Frightened by the slaughter and by Prussian mobilisation, Napoleon III made an armistice without telling his ally; Cavour resigned in a fury — and came back six months later. France received Nice and Savoy in 1860; Nice was Garibaldi's birthplace, and he never forgave it.
level.cavour.goal: The minister buys France first with blood in the Crimea, then with a secret bargain — and pays for victory with Nice and Savoy
level.cavour.hint: The Crimean War first: the minister becomes a power to be reckoned with. A strong minister and the emperor strike their bargain at Plombières. The emperor, now committed, beats the Austrian. And only then the payment: Nice and Savoy. Appealing to England is useless — she did not fight for us.
level.cavour.intro: Piedmont is a small kingdom facing the Austrian Empire. Its minister Cavour knows he cannot win alone: he needs an ally. And he sets about acquiring one the way only diplomats do — by first sending soldiers into somebody else's war.
level.cavour.source: D. Mack Smith, Cavour and Garibaldi; Cavour's correspondence
level.cavour.title: Cavour
level.cedynia_972.fact: On 24 June 972 at Cedynia, on the right bank of the Oder, Hodo's army was defeated; Thietmar of Merseburg writes that the Polish blow was struck by Czcibor, Mieszko's brother, and that of all the margrave's noble warriors only Hodo himself and the chronicler's father, Count Siegfried, escaped. The feigned retreat is a historians' reconstruction: the chronicle speaks only of the margrave's defeat, not of how he was lured. Emperor Otto I summoned both to judgement in Quedlinburg, and Mieszko had to send his son there as a hostage — the future Bolesław the Brave. Cedynia is the first battle in Polish history that we know of.
level.cedynia_972.goal: The prince retreats, the margrave gives chase — and the prince's brother strikes him from the rear
level.cedynia_972.hint: The margrave is stronger and cannot be beaten head-on — not even with a mustered retinue. Let him stretch his own line in the pursuit. But the blow must come from someone who did not run.
