level.excommunicate.hint: Let Savonarola first boldly denounce the Pope from the pulpit — and only the rebel will the Pope anathematize. Until the monk issues a challenge, there is no anathema.
level.excommunicate.intro: The monk Savonarola burns 'bonfires of the vanities' and from the pulpit denounces the corrupt Pope. Rome is divided.
level.excommunicate.title: Excommunication
level.execution.fact: On January 10, 1775, Yemelyan Pugachev was executed in Bolotnaya Square in Moscow. The rebellion was drowned in blood; Catherine II renamed the Yaik River to the Ural to erase the memory of the revolt.
level.execution.goal: The captured impostor is executed in Bolotnaya Square
level.execution.hint: First — capture by Suvorov, then — the block by the sovereign's will.
level.execution.intro: The Empress reigns; the captured impostor awaits judgment.
level.execution.title: The Execution of Pugachev
level.fabius.fact: After Lake Trasimene (217 BC), Dictator Quintus Fabius Maximus followed Hannibal along mountain ridges, avoiding battle and burning supplies. Rome nicknamed him Cunctator, «The Delayer», — and it was a mockery. The Master of Horse, Minucius, obtained equal powers with him, immediately engaged in open battle, and was surrounded; Fabius led him out of the encirclement, and Minucius publicly called him father. Once, Hannibal escaped a trap by sending a herd of oxen with burning faggots on their horns at night. A year later, Rome abandoned «delaying tactics» — and suffered Cannae.
level.fabius.goal: Hannibal is exhausted by hunger, and the hothead acknowledges the delayer's wisdom
level.fabius.hint: Hannibal is not defeated in battle – he is worn down. A hothead will learn this only through his own skin, and only he who has not been defeated can pull him out.
level.fabius.intro: Hannibal is in Italy; he has already destroyed two Roman armies. Fabius Maximus, appointed dictator, refuses battle — for this, he is called the Delayer in Rome, while the master of horse yearns to show how to fight.
level.fabius.title: The Delayer
level.falerii.fact: In 394 BC, during the siege of Falerii, a local teacher brought boys from noble families to Camillus, offering them as hostages. Camillus ordered the traitor stripped, gave the children rods, and had him driven back into the city. The Falisci, seeing this, sent word to the Senate: 'We prefer to live under Roman rule than under our own laws — so just is your general.' Livy recounts the episode as a lesson in Roman fides — faithfulness to one's word even with an enemy. It is worth remembering that a few years earlier, the same Camillus had plundered Veii and sold its inhabitants into slavery.
level.falerii.goal: A city surrenders to an enemy who refused to take it by treachery
level.falerii.hint: First, attrition — otherwise, the city has no reason to surrender. The traitor with the children must be sent home, not accepted: only an honorable general has the authority for the city to open its gates itself.
level.falerii.intro: Camillus besieges Falerii, and the siege drags on. The city teacher, whose class includes the sons of all the best families, takes the children 'for a walk' — directly into the Roman camp.
level.falerii.source: Livy, 'The History of Rome', V, 27; Plutarch, 'Camillus', 10
level.falerii.title: The Teacher of Falerii
level.fall_1453.fact: On April 6, 1453, Mehmed II besieged Constantinople; Urban's bombard, eight meters long, fired half-ton cannonballs and took three hours to load. On the night of April 22, the Ottomans dragged seventy ships over greased logs across the hill of Galata into the Golden Horn, bypassing the chain. At dawn on May 29, after a night assault, the Genoese Giovanni Giustiniani, who commanded the defense, was wounded — he ordered himself to be carried to a ship, and his men followed him; at the same time, the Kerkoporta gate was opened. Emperor Constantine XI, according to legend, tore off his insignia and rushed into battle; his body was not identified. Mehmed entered Hagia Sophia and ordered it converted into a mosque. He was twenty-one years old. Historians often mark this day as the end of the Middle Ages.
level.fall_1453.goal: The Sultan batters the walls with cannons, drags his fleet overland, the defense commander is wounded — and the last emperor tears off his purple and rushes into battle.
level.fall_1453.hint: First, the bombard — the Sultan is powerful. The powerful Sultan drags ships overland — the Emperor is besieged. Wounded Giustiniani leaves — the Emperor is no longer powerful. Then May 29: the powerful Sultan defeats the besieged and weakened Emperor — the last Emperor. To sail to Morea — he refused.
level.fall_1453.intro: Only one city remained of the empire, with seven thousand defenders; Sultan Mehmed had eighty thousand men and the cannon of the Hungarian Urban, firing half-ton cannonballs. The Genoese Giustiniani holds the defense. The Emperor is offered to flee — he stays.
level.fall_1453.source: George Sphrantzes, «Chronicle»; S. Runciman, «The Fall of Constantinople 1453»
level.fall_1453.title: May 29, 1453
level.false_dmitry.fact: In October 1604, False Dmitry crossed the Dnieper with four thousand men; cities surrendered to him without a fight, but on January 21, 1605, at Dobrynichi, the Tsar's voivodes utterly defeated him — he fled to Putivl and intended to retreat to Poland. He was saved by the death of Boris Godunov: on April 13, the Tsar rose from the table, blood gushed from his nose and ears, and two hours later he died. The army near Kromy defected to the impostor, the sixteen-year-old Tsar Fyodor Godunov and his mother were strangled, and on June 20, 'Dmitry' entered Moscow; the Tsarevich's mother, Nun Marfa, publicly recognized him as her son. He reigned for eleven months.
level.false_dmitry.goal: The impostor raises the banner — and the Tsar suddenly dies, and the entire army defects to 'Dmitry'.
level.false_dmitry.hint: First, the Tsarevich's banner — people gather under it. Do not rush into battle: a strong Tsar will defeat you. Await Boris's sudden death — the army will defect to the impostor, and he will gain the right to the crown. Then the coronation.
level.false_dmitry.intro: Fugitive monk Grigory Otrepyev declares in Poland that he is Tsarevich Dmitry, miraculously saved. With a handful of Poles and Cossacks, he marches on Moscow. Godunov is ten times stronger, but the country has been starving for three years, and everyone awaits a 'true Tsar'.
level.false_dmitry.source: R. Skrynnikov, 'Impostors in Russia in the Early 17th Century'
level.false_dmitry.title: The Impostor
level.february.fact: On February 23 (March 8), 1917, women in Petrograd took to the streets shouting 'Bread!'; four days later, the Volynsky, Litovsky, and Preobrazhensky regiments joined the crowd. Rodzianko telegraphed the Tsar at Stavka: 'The situation is serious. Anarchy in the capital'; Nicholas said: 'That fat Rodzianko has written me nonsense again.' The Tsar's train was not allowed into Tsarskoye Selo; he was stranded in Pskov; on March 2 (15), General Ruzsky and Guchkov and Shulgin, sent by the Duma, presented him with telegrams from the front commanders — all but one advised him to abdicate. Nicholas signed the abdication with a pencil — first for himself, then, 'not wishing to part with his son,' also for Alexei — in favor of his brother Mikhail, who also refused the next day. That same evening in his diary: 'Around me is treason, and cowardice, and deceit.'
level.february.goal: The capital revolts, the Duma demands, generals advise — and in the Tsar's carriage near Pskov, three hundred years of the dynasty end with a pencil signature
level.february.hint: First, bread riots: Rodzianko telegraphs the Tsar — the capital is hungry, the Duma is against the Tsar and has authority. The Duma, with authority, denounces the Tsar — he is condemned. In Pskov, a general presents the condemned Tsar with the abdication. Bribing the Duma and shooting the crowd — neither move will save him.
level.february.intro: Third year of war, bread queues in Petrograd. Women take to the streets, followed by workers, then soldiers of reserve regiments shoot officers. The Tsar is at Stavka, and the Chairman of the Duma, Rodzianko, sends him telegrams, which he calls 'nonsense.'
level.february.source: 'Diaries of Emperor Nicholas II'; V. Shulgin, 'Days'; G. Katkov, 'The February Revolution'
level.february.title: Abdication
level.fili.fact: On September 1 (13), 1812, in peasant Frolov's hut in Fili, Kutuzov listened to the generals and cut short the debate: 'With the loss of Moscow, Russia is not yet lost. I order a retreat.' The next day, the army marched through Moscow, and Napoleon entered the city after them; that same night, fires began, and three-quarters of the houses burned down in six days. For five weeks, Napoleon awaited Alexander's reply — 'I will not conclude peace as long as a single armed enemy remains in my realm' — and on October 7 (19), he left Moscow. On October 12 (24), at Maloyaroslavets, the town changed hands eight times; Kutuzov blocked the path south, and the Grande Armée had to retreat along the devastated Smolensk road, in freezing weather, towards the Berezina. The hut in Fili burned down in 1868 and was rebuilt — it is now a museum.
level.fili.goal: A draw at Borodino, Moscow is surrendered and burns — and the conqueror's starving army is defeated on its way home.
level.fili.hint: Borodino — a draw between two forces, both at war. Then the council at Fili: Kutuzov surrenders Moscow, it burns — Napoleon is hungry and no longer strong. Maloyaroslavets: a strong Kutuzov defeats him. Do not answer Napoleon's letter — a yielding Napoleon is not defeated.
level.fili.intro: The Grande Armée reached Borodino. Kutuzov gave battle — the bloodiest in history — and did not lose it. Now, in a peasant's hut in Fili, the generals decide: another battle beneath the walls of Moscow or surrender the capital without a fight. The Tsar does not answer Napoleon's letters.
level.fili.source: 'Memoirs' of A. Yermolov; E. Tarle, 'Napoleon's Invasion of Russia'
level.fili.title: Council at Fili
level.first_partition_1772.fact: On 5 August 1772 in St Petersburg the three powers signed a convention: Poland lost about a third of its territory and a third of its population. In 1773 the Sejm, under the guard of foreign troops, was to ratify the partition; the envoy Tadeusz Rejtan lay down across the threshold of the chamber, crying "Kill me, but do not kill the Fatherland!" — they stepped over him. Frederick II said of Maria Theresa, who had long hesitated: "She wept, but she took." Jan Matejko painted "Rejtan" in 1866, and the painting hangs in the Royal Castle in Warsaw.
level.first_partition_1772.goal: Three neighbours agree to carve up the Commonwealth, and a lone envoy lies across the threshold of the Sejm — but the partition is ratified all the same
level.first_partition_1772.hint: Three are dividing — and all three must agree. One man's protest will not stop the partition, but it has gone down in history. Stop it by force? Against the Prussian army there is nothing to fight with.
level.first_partition_1772.intro: 1772. The Commonwealth has been weakened by the war of the confederates and by foreign armies. Russia, Prussia and Austria decide to take a piece of its lands each — and to force the Sejm to ratify it.
level.first_partition_1772.source: St Petersburg Convention of 1772; Diary of the Sejm of 1773
level.first_partition_1772.title: The First Partition
level.flight.fact: When Justinian was preparing to flee, Theodora stopped the council with the words: «Imperial purple makes the best shroud», preferring death on the throne to flight. Her resolve saved the throne.
level.flight.goal: Theodora restrains the emperor ready to flee
level.flight.hint: Who will stay the wavering emperor? Not the advisors who urge flight — only Theodora with the words, 'Purple makes the noblest shroud.'
level.flight.intro: The rebellion rages, the ship stands ready. The council — Narses the eunuch, Belisarius the general — whispers to flee. Only one voice commands them to stay.
level.flight.title: Purple Makes the Best Shroud
level.fontainebleau.fact: From 10 to 14 February 1814, in the Six Days' Campaign, Napoleon beat the allies at Champaubert, Montmirail, Château-Thierry and Vauchamps, but on 31 March the allied armies entered Paris. On 4 April at Fontainebleau the marshals Ney, Lefebvre, Oudinot and Moncey refused to lead the army against the capital: to the words 'the army will follow me' Ney replied that the army would follow its own commanders. That same day Napoleon abdicated in favour of his son, and on 6 April signed an unconditional abdication; the terms were discussed in Paris with Alexander I by his envoy Caulaincourt. On the night of 13 April he took the poison he had carried with him since the Russian campaign — the mixture had lost its strength, and he vomited it up. By the Treaty of Fontainebleau of 11 April he was left the title of emperor, the island of Elba and two million francs of annuity. On 20 April, in the Courtyard of the White Horse, he took leave of the Old Guard, embraced General Petit and kissed the standard; ever since, the courtyard has been called the Courtyard of Farewells.
level.fontainebleau.goal: After six days of victories the marshals refuse to march on Paris — and the emperor abdicates, to take his leave of the Guard
level.fontainebleau.hint: First the six days of victories: he is a force once more. And then a marshal tells him to his face that the army will not march — the force drains away and he is left alone. The abandoned man has nothing left but to sign an unconditional abdication before the victor. The man who has abdicated goes out into the courtyard to his Guard. The vial in the amulet is a trap: that night the poison did not work.
level.fontainebleau.intro: February 1814: with forty-five thousand raw recruits he beats the allies four times in six days — and on the map it looks like a miracle. But the allies go round him and enter Paris. At Fontainebleau he spreads out the maps and announces to his marshals that tomorrow they march to retake the capital.
level.fontainebleau.title: The Courtyard of the White Horse
level.fouquet.fact: On August 17, 1661, Fouquet hosted the King at Vaux-le-Vicomte: dinner on gold, a Molière premiere, fireworks over Le Nôtre's gardens. Three weeks later, d'Artagnan — yes, that one — arrested him in Nantes. The trial lasted three years; the judges sentenced him to exile, but Louis XIV did what no other king had done — he stiffened the sentence to life imprisonment, and Fouquet died in Pignerol in 1680. The King took Vaux's architect, gardener, and artist for himself — they built Versailles. Voltaire said: 'On August 17, at six in the evening, Fouquet was King of France; at two in the morning, he was nobody.'
level.fouquet.goal: The Minister dazzles the King with luxury — and receives life imprisonment instead of the block
level.fouquet.hint: The celebration makes the minister the King's enemy. The King condemns him in a speech — the trial is rigged. But instead of execution — a fortress forever: the King neither pardons nor executes, he forgets.
level.fouquet.intro: Superintendent of Finance Nicolas Fouquet built himself the Château de Vaux-le-Vicomte — more beautiful than anything the King possessed — and invited the twenty-two-year-old Louis XIV to a celebration: fountains, Molière, fireworks. The King watched in silence.
level.fouquet.source: Voltaire, 'The Age of Louis XIV'; letters of Madame de Sévigné
level.fouquet.title: The Feast at Vaux
level.four_emperors.fact: Between 68–69 AD, Rome saw four rulers. Galba refused to pay the Praetorians what was promised ('I recruit soldiers, I don't buy them'), and they cut him down in the Forum, proclaiming Otho, who paid. Otho was defeated by Vitellius's Rhine legions, and he took his own life; Vitellius was torn apart by the mob six months later. Vespasian, raised by the legions of Judea and Egypt, emerged victorious. Tacitus drew the main lesson of the year from this: the secret of power was revealed — an emperor could be made outside of Rome.
level.four_emperors.goal: The purple goes to him whom the legions of the provinces raise
level.four_emperors.hint: The Guard kills not for an idea, but for non-payment: deny them — and another will come to pay. Then the eastern legions will raise Vespasian against the one who bought the Guard. Vitellius will approach from the Rhine, but the purple will not be his.
level.four_emperors.intro: Nero is dead, the dynasty is no more. The governor of Hispania occupied the palace, but gave no money to the Guard — and the Guard was accustomed to a new princeps paying.
level.four_emperors.title: The Year of the Four Emperors
level.francis.fact: In 1206 Francesco, son of the cloth merchant Pietro Bernardone, stripped off all his clothes on the square of Assisi before Bishop Guido and gave them back to his father: "Until now I called you father; from now on I say: Our Father, who art in heaven." In 1209 he came to Rome with eleven companions to see Innocent III, the most powerful pope of the Middle Ages. The pope first drove the ragged men away but, so the story goes, dreamed of the Lateran basilica tilting and being held up on the shoulder of that same beggar — and approved a rule made of nothing but words of the Gospel. Seventeen years later the order numbered thousands of brothers; Francis was canonised two years after his death, and in 2013 a pope took his name for the first time.
level.francis.goal: The son strips naked to renounce his father's wealth — and the pope, after a dream, hands the beggar a rule for his order
level.francis.hint: The square first: son and father — he gives back everything, his clothes included. The pope dreams of the man who renounced all and blesses him. The blessed man receives his rule. Taking over the father's shop: a man who has been bought renounces nothing.
level.francis.intro: The son of the richest cloth merchant in Assisi caroused, went to war and sat in a prison cell — and on returning began giving his father's goods away to beggars. His father hauls him before the bishop's court: let him return every thread of it.
level.francis.source: Thomas of Celano, First Life; The Little Flowers of St Francis
level.francis.title: Brother Francis
level.francis_sultan.fact: In September 1219, after the Crusaders' defeat on August 29, Francis and Brother Illuminatus crossed the front line near Damietta; Saracen patrols beat them and brought them before Sultan al-Kamil, Saladin's nephew. The Sultan listened to the sermon for several days, offered gold—Francis refused—and released both with a safe-conduct; in Assisi, the ivory horn gifted by the Sultan is still preserved. At that time, al-Kamil also offered Jerusalem to the Crusaders in exchange for their withdrawal from Egypt—Legate Pelagius refused, took Damietta in November, and in 1221 lost both it and his army in the Nile flood. Frederick II, who was awaited at Damietta, only sailed to the East in 1228 and received Jerusalem from the same al-Kamil—by treaty, without a fight.
level.francis_sultan.goal: A mendicant friar crosses the front line unarmed—and the Sultan, instead of beheading him, releases him in peace.
level.francis_sultan.hint: First—cross the line near Damietta unarmed: one who takes up a sword is no longer a pilgrim. The unarmed pilgrim is heard and released by the Sultan. The Emperor never arrived in Damietta—do not lead him into battle.
level.francis_sultan.intro: The Fifth Crusade is stalled near Damietta in the Nile Delta. The Crusaders await Emperor Frederick II, who took the cross four years ago and still has not come. A mendicant from Assisi arrives in the camp and asks the legate for permission to go to the Sultan—to preach.
level.francis_sultan.source: Jacques de Vitry, letter of 1220; Thomas of Celano, 'First Life'; Bonaventure, 'Major Legend'
level.francis_sultan.title: Francis and the Sultan
level.fratricide.fact: In June 1497, Juan Borgia was murdered, his body cast into the Tiber. Rumor accused his brother Cesare, who eliminated a rival for their father's affection and power. The murder remained unsolved.
level.fratricide.goal: Cesare secretly murders his rival brother
level.fratricide.hint: Let the fraternal feast ignite Cesare's envy — and only consumed by it will he dispose of Juan in the Tiber. Without resentment, his hand will not rise.
level.fratricide.intro: His father made Juan Gonfalonier of the Church, bypassing the capable Cesare. The younger brother's envy grows.
level.fratricide.title: Body in the Tiber
level.frederick2.fact: Gregory IX excommunicated Frederick II in September 1227 for turning his fleet back because of an epidemic. The emperor sailed anyway, and in February 1229 concluded the Treaty of Jaffa with Sultan al-Kamil: Jerusalem, Bethlehem and Nazareth passed to the Christians for ten years, the al-Aqsa mosque stayed with the Muslims, and there was no fighting at all. On 18 March he entered the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, where no one dared crown him — and set the crown on his own head. The pope declared the crusade void and laid an interdict on Jerusalem; both sides considered Frederick a traitor to his own faith. He died excommunicated in 1250, and Dante placed him in the sixth circle of hell, among the heretics.
level.frederick2.goal: The excommunicated emperor takes Jerusalem by treaty, without a single battle — and crowns himself at the Holy Sepulchre
level.frederick2.hint: The excommunication first: a pope with standing condemns the emperor. Then Jaffa: emperor and sultan — Jerusalem handed over by treaty. An excommunicate holding Jerusalem has only one way left to be crowned: himself. No need to storm the city — it was taken with words.
level.frederick2.intro: Frederick II, the Wonder of the World: raised in Palermo among Arabs and Greeks, keeping a harem and a menagerie, corresponding with sultans about mathematics. For years he put off the crusade he had promised, and Pope Gregory IX excommunicated him. Excommunicated — and off he goes on crusade.
level.frederick2.source: E. Kantorowicz, Frederick II; the chronicle of Ibn Wasil
level.frederick2.title: The Excommunicate's Crusade
level.fronde.fact: The Fronde began in August 1648 with the arrest of the parliamentary councillor Broussel: overnight Paris was covered in barricades. On the night of 6 January 1649 the court slipped away to Saint-Germain-en-Laye, where the palace had no furniture and the ten-year-old Louis XIV slept on straw. On the night of 10 February 1651 Parisians came to the Palais-Royal to check that the king had not been spirited away again; he was put to bed, and the crowd filed past in silence — he lay with his eyes closed, not asleep. Condé spent that night under arrest at Le Havre and was freed three days later. In 1652 he fought the royal army in the Faubourg Saint-Antoine, and the Grande Mademoiselle ordered the guns of the Bastille to fire on her cousin's troops; beaten, Condé went to serve the king of Spain. On 21 October 1652 Louis returned to Paris. After Mazarin's death on 9 March 1661 he told his ministers that from now on he would rule himself, with no first minister — and spent his life building a court far from Paris, at Versailles.
level.fronde.goal: The boy who slept on straw and played at sleeping before the crowd comes back to Paris — and never trusts it again
level.fronde.hint: First the straw: the minister carries the king off by night, and the humiliation stays with him forever. The humiliated boy lies with his eyes shut while the frondeurs file past his bed — and after that he is another man. The hardened king comes back and does not forgive the insolent one. Mazarin's cabinet is a trap: a bought prince cannot be broken.
level.fronde.intro: The king is ten years old; the country is ruled by his mother and an Italian cardinal whom everyone hates: the parlement, the princes and the Paris street. In January 1649 the court flees the city by night. In the empty Saint-Germain there is no furniture: they lay straw for the boy-king.
level.fronde.source: Cardinal de Retz, 'Memoirs'; F. Bluche, 'Louis XIV'
level.fronde.title: Straw at Saint-Germain
level.gaius_gracchus.fact: In 121 BC, the Senate for the first time issued a senatus consultum ultimum — an 'ultimate decree' granting extraordinary powers to Consul Lucius Opimius. Gracchus' supporters were crushed on the Aventine; Gaius himself fled across the Tiber to the grove of Furina and there ordered his slave Philocrates to stab him, after which the slave killed himself. Opimius promised as much gold for Gracchus' head as it weighed; a certain Septimuleius brought it, having first removed the brain and filled it with lead — and received seventeen pounds. Three thousand supporters were executed without trial. This marked the end of the attempt to change Rome through laws.
level.gaius_gracchus.goal: The Senate declares the tribune an enemy — and pays for his head its weight in gold.
level.gaius_gracchus.hint: The consul, with extraordinary powers, condemns the tribune with a speech and defeats him on the Aventine. The tribune will not flee across the Tiber — he will order his slave to kill him. His head will be brought to the consul.
level.gaius_gracchus.intro: Ten years after his brother's death, Gaius Gracchus is tribune, and he has more laws than Tiberius did. For the first time in history, the Senate grants Consul Opimius the right to 'save the state' by any means.
level.gaius_gracchus.title: A Head's Weight in Gold
level.galileo.fact: «Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems» was published in 1632 with censorship approval; but the argument that Urban VIII personally requested to be included — that God could arrange the world in any way — Galileo put into the mouth of the character Simplicio, the «simpleton». The Pope felt ridiculed. In 1633, the seventy-year-old Galileo was summoned to Rome; on June 22, in the Church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, he knelt and read his abjuration of the «opinion that the Sun is the center of the world and motionless». The words «Eppur si muove» first appeared in print a hundred years later. He spent the rest of his life under house arrest in Arcetri, went blind, and wrote «Discourses» there — the foundation of mechanics. The Church lifted the ban on his books in 1835 and admitted its error in 1992.
level.galileo.goal: The Pope's friend writes a book where the Pope is a simpleton; the Holy Office forces the seventy-year-old man to his knees.
level.galileo.hint: First, old friendship — allies. The friend writes «Dialogue» and implicates the Pope — the book is out, the Pope is now an enemy. The influential Pope judges the astronomer — condemned. The condemned abjures on his knees — house arrest. To flee to Venice — one who has left is not judged or brought to his knees.
level.galileo.intro: Galileo and Pope Urban VIII are old friends: Cardinal Barberini wrote odes in honor of the astronomer. The Pope permits a book on the two world systems to be written — «impartially». Galileo puts the Pope's arguments into the mouth of a simpleton named Simplicio.
level.galileo.source: «Il processo di Galileo Galilei» (process documents); J. Heilbron, «Galileo»
level.galileo.title: And yet it moves
level.garibaldi.fact: On the night of May 6, 1860, 1089 volunteers on two steamers sailed from Quarto near Genoa; on May 15, at Calatafimi, Garibaldi, in his red shirt, took the hill with bayonets against Bourbon troops — «here we make Italy or die». Palermo rebelled, and by September, he entered Naples by train, outrunning the army. On October 26, at Teano, he met Victor Emmanuel: «I salute the first King of Italy» — and, having handed over all his conquests, refused rewards and left for his island of Caprera with a bag of seeds and a box of pasta. On March 17, 1861, the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed; Rome was taken in 1870, Venice in 1866. Garibaldi was invited to be a general by Lincoln and the Paris Commune; there is no city in Italy without a street named after him.
level.garibaldi.goal: A thousand Redshirts take half a kingdom — and the general gives everything to the king, leaving with a bag of seeds.
level.garibaldi.hint: First, the Thousand set sail — the Garibaldini are raised and hold sway. Calatafimi: the raised one defeats the Bourbon — a victor. The victor at Teano shakes hands with the king — King of Italy. You cannot march on Rome — the king is not your enemy.
level.garibaldi.intro: Italy is a patchwork quilt: Piedmont of King Victor Emmanuel, Papal Rome, Austrian Venice, the Bourbon Kingdom of Naples. Garibaldi, with a thousand red-shirted volunteers, sails to Sicily — against an army of a hundred thousand.
level.garibaldi.source: G. Garibaldi, «Memoirs»; G. Trevelyan, «Garibaldi and the Thousand»
level.garibaldi.title: The Thousand
level.girondins.fact: On June 2, 1793, eighty thousand sans-culottes with cannons surrounded the Convention and would not release the deputies until they voted for the arrest of twenty-nine Girondins. Brissot and twenty of his comrades were guillotined on October 31 — all in thirty-eight minutes; on the night before their execution, they sang in prison, and one, Valazé, stabbed himself upon the reading of the verdict, and his body was taken to the execution alongside the living. Thus began the dictatorship of the Mountain — and the Terror, which eight months later would consume Danton, and a year later, Robespierre.
level.girondins.goal: Sans-culottes with cannons resolve the dispute in the Convention — and the eloquent are taken to the square
level.girondins.hint: Debating in the Convention is useless. Sans-culottes at the doors with cannons — the power of the Mountain. Then Robespierre's speech condemns Brissot, and the condemned is executed with gravity.
level.girondins.intro: In the Convention, there are two camps: Brissot's Girondins, moderate and eloquent, and Robespierre's Mountain, with the sans-culottes at their back. Debating with the Girondins is useless — there are more of them, and they speak better.
level.girondins.source: Lamartine, 'History of the Girondins'; records of the Revolutionary Tribunal
level.girondins.title: The Expulsion of the Girondins
level.giulia.fact: Giulia Farnese, the young mistress of Alexander VI, was sardonically dubbed 'Bride of Christ' by the Romans. Through her, her brother achieved a meteoric career and himself became Pope Paul III.
level.giulia.goal: A young beauty becomes the Pope's favorite
level.giulia.hint: Let Giulia first captivate the Pope during a rendezvous — and only enamored will he shower her with favors. Lucrezia is his daughter, not a mistress.
level.giulia.intro: Young Giulia Farnese captivated the old Pope. The key to papal favors lies through the pontiff's heart.
level.giulia.title: Bride of Christ
level.globe.fact: On December 28, 1598, the Lord Chamberlain's Men, with carpenter Peter Street, dismantled 'The Theatre' in Shoreditch and transported the timbers across the frozen Thames to Southwark; from these, 'The Globe' was built, opening in 1599 — likely with 'Julius Caesar'. Shakespeare owned a tenth share. In February 1601, Essex's supporters paid the troupe to stage 'Richard II' — a play about the deposition of a king — on the eve of their rebellion; the actors were interrogated and released, and the evening after Essex's execution, they performed before the Queen. The Globe burned down in 1613 from a theatrical cannon during 'Henry VIII'; only someone's breeches, which were doused with ale, were damaged.
level.globe.goal: The Theatre is moved across the Thames on timbers — and the best theatre in England opens.
level.globe.hint: First, dismantle 'The Theatre' — the timbers are the troupe's strength. Then the playwright and actor will open 'The Globe'. And playing 'Richard II' for Essex on the eve of a rebellion means facing an interrogation: don't befriend the Earl.
level.globe.intro: Burbage's troupe was denied a lease for the land under 'The Theatre'. The landowner considers the building his own. On the night after Christmas 1598, the actors dismantle it, timber by timber.
level.globe.source: Testimony of Augustine Phillips, 1601; J. Shapiro, '1599'
level.globe.title: The Globe
level.glorious.fact: On November 5, 1688, William of Orange landed in Torbay. James II's army disintegrated without a fight — commander John Churchill (the future Marlborough) defected to the Dutch. In December, James fled, on the way throwing the Great Seal of the Realm into the Thames to paralyze governance; he was caught by fishermen in Kent, but William deliberately allowed him to escape to France. Parliament declared the throne vacant and in February 1689 offered it jointly to William and Mary — under the terms of the Bill of Rights. The Revolution was called Glorious because in England it was bloodless; Ireland and Scotland paid for it in full.
level.glorious.goal: The king loses his throne without fighting a single battle — and throws the Great Seal of the Realm into the river.
level.glorious.hint: The powerful Dutchman lands — and the king's army disperses, there will be no battle. The king flees and throws the seal into the Thames — this is his departure. And then his allied daughter, with authority, proclaims her husband king alongside herself.
level.glorious.intro: The Catholic James II had a son — England feared a Catholic dynasty. Seven lords secretly invited the Dutch Stadtholder William, married to James's daughter Mary, to 'save the Protestant faith.' He landed with twenty thousand men.
level.glorious.title: The Seal in the Thames
level.gniezno_1000.fact: On 23 April 997 Adalbert was killed by the Prussians; Bolesław ransomed his body for its weight in gold and buried it in Gniezno. In March 1000 Otto III came to the tomb as a pilgrim, barefoot. Gallus Anonymus writes that the emperor took the diadem from his own head and placed it on Bolesław's, called him "brother and partner of the empire" and gave him a copy of the Holy Lance of Saint Maurice, receiving in return an arm of the saint. At that time an archbishopric was founded in Gniezno with bishoprics in Kraków, Wrocław and Kołobrzeg — the Polish Church became independent. Bolesław was crowned king only in 1025, a few months before his death.
level.gniezno_1000.goal: A saint dies among the Prussians, the prince ransoms his body for its weight in gold — and the emperor comes to the tomb as a pilgrim
level.gniezno_1000.hint: The emperor is coming not to the prince but to the saint: without the relics there is nothing to invite him to. The relics are with the Prussians — and war with them won't bring them back, it will only spoil the bargain.
level.gniezno_1000.intro: 997. Adalbert, former Bishop of Prague and friend of the young emperor Otto III, asks Prince Bolesław to let him go and preach to the pagan Prussians. Bolesław gives him a boat and an escort. The emperor dreams of a new Christian empire — a Rome that the Slavs will join.
level.gniezno_1000.source: Gallus Anonymus, I, 6; Thietmar of Merseburg, IV, 45–46; Life of Saint Adalbert
level.gniezno_1000.title: The Congress of Gniezno
level.godunov.fact: On May 15, 1591, eight-year-old Tsarevich Dmitry died in Uglich with his throat slit; Prince Vasily Shuisky's commission ruled that the boy, playing with knives during an epileptic fit, 'stabbed himself.' The residents of Uglich who tore apart Godunov's men were executed and exiled to Siberia, and the veche bell, which raised the alarm, was 'punished' – its clapper removed and exiled to Tobolsk. When the childless Tsar Fyodor died in January 1598, Boris secluded himself in the Novodevichy Convent with his sister, Tsarina Irina; Patriarch Job, with a procession and a crowd, went three times to beg him to accept the throne, and he agreed 'with tears.' The same Shuisky, eight years later, would declare that the Tsarevich had indeed been murdered on Boris's orders.
level.godunov.goal: The ruler emerges clean from the Uglich affair — and 'reluctantly' accepts the crown from the hands of the pleading crowd.
level.godunov.hint: First, Shuisky's investigation in Uglich: an accident, the ruler is clean, and Shuisky is with him. Then Novodevichy: the clean ruler is begged three times, and he gains the right to the crown. The coronation is at the end. To renounce the crown means to leave for good.
level.godunov.intro: Tsar Fyodor is weak-minded; his brother-in-law, Boris Godunov, rules. In Uglich, under strange circumstances, Ivan the Terrible's youngest son, Tsarevich Dmitry, dies. Prince Shuisky leads the investigation. And when Fyodor dies, the throne is empty for the first time in seven hundred years.
level.godunov.title: Boris Godunov
level.gracchus.fact: In 133 BC, Tribune Tiberius Gracchus proposed returning surplus public land to the state and distributing it to the landless. His colleague Marcus Octavius vetoed it — and Gracchus secured a vote for his removal, which the Roman constitution did not recognize. The law passed. When Gracchus ran for a second consecutive term (also an unprecedented act), senators led by Scipio Nasica Serapio, wrapping their togas around their arms and armed with bench legs, beat him to death near the Capitoline — about three hundred people died with him. This was the first political assassination in Rome in 380 years of the Republic; from then on, the count would be in the thousands.
level.gracchus.goal: The agrarian law is passed — and the tribune is killed for it on the Capitoline.
level.gracchus.hint: First, remove a colleague with his veto through a speech, then the law – and only then the senator with a club.
level.gracchus.intro: The land of Italy is being bought up into vast estates, while veterans return from wars to nothing. Tribune Tiberius Gracchus wants to distribute surplus public land to them — and runs into the veto of his own colleague. A tribune is inviolable, as long as he is a tribune.
level.gracchus.source: Plutarch, 'Tiberius Gracchus'; Appian, 'The Civil Wars', I
level.gracchus.title: The Fall of the Tribune
level.great_fire.fact: The fire began on September 2, 1666, in Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane. Lord Mayor Thomas Bloodworth, woken at night, refused to demolish houses for firebreaks — 'Pish! A woman might piss it out!' — and missed the only opportunity. In four days, 13,200 houses, 87 churches, and St. Paul's Cathedral burned; officially, six people died. Charles II and the Duke of York personally commanded the demolition of houses by explosion in the fire's path. The French and Catholics were blamed; the French watchmaker Robert Hubert, who confessed to arson, was hanged, even though he was not yet in England on the day the fire started. Wren rebuilt the cathedral in thirty-five years.
level.great_fire.goal: A spark from the oven burns London because the mayor won't demolish houses — and the king stops the fire.
level.great_fire.hint: The baker won't extinguish the oven. The mayor won't demolish houses — and the city will ignite; if he undertakes to demolish them immediately, there will be no fire, and then nothing to stop. The king will stop the fire by blowing up houses with gunpowder.
level.great_fire.intro: September 1666, a dry summer, an east wind. At two in the morning, the royal baker Farriner went to sleep without extinguishing his oven. Woken, Mayor Bloodworth looked at the fire and returned to bed.
level.great_fire.title: Pudding Lane
level.greek_fire.fact: According to Theophanes, around 672, the architect Kallinikos from Syrian Heliopolis (Baalbek) fled to Constantinople and brought «sea fire» — a petroleum-based mixture that was ejected under pressure from bronze siphons on the prows of dromons; it burned on water and could only be extinguished with sand, vinegar, or urine. In 674–678, the Arab fleet, wintering near Cyzicus, was burned, the siege was lifted, and Caliph Muawiyah paid tribute. The composition was kept in the strictest secrecy: Constantine Porphyrogennetos wrote to his son that the fire was «shown by an angel to Constantine the Great» and to reveal it was a sin; an official who tried to sell the secret was «consumed by fire from heaven». The secret is indeed lost — the exact composition is unknown to this day.
level.greek_fire.goal: A refugee brings burning water, the Caliph's fleet burns at the Golden Horn — and the recipe becomes the empire's secret for five centuries.
level.greek_fire.hint: First, a refugee brings the recipe to the Emperor — the Emperor is powerful and has fire. Battle at the Golden Horn: the powerful Emperor defeats the Caliph. The victor with fire declares the composition a secret. To sell the recipe to the Caliph — a bought engineer will not bring the fire.
level.greek_fire.intro: The Arab fleet of Caliph Muawiyah has stood before Constantinople for four years. From captured Syria, the architect Kallinikos flees to the capital — with the recipe for a liquid that burns on water and cannot be extinguished.
level.greek_fire.source: Theophanes the Confessor, «Chronographia»; Constantine Porphyrogennetos, «De Administrando Imperio», ch. 13
level.greek_fire.title: Greek Fire
level.grunwald_1410.fact: The heralds of Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen brought Jagiełło two naked swords — these swords later became a symbol of the victory. Vytautas's Lithuanian banners withdrew — whether this was flight or a feigned manoeuvre, historians still argue — and some of the Order's knights rushed after them. Jagiełło committed his reserves, the Order's army was surrounded, and the Grand Master fell along with most of the brethren of the Order. Zawisza the Black of Garbów distinguished himself in the battle — ever since, Poles say "to rely on someone as on Zawisza". Malbork could not be taken after the battle, but the power of the Order was broken.
level.grunwald_1410.goal: The Grand Master sends the king two swords in mockery, the Lithuanians withdraw, the knights give chase — and the king strikes the disordered army
level.grunwald_1410.hint: The Order is strong as long as it holds its formation — even the finest knight cannot beat it alone. Let it break its own line in the pursuit. And the king is waiting for a challenge.
level.grunwald_1410.intro: 15 July 1410, a scorching day. On the field between Grunwald and Tannenberg the army of the Teutonic Order meets the allied armies of Poland and Lithuania — one of the largest battles of medieval Europe. King Jagiełło stands in the forest, hears Mass and does not begin.
level.grunwald_1410.source: Jan Długosz, Annals, XI; Chronicle of the Conflict of Władysław, King of Poland, with the Teutonic Knights
level.grunwald_1410.title: Grunwald
level.gunpowder.fact: On October 26, 1605, the Catholic Lord Monteagle received an anonymous letter advising him not to attend the opening of Parliament; he took it to Robert Cecil. On the night of November 5, Guy Fawkes was found in the cellar beneath the House of Lords with a fuse and thirty-six barrels of gunpowder. Under torture, he betrayed the others; Catesby died during arrest, eight were hanged and quartered in January 1606 — Fawkes jumped from the gallows ladder and broke his neck before being quartered. The day of the king's salvation is still celebrated with bonfires, and Fawkes' mask became the face of protest four centuries later.
level.gunpowder.goal: An anonymous letter reveals the plot — and the gunpowder remains in the barrels.
level.gunpowder.hint: First, the plot in the tavern. Then the letter will land on the royal spy's table — and the conspirator is condemned; the spy, with authority, executes him. If no one interferes — the fuse will be lit.
level.gunpowder.intro: Catholics hoped that the Scottish James would grant them freedom of religion. He did not. Robert Catesby gathered conspirators and hired former soldier Guy Fawkes to blow up the king and Parliament. Thirty-six barrels of gunpowder are already in the cellar.
level.gunpowder.source: 'The King's Book' (protocols 1606); A. Fraser, 'The Gunpowder Plot'
level.gunpowder.title: Remember, Remember the Fifth of November
level.hagia.fact: After the Nika fire, Justinian rebuilt the Hagia Sophia (537) — for a thousand years the greatest temple of Christianity. Upon entering its colossal dome, the emperor, according to legend, exclaimed: «Solomon, I have surpassed you!».
level.hagia.goal: The emperor erects the greatest temple of Christianity
level.hagia.hint: Let the emperor himself conceive the cathedral amidst the ruins — and only then will he erect the Hagia Sophia. Courtiers do not build temples.
level.hagia.intro: The Nika riot burned the old temple to ashes. Amidst the ruins, Justinian conceives the unprecedented.
level.hagia.title: Hagia Sophia
level.hannibal_alps.fact: In the autumn of 218 BC, Hannibal led his army across the Alps in fifteen days — according to Polybius, out of 46,000, about 26,000 and a handful of elephants survived; avalanches, landslides, and mountain tribes did the rest. But he emerged into the Po Valley, where the Boii Gauls, who had just revolted against Rome, provided him with men and grain. In the spring of 217 BC, at Lake Trasimene, in the morning fog, he ambushed the entire army of Consul Flaminius: fifteen thousand Romans perished, as did the consul. It is said that an earthquake that occurred during the battle went unnoticed by any of the combatants.
level.hannibal_alps.goal: The Carthaginian arrives in Italy from an unexpected direction — and the first consul perishes in the fog
level.hannibal_alps.hint: By sea — they will be intercepted. Half the army will make it through the mountains, but that will be its strength. The Gauls, who hate Rome, must be taken as allies. And only then — the lake in the fog.
level.hannibal_alps.intro: Hannibal departed from Spain with his army and elephants. The sea is held by the Roman fleet, and there is no direct road to Italy — only mountains, where it is already snowing in October. Consul Flaminius awaits him in Etruria.
level.hannibal_alps.title: Across the Alps
level.hastings.fact: On September 25, 1066, Harold Godwinson defeated the Norwegian King Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge — the latter fell in battle. Three days later, William landed in Sussex. Harold marched his army three hundred miles in nine days and on October 14, engaged in battle near Hastings, tired and with depleted forces. The Normans feigned retreat, breaking the English shield wall; by evening, Harold died — according to the Bayeux Tapestry, from an arrow to the eye. William was crowned in Westminster on Christmas Day. A century later, one third of the English language would become French.
level.hastings.goal: One king defeats another — and comes to the third without strength.
level.hastings.hint: The Norwegians must be defeated first — both are strong, but there you are home. A week's march south will exhaust the army, and it will cease to be a force. Only then will the Norman prevail; wait in London — and he will not.
level.hastings.intro: In one year, three contenders emerged for the English throne: Harold, crowned in London; Harald Hardrada, who landed with the Norwegians in the north; and William of Normandy, awaiting the wind across the Channel. Harold can reach both — but not fresh.
level.hastings.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, 1066; William of Poitiers; Bayeux Tapestry
level.heir.fact: Justin I, an illiterate soldier who became emperor, brought close and adopted his gifted nephew Justinian, making him co-ruler and heir to the throne.
level.heir.goal: Old Justin makes his nephew heir
level.heir.hint: First, let Justin entrust the gifted Justinian with the palace guard — and only then declare the proven man his heir. Germanus is superfluous here.
level.heir.intro: The illiterate soldier Justin became emperor — but which of his nephews should he make his heir? Ambitious Germanus also awaits his hour.
level.heir.source: History of the Eastern Roman Empire
level.heir.title: Justin's Heir
level.henri_flight.fact: Charles IX died on 30 May 1574; the news reached Kraków on 14 June. On the night of 19 June, after a feast, Henry slipped out of Wawel and galloped for the border of the Empire. Chamberlain Jan Tęczyński caught up with him near Pszczyna; the king, it is said, gave him a ring and promised to return. He did not: in Paris he became Henry III, and in 1589 he was killed by the monk Jacques Clément. A year later Poland declared the throne vacant, and Stephen Báthory was elected king — together with that same Anna Jagiellon.
level.henri_flight.goal: A French prince, king of Poland for only half a year, learns of his brother's death and flees Wawel by night — he is caught only at the border
level.henri_flight.hint: He would not have fled without a reason — first the news from Paris. Married to the Jagiellonian, he would have found it much harder to flee; the wedding never took place.
level.henri_flight.intro: 1574. Henry of Valois has been crowned in Kraków, but he is bored: a foreign language, endless Sejms, a promised marriage to the no-longer-young Anna Jagiellon. In France his brother, King Charles IX, is ill.
level.henri_flight.source: Jan Dymitr Solikowski, A Brief Commentary on Polish Affairs; Philippe Desportes, Farewell to Poland
level.henri_flight.title: The Flight of Henry of Valois
level.henry6.fact: From August 1453 to December 1454, Henry VI neither spoke nor moved; doctors offered no help. Parliament appointed Richard of York as Protector, removing Queen Margaret. Upon awakening, the King restored power to her party — and on May 22, 1455, York and Warwick attacked the royal court at St Albans: the Duke of Somerset and about sixty others died, the King was wounded by an arrow in the neck. Thus began the Wars of the Roses — thirty years of slaughter between the descendants of one king. The only things Henry VI built still stand today: Eton and King's College, Cambridge.
level.henry6.goal: While the King is silent, the Protector seizes power — and the first blood of the Wars of the Roses is shed in the streets of St Albans.
level.henry6.hint: Stupor renders the King an empty vessel — without weight or power. Then a strong duke becomes Protector to an empty king, not the queen. Upon awakening, the King will strip him of power — and St Albans: battle, the King defeated.
level.henry6.intro: Henry VI, son of the victor of Agincourt, is meek, pious, and weak. In August 1453, upon learning of the loss of Gascony, he fell into a stupor: he does not speak, does not eat on his own, and does not recognize his newborn son. Queen Margaret demands regency. The Duke of York — also.
level.henry6.source: 'The Chronicle of John Benet'; R. Griffiths, 'The Reign of Henry VI'
level.henry6.title: The Sleeping King
level.heraclius.fact: In 622, Heraclius, borrowing gold and silver from the church, for the first time in two hundred years personally led an army on campaign — deep into Armenia and Persia, leaving the capital under the protection of its walls and the patriarch; in 626, the Avars and Persians besieged Constantinople and retreated. On December 12, 627, at Nineveh, he defeated the Persians — according to legend, personally slaying three commanders; in February 628, Khosrow II was overthrown and killed by his own son. On March 21, 630, the Emperor carried the returned Cross into Jerusalem — on foot and in simple clothes, as the patriarch demanded. Six years later, he would lose that same Syria forever — at Yarmouk.
level.heraclius.goal: The Emperor, with church money, goes to Persia, defeats the King of Kings — and on his shoulders carries the Cross into Jerusalem.
level.heraclius.hint: First, church silver — the Emperor is powerful and influential. Nineveh: the powerful Emperor defeats Khosrow's army. The victor carries the Cross into Jerusalem. To move the capital to Carthage — one who has left will not be given silver.
level.heraclius.intro: The Persians took Jerusalem and carried away the True Cross, standing at Chalcedon opposite the capital; the treasury is empty. Emperor Heraclius, advised to flee to Carthage, borrows church silver and personally leads an army into the heart of Persia.
level.heraclius.source: Theophanes the Confessor, 'Chronographia'; W. Kaegi, 'Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium'
level.heraclius.title: The True Cross
level.heraclius_coup.fact: In 608, Heraclius the Elder, Exarch of Africa, rebelled and cut off supplies of African and Egyptian grain to Constantinople; famine began in the capital. Meanwhile, the Persians of Khosrow II took Edessa and Amida and reached the Euphrates. In the autumn of 610, Heraclius the Younger brought a fleet from Carthage; the Blues opened the harbor, and the guard defected to his side. The bound Phocas was dragged onto the ship, and Heraclius asked: 'Is this how you have ruled the empire?'—'And will you rule better?'—he replied. Phocas was beheaded, his body burned in the Forum Bovis; on October 5, 610, Patriarch Sergius crowned Heraclius, and on the same day, he married. The new emperor immediately offered Khosrow peace—he refused, and the war, begun 'for Maurice', lasted another eighteen years.
level.heraclius_coup.goal: Africa cuts off grain to the capital, the Persians strike the tyrant—and the Exarch's son enters the harbor to ask the bound Phocas one question.
level.heraclius_coup.hint: First, grain: the tyrant without African grain loses his army. The weakened one is struck by the mighty Khosrow—he who avenges Maurice. The fleet is the Exarch's son's strength. And only the strong one, who has not warred with the Persians, judges the defeated and starving tyrant. Do not go to Khosrow with gold—he will not accept peace.
level.heraclius_coup.intro: For eight years Phocas rules by terror; Khosrow II wages war 'for Maurice' and takes city after city. In Carthage, the Exarch of Africa and his son Heraclius decide that the empire will not survive this emperor. They have the grain that feeds the capital, and a fleet.
level.heraclius_coup.source: John of Nikiû, 'Chronicle', CIX–CX; Theophanes the Confessor, 'Chronographia'; Chronicon Paschale
level.heraclius_coup.title: 'Is this how you ruled?'
level.horatii.fact: Tullus Hostilius, the third king of Rome, waged war with Alba Longa, and by agreement, the outcome was decided by a duel between three Horatii and three Curiatii. The last Horatius feigned flight, the wounded enemies spread out — and he killed them one by one. At the gates, his sister, betrothed to one of the Curiatii, burst into tears upon recognizing her fiancé's cloak — and her brother stabbed her, saying: 'So perish every Roman woman who mourns an enemy.' He was tried for murder and acquitted at his father's plea, but was made to pass under a beam — the 'sister's beam,' which was still shown in Rome during Augustus's time.
level.horatii.goal: One defeats three — and kills his own sister for weeping over an enemy
level.horatii.hint: One against three will not stand — one must flee so that the pursuers spread out, and strike them down one by one: this is strength. And the sister at the gates is met by the victor.
level.horatii.intro: Rome and Alba Longa decided not to destroy two armies, but to pit three brothers against three. Two Horatii fell immediately; the third remained alone against three wounded Curiatii. And his sister is betrothed to one of them.
level.horatii.title: The Horatii and the Curiatii
level.hotspur.fact: On July 21, 1403, at Shrewsbury, Henry IV defeated Henry Percy, nicknamed Hotspur. Hotspur died, having raised his visor in the heat — an arrow struck him in the face. For the Prince of Wales, the future Henry V, an arrow entered his cheek six inches below his eye; he refused to leave the field, and later surgeon John Bradmore extracted the arrowhead with special forceps and washed the wound with honey and wine — the prince survived, the scar remained for life. Hotspur's body was quartered and sent to various towns. Shakespeare made Hotspur a contemporary of Hal and his mirror image; in life, he was twenty-three years older.
level.hotspur.goal: The rebel dies at Shrewsbury, and the idle prince, with an arrow in his face, becomes the future Henry V.
level.hotspur.hint: Percy's muster is the rebel's strength. At Shrewsbury, a strong king meets him, and in the third slot — the prince: while the boy holds the flank, the rebel loses strength, and with an arrow in his face, he does not leave the field — the defeated are finished off. If you lead the prince away, there will be neither victory nor a hero.
level.hotspur.intro: The Percys helped Bolingbroke take the throne — and decided he owed them. Harry Hotspur, the best knight of the North, raised a rebellion. Against him are the King and his sixteen-year-old son Hal, whom his father considers idle.
level.hotspur.source: T. Walsingham; J. Bradmore, 'Philomena' (a surgeon's treatise)
level.hotspur.title: Hotspur
level.howard.fact: Catherine Howard, the fifth wife, was very young. Her pre-marital affairs and accusations of treason with courtier Thomas Culpeper surfaced. On February 13, 1542, she was beheaded in the Tower. According to legend, the day before, she requested the block be brought so she could 'dignifiedly' rehearse her execution.
level.howard.goal: The young queen — and the block once more
level.howard.hint: Marriage, then accusation: Cranmer, with authority, condemns the Queen with a speech in the tribunal. The condemned is executed by the King.
level.howard.intro: The fifth wife, nineteen-year-old Catherine Howard, — 'a rose without thorns,' as the King called her. A year later, Archbishop Cranmer hands him a note: before the wedding, she had lovers, and after — too.
level.howard.title: Catherine Howard
level.hypatia.fact: Hypatia, daughter of the mathematician Theon, taught philosophy in Alexandria, commented on Diophantus and Ptolemy, and, according to Socrates Scholasticus, 'surpassed all the philosophers of her time.' She was an advisor to Prefect Orestes in his struggle against Bishop Cyril; a rumor spread in the city that she was hindering reconciliation. In March 415, a mob led by the lector Peter dragged her from her chariot, hauled her to the Caesareum church, stripped her clothes, and killed her with pottery shards (or oyster shells — 'ostracon' means both), then burned her body. Cyril was later canonized; Orestes was recalled; the Alexandrian school faded. Gibbon made her a symbol of the end of antiquity, and Raphael, according to tradition, included her in 'The School of Athens'.
level.hypatia.goal: A bishop preaches against a woman philosopher, friendly with the prefect, — and a mob of monks tears her apart with pottery shards.
level.hypatia.hint: First, the prefect's friendship with the philosopher — allies. The bishop preaches against her with authority — condemned. The bishop's parabolani drag the condemned woman from her chariot. Leave for Athens — the one who left will not be touched.
level.hypatia.intro: Alexandria, 415 AD. Hypatia — mathematician, astronomer, head of the Neoplatonic school; Prefect Orestes and half the city seek her counsel. The new bishop Cyril battles the prefect for power — and declares the pagan woman the cause of discord.
level.hypatia.source: Socrates Scholasticus, 'Ecclesiastical History', VII, 15; M. Dzielska, 'Hypatia of Alexandria'
level.hypatia.title: Hypatia
level.hypatius.fact: On January 10, 1775, Yemelyan Pugachev was executed on Bolotnaya Square in Moscow. The rebellion was drowned in blood; Catherine II renamed the Yaik River to the Ural to erase the memory of the revolt.
level.hypatius.goal: The captured impostor is executed on Bolotnaya Square
level.hypatius.hint: First, let Theodora reject mercy and harden the emperor's resolve — and only then will Justinian send the usurper to the block. Without her word, he would pardon him.
level.hypatius.intro: Hypatius is captured. He swears the mob raised him by force — and Justinian is ready to forgive. But Theodora holds a different view.
level.hypatius.title: Pugachev's Execution
level.imola_1502.fact: A patent dated August 18, 1502, ordered all of Cesare's officers to allow passage to 'our most excellent and beloved architect and general engineer Leonardo da Vinci,' to provide him with men, and to heed his advice on fortresses. In Imola, Leonardo drew a city plan, measuring streets with paces and a wheeled odometer — the first accurate 'top-down' rather than 'side-view' city plan in European history (Windsor Collection, RL 12284). Machiavelli arrived in Imola on October 7, 1502, and spent three months with the Duke, sending dispatches almost daily: 'This lord is magnificent and majestic... in his affairs, he knows no rest.' Cesare asked Florence for a condotta and money — the Signoria responded evasively, and the ambassador received no authority for anything. Whether Leonardo and Machiavelli met in Imola, the documents are silent; but in the summer of 1503, they would together attempt to divert the Arno from Pisa.
level.imola_1502.goal: Duke Valentino buys Italy's best engineer, who draws the world's first 'bird's-eye view' city plan — while the Florentine ambassador observes the Duke and writes dispatches from which 'The Prince' will grow.
level.imola_1502.hint: First, the patent: the Duke hires an artist — he is bought and in the retinue. The hired engineer draws Imola — the Duke's fortresses are in order. The ambassador observes the fortified Duke and records. Do not let the Duke buy the ambassador: Florence did not give him a condotta, and Machiavelli remained an observer, not a servant.
level.imola_1502.intro: Autumn 1502. Cesare Borgia has taken Romagna and is in Imola, while his condottieri conspire against him in Magione. In the Duke's retinue is Leonardo da Vinci with a patent as 'architect and general engineer'; the Florentine ambassador Niccolò Machiavelli arrives at the palace with orders to stall for time and promise nothing. Three people who will never again be in the same room.
level.imola_1502.source: N. Machiavelli, 'Legations', dispatches from Imola, October–December 1502; Cesare Borgia's patent of 18.08.1502; W. Isaacson, 'Leonardo da Vinci'
level.imola_1502.title: Imola
level.irene.fact: In 787, Irene convened the Seventh Ecumenical Council in Nicaea, which restored icon veneration; for this, she is revered as a saint in Orthodoxy. Her son Constantine VI deposed her in 790, but restored her two years later; on August 15, 797, by her order, he was seized and blinded — in the Porphyra chamber of the Great Palace, where she herself had given birth to him; the chronicler Theophanes writes that the sun darkened for seventeen days. She ruled alone for five years and signed herself 'Irene, faithful basileus' — in the masculine gender: the law had no word for a woman on the throne. In the West, it was decided that the throne was vacant — and in 800, the Pope crowned Charlemagne emperor; Charlemagne proposed to Irene, but in 802 she was overthrown and exiled to Lesbos, where she spun wool.
level.irene.goal: A regent restores icons, blinds her own son in the room where she bore him, — and is the first woman to be called basileus.
level.irene.hint: First, the Council of Nicaea — the ruler restores icons, is Orthodox and influential. Porphyra chamber: Orthodox mother and son — the son is blinded, she rules alone. The sole ruler takes a masculine title. Charlemagne's proposal — one who spares her son will not be touched and will not remain alone.
level.irene.intro: Irene, an Athenian, is the emperor's widow and regent for her son Constantine VI. She restores the icons that her father-in-law and husband had burned for half a century. Her son grows up and wants to rule himself.
level.irene.source: Theophanes the Confessor, 'Chronographia', sub anno 6289; J. Herrin, 'Women in Purple'
level.irene.title: Basileus Irene
level.isabella.fact: In 1326, Isabella of France and her lover Roger Mortimer landed in Suffolk with mercenaries; Edward II's army scattered. Hugh Despenser the Younger was hanged, castrated, and quartered in Hereford on a fifty-foot gallows; the king abdicated in favor of his son. In September 1327, Edward II died in Berkeley Castle — according to a later legend, a red-hot poker was inserted into him to leave no marks; chroniclers of the time simply speak of murder, and some historians believe he fled to Italy. Three years later, the seventeen-year-old Edward III arrested Mortimer in his mother's bedroom and hanged him; Isabella was sent into honorable confinement — for twenty-eight years.
level.isabella.goal: The queen and her lover overthrow her husband — and the husband dies in Berkeley Castle.
level.isabella.hint: First, love in Paris. Then powerful Mortimer lands and defeats the king. Despenser will be hanged without your intervention — but the king in the castle needs a killer, and that is his enemy.
level.isabella.intro: Edward II gave England to his favorite Despenser, and Queen Isabella to humiliation. Sent as an envoy to Paris, she met the exiled Roger Mortimer there. She will return with him and an army.
level.isabella.title: She-Wolf of France
level.izmail.fact: Potemkin, despairing of the siege of Izmail, handed command to Suvorov in November 1790: 'My hope is in God and your bravery.' Suvorov, in a week, built a replica of the rampart and moat near the camp and trained soldiers for the assault at night. He sent an ultimatum to Commandant Aidozle-Mehmed Pasha: 'A day to reflect – freedom. My first shot – already captivity. Assault – death.' The Pasha replied that the Danube would sooner flow backward and the sky fall to earth. On December 11 (22), at half past five in the morning, nine columns advanced on the walls; by four in the afternoon, the city was taken. Only a handful of the garrison survived, and the Russians lost four thousand killed. Catherine minted a medal 'For Exceptional Bravery,' and Suvorov, who had fallen out with Potemkin, was sent to Finland to build fortifications.
level.izmail.goal: The commander trains soldiers on a replica of the walls, gives the Pasha a day — and takes the impregnable fortress in one night.
level.izmail.hint: First, Potemkin's order — Suvorov gains influence. The training rampart — Suvorov shows strength. A strong commander with influence sends an ultimatum to the Pasha — who replies defiantly. The assault on the stubborn Pasha — the fortress is taken. Lifting the siege is not an option.
level.izmail.intro: A Turkish fortress on the Danube is considered impregnable: a ten-meter rampart, a moat, a thirty-five-thousand-strong garrison. The Russian army has besieged it for months and is suffering from illness. Potemkin hands the fortress over to Suvorov — who arrives and orders a replica of the rampart to be built.
level.izmail.source: A. Petrushevsky, 'Generalissimo Prince Suvorov'; Suvorov's report to Potemkin, 1790
level.izmail.title: Izmail
level.jacobins.fact: The Jacobin Club became the engine of the Revolution. Robespierre and his young comrade Louis de Saint-Just transformed it into a stronghold of radicals, from which the Terror emanated. Saint-Just was dubbed the 'Archangel of Terror.'
level.jacobins.hint: Let Robespierre first ignite into a radical in the debate — and only then shall he infect Saint-Just with radicalism. The Girondin Corday cannot be turned into a Jacobin.
level.jacobins.intro: The Jacobin Club is seething. Robespierre inflames his comrades, while moderate Girondins try to cool him down.
level.jacobins.title: The Jacobin Club
level.jadwiga_axe.fact: Jadwiga was crowned on 16 October 1384. William came to Kraków, but the lords drove him out; according to Długosz, the queen wanted to hack through the gates of Wawel with an axe and was stopped by Vice-Chancellor Dymitr of Goraj. On 14 August 1385 at Krewo, Jagiełło undertook to be baptised, to baptise Lithuania and to join it to the Crown. On 15 February 1386 in Kraków he was baptised with the name Władysław, three days later he married Jadwiga, and on 4 March he was crowned. Thus began the union of Poland and Lithuania and the Jagiellonian dynasty; Lithuania became the last pagan country in Europe to adopt Christianity.
level.jadwiga_axe.goal: The young queen gives up her beloved betrothed and marries a pagan Lithuanian prince — and two countries are joined for four centuries
level.jadwiga_axe.hint: The queen's heart belongs to William, and a secret wedding seems so simple. But then there will be no union and no baptism of Lithuania. First she must say no — and only then summon the Lithuanian.
level.jadwiga_axe.intro: 1384. Poland is ruled by ten-year-old Jadwiga — crowned "king", not queen, because a woman on the throne is not provided for. Since childhood she has been betrothed to the Austrian prince William. The Polish lords are seeking another husband for her: the Grand Duke of Lithuania, Jogaila, a pagan whose country is vast and surrounded by enemies.
level.jadwiga_axe.source: Jan Długosz, Annals, X; Act of Krewo (1385)
level.jadwiga_axe.title: Jadwiga and Jagiełło
level.jane_grey.fact: In July 1553, the Duke of Northumberland proclaimed Lady Jane Grey — his daughter-in-law — as Queen. But the people and nobility rallied behind Henry VIII's daughter, Mary; nine days later, Jane was deposed. Northumberland was executed immediately; sixteen-year-old Jane, in February 1554. Mary I ascended the throne.
level.jane_grey.goal: Northumberland's puppet is overthrown by Mary — and Jane ascends the scaffold
level.jane_grey.hint: An influential patron proclaims the girl queen. Nine days later, Mary condemns her with a speech — and the condemned is executed.
level.jane_grey.intro: Edward VI is dead. The Duke of Northumberland places his daughter-in-law, Jane Grey, on the throne — bypassing the rightful Mary.
level.jane_grey.title: The Nine Days' Queen
level.jane_seymour.fact: On May 19, 1536, Anne Boleyn was beheaded at the Tower; just 11 days later, Henry VIII married Jane Seymour. In October 1537, she gave birth to the long-awaited son — the future Edward VI — and died twelve days later of puerperal fever. Jane was the only wife Henry mourned.
level.jane_seymour.goal: After executing Boleyn, Henry marries Jane — she bears an heir and dies.
level.jane_seymour.hint: The condemned queen is executed first — otherwise the wedding will not take place. The new queen will bear an heir, and childbed fever will claim her.
level.jane_seymour.intro: Anne Boleyn is condemned. Henry already gazes upon Jane Seymour — but the path to a new wedding lies through the executioner's block.
level.jane_seymour.title: Jane Seymour
level.january_1863.fact: The January Uprising began on 22 January 1863. The National Government operated underground: press, taxes, post, its own courts and police — and almost no one knew who belonged to it. On 2 March 1864, by decree of Alexander II, the peasants of the Kingdom of Poland received their land as property on more favourable terms than in Russia — largely to turn them away from the uprising. Traugutt was arrested in April 1864 and executed on 5 August on the slopes of the Warsaw Citadel together with four members of the government. Thousands of participants were exiled to Siberia.
level.january_1863.goal: The insurgents create an underground state with taxes and a postal service — and the emperor responds by giving the peasants land
level.january_1863.hint: In open battle against the empire's army they cannot hold out. The state is built in secret: first the government, then everything else. The emperor answers with more than troops.
level.january_1863.intro: 1863. An uprising begins in the Kingdom of Poland — a guerrilla war in the forests, without an army or fortresses. To hold out, the insurgents need an invisible state. In the autumn it is headed by a former officer, Romuald Traugutt.
level.january_1863.source: Documents of the National Government, 1863–1864; decree of 2 March 1864
level.january_1863.title: The Secret State
level.jasna_gora_1655.fact: From 18 November to 27 December 1655 some three thousand Swedes besieged Jasna Góra, defended by about seventy monks and a couple of hundred soldiers and nobles under Prior Augustyn Kordecki; the monastery held out. News of the defence spread across the country and helped raise an uprising against the Swedes. On 1 April 1656 in Lwów, John Casimir proclaimed the Mother of God Queen of Poland and promised to ease the lot of the peasants — a promise that was never kept. Henryk Sienkiewicz made the siege the centrepiece of his novel The Deluge, adding the fictional Kmicic, who blew up a Swedish cannon.
level.jasna_gora_1655.goal: A monastery defended by monks and a handful of nobles beats off the Swedes — and the whole country rises against the invaders
level.jasna_gora_1655.hint: The general will offer an honourable surrender; the prior did not yield. The king cannot take vows from Silesia — first he must return. And he took the vow once the monastery had already held out.
level.jasna_gora_1655.intro: 1655, the Deluge. The Swedish army has occupied almost the entire Commonwealth, magnates are going over to the Swedish king, and John Casimir has fled to Silesia. The Swedish general Burchard Müller approaches the Pauline monastery on Jasna Góra in Częstochowa — a shrine holding an icon of the Mother of God.
level.jasna_gora_1655.source: A. Kordecki, Nova Gigantomachia (1658); Samuel Pufendorf, On the Deeds of Charles Gustav
level.jasna_gora_1655.title: Jasna Góra
level.jena.fact: On October 14, 1806, at Jena and Auerstedt, Napoleon and Davout crushed the Prussian army — within a week, Prussia ceased to exist as a military power; Blücher was the last to surrender at Lübeck, writing in his capitulation: 'for want of bread and cartridges.' On November 21 in Berlin, Napoleon signed the decree on the Continental Blockade — prohibiting all of Europe from trading with Britain. The blockade hit France harder than England, and it was precisely because of it that he would march on Russia six years later.
level.jena.goal: The Prussian army vanishes in a day, and from Berlin, Napoleon closes Europe to England
level.jena.hint: The Grand Army — preparation. Then mighty Prussia is crushed at Jena in a day. And from conquered Berlin — a decree: the continent is forbidden to trade with the English.
level.jena.intro: Frederick the Great's Prussia declared war — with an army unchanged for half a century. Napoleon leads the Grand Army through Thuringia; Blücher, a desperate hussar, commands the Prussian rearguard.
level.jena.source: Bulletins of the Grand Army, 1806; C. Clausewitz, 'The Year 1806'
level.jena.title: Jena
level.joan_reims.fact: In May 1429, Joan of Arc lifted the Siege of Orléans in nine days, and on July 17, she stood with her banner in Reims Cathedral, where the Dauphin was anointed as Charles VII — a legitimacy no victory could bestow. In September, she marched on Paris without the king's support, was wounded by an arrow in the thigh at the Porte Saint-Honoré, and repelled; the court deemed her task complete. A year later, the Burgundians captured her near Compiègne — and Charles VII, crowned by her, paid not a sou for her. What happened next, you saw in Rouen.
level.joan_reims.goal: The Maid lifts the siege and makes the Dauphin king — and she must go no further.
level.joan_reims.hint: First, victory at Orléans — with it, the Maid gains the authority to vouch for the Dauphin. Then, the coronation in Reims. Do not march on Paris: there she will be defeated, and a defeated Maid would crown no one.
level.joan_reims.intro: Dauphin Charles sits in Chinon, doubting even his own birth. Orléans has been besieged by the English for seven months. A peasant girl is brought to the Dauphin, claiming voices have commanded her to lift the siege and crown him in Reims.
level.joan_reims.source: Rehabilitation Protocols of 1456; "Journal of the Siege of Orléans"
level.joan_reims.title: The Road to Reims
level.joan_stake.fact: In May 1429, Joan of Arc lifted the seven-month siege of Orléans in nine days. In May 1430, the Burgundians captured her near Compiègne and sold her to the English for ten thousand livres; the French King Charles VII, whom she had crowned, offered not a sou for her. An ecclesiastical court presided over by Bishop Pierre Cauchon — a scholar, Anglophile, and ambitious man — condemned her for heresy and wearing men's clothing; on May 30, 1431, she was burned at the stake in the Old Market in Rouen, at the age of nineteen. Her ashes were thrown into the Seine. Twenty-five years later, the same ecclesiastical court annulled the verdict, and five hundred years later, declared her a saint.
level.joan_stake.goal: The victor over the English is tried as a heretic — and burned by those she defeated.
level.joan_stake.hint: First, her victory at Orléans — Bedford is defeated. Then the ecclesiastical court: the bishop, with authority, condemns her with a speech. The regent executes the condemned. No one will come to ransom her.
level.joan_stake.intro: A peasant girl in armor lifted the siege of Orléans and crowned the Dauphin in Reims. A year later, the Burgundians captured her and sold her to the English. The Duke of Bedford, Regent of France, wants not an execution — he wants a trial that will declare her a witch.
level.joan_stake.source: Trial records of 1431; Rehabilitation records of 1456
level.joan_stake.title: The Pyre in Rouen
level.john_fall.fact: Theodora and her friend Antonina, Belisarius's wife, used intrigue to lure John of Cappadocia into a fabricated conspiracy against the emperor. Exposed, the all-powerful minister fell and was sent into exile.
level.john_fall.goal: Theodora and Antonina ruin the hated minister
level.john_fall.hint: Let Antonina first lull John's vigilance with false friendship — and only then lure him into a nocturnal trap. Tribonian is not her target.
level.john_fall.intro: Theodora yearns for the downfall of John the Cappadocian. Her confidante Antonina, Belisarius's wife, weaves a snare — with feigned friendship.
level.john_fall.title: Trap for John
level.juan.fact: Alexander VI openly preferred his younger son Juan, making him Gonfalonier of the Church and a Duke. This ignited a burning envy in his elder brother, Cesare.
level.juan.goal: The Pope showers Cesare's brother, Juan, with favors
level.juan.hint: The favor goes not to the cardinal, but to his brother.
level.juan.intro: Alexander VI is on the throne and showers his favorite son with favors.
level.juan.source: History of the House of Borgia
level.juan.title: The Favorite Son
level.julius.fact: In 1503, Giuliano della Rovere became Pope Julius II, a long-standing enemy of the Borgias. The 'Warrior Pope' and patron of Michelangelo, he aimed to destroy everything Cesare had created.
level.julius.goal: The sworn enemy of the Borgias ascends to the throne
level.julius.hint: Let della Rovere first unite the enemies of the Borgia — and only having risen will he take the throne as Julius II. Cesare is a Borgia; he will not see the tiara.
level.julius.intro: Alexander VI is dead. The sworn enemy of the Borgia, della Rovere, sees his hour — but Cesare is still strong in the conclave.
level.julius.source: History of the Pontificate of Julius II
level.julius.title: Julius II
level.kazan.fact: On October 2, 1552, Ivan the Terrible's troops captured Kazan, annexing the Kazan Khanate to the Russian Tsardom. This opened the way to the east and to the conquest of Astrakhan and Siberia.
level.kazan.goal: The Tsar conquers the Kazan Khanate
level.kazan.hint: First, the tsar must be crowned in the cathedral — and only the reigning Ivan will conquer Kazan. Boyar Shuisky will not lead the troops.
