level.necklace.fact: In 1785, Countess de La Motte arranged a nocturnal rendezvous for Cardinal de Rohan in the groves of Versailles with a prostitute disguised as Marie Antoinette, and in the Queen's name, obtained through him a necklace worth 1.6 million livres, which her husband sold off stone by stone in London. The Queen, knowing nothing, demanded a public trial; Parliament acquitted Rohan — and Paris applauded, while the Queen was booed: everyone believed she had wanted the necklace. La Motte was branded and imprisoned in the Salpêtrière, she escaped and wrote memoirs. Napoleon believed that "the Queen's death began with the affair of the necklace."
level.necklace.goal: The Cardinal is fooled by a fake queen — but the real one pays with her reputation.
level.necklace.hint: At night in the Grove of Venus, the Cardinal will be deceived by a "queen." He will buy the necklace through the adventuress. The Queen, with her authority, demands a trial — and the Cardinal is condemned; but no one will believe her denials: she will not yield, yet the scandal will remain.
level.necklace.intro: Cardinal de Rohan is out of favor with the Queen and dreams of regaining her good graces. The adventuress La Motte convinces him: the Queen desires a necklace worth one million six hundred thousand livres, but secretly — let the Cardinal buy it for her on credit.
level.necklace.source: J. Michelet; F. Mossiker, "The Queen's Necklace"
level.necklace.title: The Queen's Necklace
level.nepotism.fact: At 18, Cesare Borgia became a cardinal by his father-Pope's will—a blatant example of nepotism. He hated his ecclesiastical career, dreaming of a sword, not a cassock.
level.nepotism.goal: The Pope elevates his young son to cardinal
level.nepotism.hint: First the throne, then the Pope bestows the cardinal's hat upon his son.
level.nepotism.title: Cardinal at Eighteen
level.nero_fire.fact: In July 64 AD, a fire completely destroyed three districts of Rome and damaged seven more. Nero, according to Tacitus, was in Antium and returned to fight the fire, but the rumor that he sang of the fall of Troy while watching the blaze proved more persistent than the facts. To quell the rumors, Christians were declared guilty — the first state persecution of this community in history. On the site of the burnt-out quarters rose the Golden House with a lake and a thirty-meter statue of its owner; upon moving in, Nero, according to Suetonius, said that he would finally live like a human being.
level.nero_fire.goal: The rumor of the arsonist fades, and a palace rises from the ashes.
level.nero_fire.hint: Suspicion is removed from oneself by pointing to others — and only after that can the burnt-out quarters be occupied for construction. But singing about burning Troy while watching the blaze is not advisable: that will never be forgotten.
level.nero_fire.intro: Rome has been burning for six days. Whispers spread through the city that the emperor himself set the fire — his palace has long felt too small for him. Beside him is Tigellinus, the Praetorian Prefect, ready for anything, and Senator Thrasea Paetus, who silently remembers everything.
level.nero_fire.title: The Fire of Rome
level.new_rome.fact: On September 18, 324, at Chrysopolis, opposite Byzantium, Constantine defeated Licinius; who surrendered under a promise of clemency given by Constantine's sister, but was strangled a year later 'for conspiracy'. The emperor sought a capital in the East — he considered Troy and Serdica ('Serdica is my Rome'), but chose Byzantium on a promontory between the Sea of Marmara and the Golden Horn. The city was built for six years and on May 11, 330, was consecrated with forty days of festivities as New Rome; the name Constantinople became established on its own. Statues were brought from across the empire — including the Serpent Column from Delphi, which still stands in the Hippodrome. The city remained the capital for 1123 years.
level.new_rome.goal: An emperor defeats his co-ruler, chooses a town on the Bosphorus — and on May 11, 330, consecrates New Rome.
level.new_rome.hint: First, Chrysopolis — a powerful emperor defeats Licinius. The victor chooses a site — Byzantium, founder. The founder consecrates the city — capital. No need to spare the rival: one who spares will not seek a capital.
level.new_rome.intro: Constantine defeated Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge, but the empire is still divided with Licinius, ruler of the East. Ahead lies the final war — and the choice of a new capital for the Christian empire.
level.new_rome.title: New Rome
level.nicaea_return.fact: On the night of 25 July 1261 the detachment of the caesar Alexios Strategopoulos — about eight hundred men, mostly Cumans — stood outside Constantinople. Local people, the 'thelematarioi' who lived outside the walls and served the Latins, reported that the whole garrison and the Venetian fleet had gone off to ravage the island of Daphnousia in the Black Sea, and showed them an underground passage beneath the wall. A small party got inside, cut down the guard at the Gate of the Spring and opened it. By morning the city was in the hands of the Nicaeans; the Latin emperor Baldwin II fled to a Venetian ship, leaving his crown and sceptre behind in the palace — they were later pawned in Venice. Michael VIII was asleep in camp in Asia Minor, and his sister woke him with the words that he was master of Constantinople; he did not believe her until the abandoned regalia were brought to him. On 15 August 1261 he entered the Golden Gate on foot, with the icon of the Virgin Hodegetria carried before him. The empire lived another hundred and ninety-two years after that.
level.nicaea_return.goal: Eight hundred men take the capital of the world without a fight — because the garrison had sailed away and a passage was found under the wall
level.nicaea_return.hint: First Daphnousia: the garrison and the fleet sail off, the Latin is left alone, and the man from Nicaea learns of it. The one who knows goes in at night through the passage. The one who is inside raises the empty city, and the Latin flees. And only then does the basileus enter the Golden Gate. The Venetian fleet is a battle: a man beaten in battle will not go crawling through a tunnel.
level.nicaea_return.intro: For fifty-seven years Constantinople has belonged to the Latins. The empire in exile sits at Nicaea gathering strength; its basileus Michael Palaiologos is preparing a great war. And the caesar Strategopoulos is marching past with a detachment of eight hundred men, on his way to Selymbria — simply to scout the district.
level.nicaea_return.source: George Akropolites, 'History'; George Pachymeres, 'On Michael and Andronikos Palaiologos'
level.nicaea_return.title: The Empty City
level.nika.fact: In January 532 AD, the circus factions of the 'Blues' and 'Greens,' usually hostile, united with the cry 'Nika!' ('Conquer!'). Half the city burned; the mob, against its will, proclaimed the noble Hypatius, nephew of the former emperor, as their ruler.
level.nika.goal: The Rebellious Mob Proclaims Hypatius Emperor
level.nika.hint: Let the fury against the corrupt John ignite the rebellion — and then the already incensed mob will proclaim Hypatius. Germanus is noble, but the crowd did not raise him.
level.nika.intro: January 532 AD. The Blues and Greens, eternal rivals, united against the levies of the hated John. The mob demands an emperor in place of Justinian.
level.nika.title: The Nika Revolt
level.november_11_1918.fact: On 10 November 1918 Piłsudski arrived in Warsaw by train. On 11 November — the day of the armistice on the Western Front — the Regency Council handed him supreme command of the army, and on 14 November it dissolved itself, handing over all power. German garrisons were disarmed by units of the Polish Military Organisation and volunteers, but mostly without a fight: the garrison's soldiers' council agreed to go home. Thus, after 123 years, Poland returned to the map; 11 November is Independence Day. Ahead lay years of wars over the borders — but that is another story.
level.november_11_1918.goal: The prisoner of Magdeburg returns to Warsaw, the Regency Council hands him power — and the German garrison leaves almost without a shot
level.november_11_1918.hint: He can only take command once he has returned. Power is not seized by storm — it is handed over. And the Germans are not stormed: they are disarmed and go home.
level.november_11_1918.intro: November 1918. Germany is losing the war, and there is revolution in Berlin. Warsaw is governed by the Regency Council, created by the Germans, and a German garrison is stationed in the city. In Magdeburg, Piłsudski is being released.
level.november_11_1918.source: Documents of the Regency Council, November 1918; Andrzej Garlicki, Józef Piłsudski
level.november_11_1918.title: 11 November
level.oath.fact: On June 20, 1789, deputies of the Third Estate, locked out of their assembly hall, gathered in the Royal Tennis Court and swore not to disperse until they had given France a constitution. The 'Tennis Court Oath' became the first act of the Revolution.
level.oath.goal: Deputies unite into a revolutionary bloc
level.oath.hint: Let the royal lockout in the hall embitter the deputy — and only then shall the unyielding swear in the tennis court not to disperse. The King will not take the oath.
level.oath.intro: June 1789. The King locks the assembly hall before the deputies of the Third Estate. But they cannot be broken so easily.
level.oath.title: Oath of the Third Estate
level.oath_crisis_1917.fact: On 6 August 1914 the First Cadre Company marched out of Kraków. In July 1917 most of the legionnaires of the First and Third Brigades, following Piłsudski, refused to take the oath; on 22 July Governor-General Hans von Beseler ordered Piłsudski's arrest, and he spent more than a year in the fortress of Magdeburg. The arrest made him, in the eyes of Poles, a symbol of independence — one who had served none of the powers.
level.oath_crisis_1917.goal: The commander of the legions refuses to swear allegiance to the German emperor — and, as the prisoner of Magdeburg, becomes a hero
level.oath_crisis_1917.hint: First he needs the legions. Had he sworn, he would have become an officer of a foreign army — instead he became a prisoner.
level.oath_crisis_1917.intro: The First World War. In 1914 Józef Piłsudski led the First Cadre Company out of Kraków and created the Polish Legions, fighting on the side of Austria and Germany against Russia. In 1916 Germany and Austria proclaimed a "Kingdom of Poland" — without a king or borders. Now the legionnaires must swear an oath of "brotherhood in arms" with the armies of the Central Powers.
level.oath_crisis_1917.source: Documents of the 1917 Oath Crisis; J. Piłsudski, My First Battles
level.oath_crisis_1917.title: The Oath Crisis
level.odnowiciel_1039.fact: In 1038 or 1039 Bretislav sacked Gniezno and Poznań and carried off the relics of Saint Adalbert to Prague — Gniezno never recovered. In 1039 Casimir returned with a force that Gallus Anonymus puts at five hundred knights — help was provided by Emperor Henry III. The duke made Kraków, which had barely been touched by the devastation, the centre of the country — Kraków remained the capital until 1596. Casimir recovered Silesia only in 1050, and peace with Bohemia was concluded in 1054 through the emperor's mediation, in exchange for an annual tribute. The nickname "the Restorer" — Odnowiciel — was given to him by later historians.
level.odnowiciel_1039.goal: An exiled duke returns with knights obtained by his mother — and restores the country, making Kraków its capital
level.odnowiciel_1039.hint: Without help from abroad there is nothing to return with. Once back, don't rush to win back Silesia: first the country must be raised from the ruins, and a war with Bohemia now would lose even what remains.
level.odnowiciel_1039.intro: The 1030s. After the death of Mieszko II the Piast state collapsed: the pagans revolted, the nobles scattered, and the young Casimir was driven out. His mother Richeza, a niece of Emperor Otto III, lives in Germany. And the Bohemian duke Bretislav sees that Poland is defenceless.
level.odnowiciel_1039.source: Gallus Anonymus, I, 19; Cosmas of Prague, II, 2–5
level.odnowiciel_1039.title: Casimir the Restorer
level.olszynka_1831.fact: On 25 February 1831 at Olszynka Grochowska, Polish troops under General Chłopicki, who was severely wounded in the battle, held the grove all day, and Diebitsch abandoned the assault on Warsaw — the war lasted another half year. In September, during the storming of Warsaw, Redoubt No. 54 at Wola fell; Adam Mickiewicz wrote the ballad "Ordon's Redoubt", in which the artilleryman Julian Ordon blows it up together with himself. In reality Ordon survived, emigrated and died in 1887 — it is said that he read the ballad about his own death himself.
level.olszynka_1831.goal: The Polish army holds an alder grove outside Warsaw all day, and the artilleryman Ordon becomes a legend of the defence
level.olszynka_1831.hint: In the open field the field marshal's army is stronger — hold on to the grove. And Ordon's redoubt stands to the end, whatever was said about it later.
level.olszynka_1831.intro: February 1831. Field Marshal Diebitsch's army is marching on Warsaw to end the war with a single blow. Before the capital, near Grochów, there is an alder grove — Olszynka.
level.olszynka_1831.source: Adam Mickiewicz, Ordon's Redoubt (1832); Ignacy Prądzyński, Memoirs
level.olszynka_1831.title: Olszynka and Ordon's Redoubt
level.oprichnina.fact: In 1565, Ivan the Terrible established the Oprichnina – a special domain with a personal army. The Oprichniki, led by Malyuta Skuratov, sowed terror; the Novgorod massacre of 1570 claimed thousands of lives.
level.oprichnina.goal: The Tsar introduces the Oprichnina and unleashes terror.
level.oprichnina.hint: Let boyar treason in the Duma embitter the tsar — and only the loyal Ivan with Malyuta will establish the oprichnina. Shuisky is not fit to be an oprichnik.
level.oprichnina.intro: The boyars are plotting sedition, and Ivan sees treason everywhere. He needs an instrument of reprisal — and his loyal hound Malyuta.
level.oprichnina.title: The Oprichnina
level.paderewski_1918.fact: Paderewski gave hundreds of concerts and speeches in America for Poland's cause and became friends with Colonel Edward House, Wilson's closest adviser. On 8 January 1918, in Wilson's Fourteen Points, the thirteenth stated that an independent Polish state should be created with free and secure access to the sea. In 1919 Paderewski became prime minister and signed the Treaty of Versailles.
level.paderewski_1918.goal: A famous pianist, through his concerts and his friendship with the president's adviser, gets an independent Poland written into the peace programme
level.paderewski_1918.hint: Without fame no one would have listened to him. You don't go to the president directly, but through someone he trusts. And demanding borders right away would spoil everything.
level.paderewski_1918.intro: 1915–1917. Ignacy Paderewski is the most famous pianist in the world. He tours America giving concerts, raising money for starving Poland, and in every appearance speaks of Polish independence. President Woodrow Wilson is preparing a programme for the post-war peace.
level.paderewski_1918.source: W. Wilson, Fourteen Points (1918); diary of E. House
level.paderewski_1918.title: The Thirteenth Point
level.paris_mass.fact: On July 25, 1593, Henry IV converted to Catholicism at the Abbey of Saint-Denis — the phrase "Paris is worth a mass" was attributed to him later, but he uttered something to that effect. In March 1594, Paris opened its gates, and in 1595, the Pope lifted his excommunication. In 1598, the Edict of Nantes, for the first time in Europe, granted Protestants freedom of worship and fortified cities. On May 14, 1610, when his carriage got stuck on Rue de la Ferronnerie, the Catholic fanatic Ravaillac jumped onto the footboard and stabbed the king. Ravaillac was quartered; Henry remained France's most beloved king — "a chicken in every peasant's pot on Sundays."
level.paris_mass.goal: The Huguenot changes faith for the capital, grants freedom of worship — and perishes by a fanatic's knife.
level.paris_mass.hint: Starving Paris can last forever. A mass at Saint-Denis — and he is king with authority; the Pope will yield, the Edict of Nantes will grant Huguenots freedom. But on Rue de la Ferronnerie, an enemy with a knife awaits him.
level.paris_mass.intro: Henry of Navarre is the rightful King of France, but a Huguenot, and Paris has kept him outside its gates for four years. The Pope has excommunicated him. He can starve the city for another ten years — or attend mass.
level.paris_mass.title: Paris is Worth a Mass
level.parr.fact: Catherine Parr, the sixth wife, sympathized with Protestants; conservative enemies at court obtained a warrant for her arrest on charges of heresy. Upon learning of this, she humbly confessed to the King, stating that she had only argued to distract him from his pains. Henry forgave her. She outlived the King (d. 1547) — she 'survived'.
level.parr.goal: Enemies weave a net — but the Queen will survive
level.parr.hint: Marriage, Norfolk's accusation — and a private conversation: this queen has influence, and the King will yield. She will not go to the Tower.
level.parr.intro: The sixth wife, Catherine Parr, is too clever and too Protestant. The Duke of Norfolk obtained an arrest warrant for her from the ailing King — for disputes over faith.
level.parr.title: Catherine Parr
level.paul_murder.fact: On the night of March 12 (24), 1801, conspirators led by Bennigsen and the Zubov brothers entered the bedroom of Paul I in the newly built Mikhailovsky Castle; the emperor hid behind a screen, was overthrown, struck on the temple with a golden snuffbox, and strangled with a scarf. The organizer — Governor-General Pahlen — prudently arrived late. The heir Alexander knew about the conspiracy but had been given his word that his father would not be harmed; upon learning of the death, he burst into tears, and Pahlen said: 'Stop acting like a child, go and reign.' Officially, an 'apoplectic stroke' was announced; in St. Petersburg, people joked — 'a snuffbox to the temple.' Alexander suffered from guilt his entire life; contrary to tradition, Paul was hardly mentioned at court even after his death.
level.paul_murder.goal: Pahlen sends the guard to the Emperor's bedroom, and the heir, knowing everything, takes the oath the next morning.
level.paul_murder.hint: First, Pahlen's conspiracy with the heir — Alexander is involved. Pahlen sends the guard to the bedroom — the Emperor is dead. The heir, who participated in the conspiracy, takes the oath administered by Pahlen. Go to Gatchina — the throne will go to another.
level.paul_murder.intro: Paul I has ruled for four years and managed to turn everyone against him: the Guard is exiled to Siberia for the wrong collar. The military governor of St. Petersburg, Count Pahlen, weaves a conspiracy — and receives the silent consent of the heir Alexander. The Emperor moves into a new castle with moats and drawbridges.
level.paul_murder.source: N. Eidelman, 'The Edge of Centuries'; memoirs of Bennigsen and Sablukov
level.paul_murder.title: Mikhailovsky Castle
level.pavia.fact: The battle of Pavia was fought on 24 February 1525 — Charles V's birthday. In the night the imperials broke through the wall of the park of Mirabello; the French heavy cavalry charged so fast that it masked its own artillery, and fifteen hundred Spanish arquebusiers shot the knights down at point-blank range from a copse. France lost about ten thousand men, among them La Palice and Bonnivet; King Francis I fought on foot and gave himself up. From captivity he wrote to his mother, Louise of Savoy: 'of everything, nothing is left me but honour and my life, which is safe' — the phrase went round as 'All is lost save honour'. He spent a year in Madrid, signed a treaty in January 1526 that surrendered Burgundy, and went free in exchange for his two small sons, who spent four years in Spain — and at once declared the treaty void as signed under duress. Louise of Savoy governed France as regent, concluded the Ladies' Peace of 1529 and opened negotiations with Sultan Suleiman.
level.pavia.goal: The knightly charge masks its own guns, the arquebusiers take the king alive — and he writes to his mother that only honour is left
level.pavia.hint: First the breach in the park wall — the imperials are strong. Against that strength the king leads his gendarmes in a charge and masks his own guns with them — now he is out in the open. The arquebusiers fire on the exposed king and take him alive. The prisoner has nothing left but to write a letter to his mother. The road to Milan is a trap: a king who has ridden away will lead no charge.
level.pavia.intro: For four months the French army has stood before Pavia, and the king is certain: the town will fall, Milan will be his. In the night the imperials break down the wall of the hunting park of Mirabello and come out right at the French camp. They have fifteen hundred arquebuses — a weapon the world of chivalry holds to be base.
level.pavia.source: Francis I's letter to Louise of Savoy (1525); J. Jacquart, 'Francis I'
level.pavia.title: All Is Lost Save Honour
level.pazzi.fact: On April 26, 1478, during Sunday Mass in Santa Maria del Fiore Cathedral, at the signal — the bell at the Elevation of the Host — Francesco de' Pazzi and Bernardo Baroncelli inflicted nineteen wounds upon Giuliano de' Medici; Lorenzo, wounded in the neck, fought them off and locked himself in the sacristy. Sixtus IV had previously told the conspirators: 'I do not desire anyone's death, but I do desire a change of government.' Florence did not rise — the crowd shouted 'Palle! Palle!', the balls of the Medici coat of arms; Archbishop Salviati and Francesco de' Pazzi were hanged the same day from the windows of Palazzo Vecchio; Botticelli painted the hanged men on the wall. Baroncelli fled to Constantinople — the Sultan extradited him, and Leonardo sketched him in the noose. The Pope excommunicated Lorenzo and declared war; Lorenzo traveled alone to Naples to the Pope's ally and persuaded him to make peace.
level.pazzi.goal: With papal blessing, brothers are cut down at Mass — one is killed, the other escapes, and the mob hangs the conspirators from windows.
level.pazzi.hint: First, Sixtus's blessing — the conspirator is in. Mass in the Duomo: conspirator and younger brother — Giuliano is dead, the conspirator is condemned. Lorenzo with authority executes the condemned — 'Palle!'. Give the Pazzi credit — a bribed man will not conspire.
level.pazzi.intro: Florence is ruled by the Medici brothers — Lorenzo and Giuliano. The Pazzi bankers, with the support of Pope Sixtus IV, from whom the Medici had taken profitable business, decide to kill both — in the cathedral, during Mass, when everyone is kneeling.
level.pazzi.source: A. Poliziano, 'Commentary on the Pazzi Conspiracy'; L. Martinez, 'April Blood'
level.pazzi.title: The Pazzi Conspiracy
level.petersburg.fact: On May 1, 1703, after a week-long siege, the Swedish fortress of Nyenschanz at the mouth of the Neva surrendered. On May 16 (27), the Peter and Paul Fortress was laid on Zayachy Island — this day is considered the birthday of St. Petersburg; Peter himself was likely elsewhere on that day. Up to forty thousand laborers were driven to the construction site each year from all over the country; they lived in dugouts and died by the thousands from disease and hunger — hence the 'city on bones.' In 1714, the Tsar forbade stone construction everywhere except St. Petersburg, and every incoming cart had to bring stones. From 1712, the court moved here — the capital stood on the very edge of the country, 'cutting a window into Europe,' as Pushkin would later say, quoting Algarotti.
level.petersburg.goal: The Tsar takes the mouth of the Neva, lays a fortress on a swampy island — and makes it the capital.
level.petersburg.hint: First, the Swedish fortress on the Neva — the mighty Tsar defeats the Swedes, whose king has gone to Poland. The victor lays the foundation for a fortress on Hare Island — the founder. Then he gathers laborers — a city built on bones becomes the capital. Return to Moscow — leave the island to the gulls.
level.petersburg.intro: Charles is bogged down in Poland, and the new Russian army reaches the Neva. At its mouth is the Swedish fortress Nyenschanz, beyond it — a swamp, seagulls, and the sea. The Tsar needs not a city, but an outlet.
level.petersburg.source: 'Journal of Peter the Great'; E. Anisimov, 'The Young City'
level.petersburg.title: Window to Europe
level.pharsalus.fact: On August 9, 48 BC, at Pharsalus, Pompey had twice as much infantry and four times as much cavalry. Caesar hid a fourth line of cohorts against the cavalry wing and ordered his men to strike the young nobles in the face with pila — they could not endure it and fled, exposing their flank. The victors found tents adorned with myrtle and tables set for a feast in Pompey's camp: they had considered the outcome decided in advance. Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was killed.
level.pharsalus.hint: Pompey has more troops, and he cannot be taken head-on. Let tables be set for a feast in his camp — one who celebrates prematurely loses formation. But one's own must be arrayed.
level.pharsalus.intro: Year after year, Caesar pursued Pompey through Italy and Greece. At Pharsalus, the rival has twice as much infantry — and complete confidence in victory.
level.pharsalus.source: Caesar, Commentaries on the Civil War, III; Plutarch, Pompey
level.pharsalus.title: Pharsalus
level.philip.fact: On March 22, 1568, in the Dormition Cathedral, Metropolitan Philip refused Ivan IV his blessing: 'In this guise, in this strange attire, I do not recognize the Orthodox Tsar.' The Tsar convened an obedient council, and false witnesses from the Solovetsky monks accused Philip of a 'vicious life'; in November, Oprichniki burst into the cathedral during a service, stripped him of his vestments, and took him away on a sled. A year later, on December 23, 1569, Malyuta Skuratov arrived at the Otroch Monastery in Tver, ostensibly for a blessing for the Novgorod campaign, and strangled the prisoner with a pillow; the abbot was told that he 'died from carbon monoxide poisoning.' The Church canonized Philip in 1652, and Tsar Alexis Mikhailovich repented before his relics for his great-grandfather.
level.philip.goal: The Tsar breaks the only one who dares to denounce him: trial, deposition — and a pillow in a monastic cell.
level.philip.hint: First, the Metropolitan publicly refuses the Tsar his blessing — now the Tsar is his enemy. The Tsar, with his authority, judges him by a council court — condemned. The condemned prisoner in the monastery is strangled by an Oprichnik. Solovki is a path to nowhere: one who has left cannot be condemned.
level.philip.intro: The Oprichnina has been cutting down boyar families for a second year. Metropolitan Philip Kolychev of Moscow is the only one who speaks to the Tsar's face. In the Dormition Cathedral, before the people, the Tsar, in Oprichnik attire, approaches for a blessing.
level.philip.source: Life of Metropolitan Philip; R. Skrynnikov, 'Ivan the Terrible'
level.philip.title: Metropolitan Philip
level.philippi.fact: In October 42 BC, two battles were fought at Philippi. In the first, Brutus crushed Octavian's wing (Octavian himself, ill, was hiding in the swamps), but Cassius on his wing was repulsed and, mistaking a cloud of dust for a general rout, ordered his freedman to stab him — unaware that his comrade was winning. Three weeks later, Brutus lost the second battle and fell on his sword. According to Plutarch, the shadow of Caesar appeared in his tent the night before, saying, 'We shall meet again at Philippi.'
level.philippi.goal: Both assassins perish at Philippi, and Antony becomes the avenger.
level.philippi.hint: Caesar's heir lies in a fever — he does not lead the battles. Philippi is two battles: in the first, they defeat the one who will later be told that all is lost, and he will take his own life; in the second, they finish off the last.
level.philippi.intro: Caesar's assassins gathered an army in Macedonia. Antony and Caesar's heir crossed the sea to put an end to them.
level.philippi.title: Philippi
level.phocas.fact: In the autumn of 602 Maurice ordered the army to winter beyond the Danube; the troops mutinied and proclaimed the centurion Phocas emperor. Maurice fled across the Bosphorus, was seized and executed at Chalcedon on 27 November: five of his sons were killed before his eyes, and at each execution he repeated 'Just art Thou, O Lord, and righteous are Thy judgements.' Phocas's eight years of rule meant terror, the loss of the Balkans and catastrophe on the Persian front: Khosrow II opened a war 'to avenge Maurice' and reached Chalcedon. In 610 Heraclius, son of the exarch of Africa, brought a fleet from Carthage with an icon of the Virgin on the mast; the city opened its harbour. According to the chronicler, Heraclius asked the bound Phocas, 'Is this how you have ruled the empire?' and heard in reply, 'And will you rule it better?' Phocas was executed and hacked to pieces, and Heraclius was crowned on 5 October 610; he would reign for thirty-one years.
level.phocas.goal: The army raises a centurion on its shields, a dynasty dies on a jetty — and eight years later a fleet arrives from Carthage
level.phocas.hint: First the wintering: the army raises the centurion, and the emperor is deposed. The man proclaimed finishes off the deposed one on the jetty — and from that day he is hated. It is the hated crowned man whom the newcomer from Africa brings down. The Persian frontier is preparation: the army will not raise anyone on its shields while the emperor is strong.
level.phocas.intro: The emperor Maurice campaigned for twenty years and counted every coin: he refused to ransom twelve thousand prisoners from the Avars — they were slaughtered — and in the autumn he ordered his exhausted army to winter not at home but beyond the Danube, in enemy country. In the camp there is a centurion named Phocas, a loudmouth with a scarred face.
level.phocas.source: Theophylact Simocatta, 'History', VIII; Theophanes the Confessor, 'Chronographia'
level.phocas.title: The Centurion
level.phokas.fact: On the night of December 11, 969, John Tzimiskes and his accomplices approached the Boukoleon Palace by boat; Theophano, the empress, left the bedroom window open, and the conspirators were pulled in by basket. The emperor was found sleeping on the floor on a leopard skin; he was kicked, Tzimiskes knocked out his teeth with the hilt of his sword, then they killed him. Patriarch Polyeuctus did not allow the murderer into Hagia Sophia until he exiled Theophano, revoked Nikephoros's decree concerning bishops, and repented; then he was crowned. Theophano was sent to the Princes' Islands; according to tradition, before her exile, she lunged at Tzimiskes with her fists. Nikephoros was an excellent general — he reconquered Crete and Antioch — and his tomb was inscribed: 'You conquered all, except a woman'.
level.phokas.goal: An empress lets her lover in through a window, the emperor is killed on a skin — and the patriarch crowns the murderer, only after exiling her.
level.phokas.hint: First, the love of the empress and the general. She leaves the window open — the lovers are in conspiracy, the general is inside. The general kills the sleeping emperor — right to the crown. The patriarch crowns him on condition of exiling the conspiring empress. Warning the emperor — not part of this story.
level.phokas.intro: Nikephoros Phokas — an ascetic and general, 'the pale death of the Saracens'; he is disliked in the capital, and his young wife Theophano — a beauty from a tavern — loves his nephew John Tzimiskes. The emperor sleeps on the floor, on a leopard skin, and places no guard at the window.
level.phokas.source: Leo the Deacon, 'History', V; John Skylitzes
level.phokas.title: The Bedroom Window
level.pilgrimage.fact: In the autumn of 1536, Yorkshire and all of northern England rebelled against the dissolution of the monasteries and the king's 'evil counselors'. Robert Aske, a London lawyer, led the 'Pilgrimage of Grace' – up to forty thousand people. The Duke of Norfolk, lacking forces, promised a general pardon and a parliament in York in the king's name; Aske disbanded his army and even stayed with the king for Christmas. In the spring, after a new minor uprising, Henry declared the promises void; Aske was hanged in chains on the walls of York in July 1537. Over two hundred people were executed. All monasteries were closed.
level.pilgrimage.goal: The king promises the rebels everything – and hangs their leader in chains once they disperse
level.pilgrimage.hint: The pilgrims must become a force – then their leader will have leverage, and Norfolk will yield: a promise, a pardon. There is no need to march on London. But when all disperse, the king's word will prove to be mere words and chains.
level.pilgrimage.intro: The king closes monasteries and destroys the old faith. The North rose: forty thousand under banners with the Five Wounds of Christ follow the lawyer Robert Aske. The royal army of the Duke of Norfolk is three times smaller.
level.pilgrimage.source: Letters and Papers of Henry VIII, XI–XII; M. Booth, 'The Pilgrimage of Grace'
level.pilgrimage.title: The Pilgrimage of Grace
level.pirates.fact: By 67 BC, Cilician pirates were plundering the coast of Italy and cutting off grain supplies. The tribune Aulus Gabinius passed a law granting one man authority over the entire Mediterranean and the coast up to 50 miles inland — Quintus Lutatius Catulus opposed it, warning that such power would destroy the republic. Pompey divided the sea into 13 sectors and cleared it in three months. He dealt with the captives unexpectedly: instead of executions, he settled them as farmers far from the sea — and piracy ceased for a generation. The precedent of extraordinary powers for one man remained; Caesar would later use it.
level.pirates.goal: One man gains power over all the sea – and pirates become farmers
level.pirates.hint: The law will pass only if Catulus is not allowed to object — leave the objector's place empty. A defeated pirate is not executed — he is negotiated with: an executed pirate means another pirate tomorrow.
level.pirates.intro: Cilician pirates plunder the Italian coast and have cut off the grain supply — Rome is on starvation rations. Catching them one by one is useless: power over the entire sea is needed at once, and they propose to give it to one man.
level.pirates.title: Power Over All the Sea
level.plague_justinian.fact: The first known plague pandemic began at Pelusium in Egypt in the summer of 541 and reached Constantinople in the spring of 542. Procopius of Caesarea, who served at court, described it as an eyewitness: buboes in the groin and under the arms, delirium, and no logic whatever in who died and who survived; he gives a figure of up to ten thousand deaths a day at the peak — historians consider it greatly inflated, but nobody disputes the scale of the disaster. Justinian fell ill himself and survived, as about one in five did. While he lay ill Theodora ruled the empire; on learning that the generals on the eastern frontier were discussing whom to make emperor should he die, she recalled Belisarius and put Bouzes in an underground cell for two years. Outbreaks recurred for two hundred years and, by various estimates, cost the Mediterranean between a quarter and a half of its population — along with any plan to revive a single empire.
level.plague_justinian.goal: The plague strikes down the emperor himself — and the empress holds power while he lies delirious
level.plague_justinian.hint: First the ships from Egypt: the chronicler counts the dead, and the emperor carries the infection. The infected man takes to his bed with a bubo and loses his standing. And then the empress takes power upon herself, and he survives. The country palace is a departure: a woman who has gone away will hold nothing.
level.plague_justinian.intro: The empire has just taken back Africa and Italy, great building works are under way, the treasury is strained — and then the grain ships arrive from Egypt. A few months later so many people are dying in the capital that they stop counting them. At court the historian Procopius is writing all of it down.
level.plague_justinian.source: Procopius, 'History of the Wars', II, 22–23; John of Ephesus, 'Ecclesiastical History'
level.plague_justinian.title: The Plague of Justinian
level.plassey.fact: On June 23, 1757, at Plassey, Clive, with 3,000 men (800 of whom were Europeans), defeated the Nawab's 50,000-strong army, losing 22 killed. Mir Jafar, commanding the larger part of the Nawab's forces, did not engage in battle due to a secret agreement; monsoon rain dampened the Bengalis' gunpowder, while the British covered theirs with tarpaulins. Siraj was captured and killed; Mir Jafar became Nawab and paid the Company and Clive personally over 2 million pounds. Thus began British rule in India – with bribery, not battle, and Clive would later say in Parliament: 'I am astonished at my own moderation.'
level.plassey.goal: Three thousand defeat fifty thousand because the enemy commander was bought beforehand
level.plassey.hint: First, secure Mir Jafar. The battle is in the grove — but the secured one must be positioned nearby: he will lead away the army, and the Nawab will lose his power. Then Clive, as a powerful ally, will proclaim the secured one as Nawab.
level.plassey.intro: Nawab of Bengal Siraj-ud-Daulah took Calcutta and imprisoned captives in the 'Black Hole'. Robert Clive, an East India Company clerk turned general, led three thousand against fifty. But the Nawab's commander, Mir Jafar, wants to be Nawab himself.
level.plassey.source: R. Orme, 'A History of the Military Transactions of the British Nation in Indostan'
level.plassey.title: The Mango Grove
level.plowce_1331.fact: On 27 September 1331 at Płowce, Łokietek attacked a detachment of the Order that had fallen behind in the fog and defeated it; when the main forces arrived the battle ended in a draw, but for Poland it was the first field victory over the Teutonic Knights. According to the chroniclers, Prince Casimir was sent away from the field before the battle so as not to risk the heir. Płowce is linked to the legend of the knight Florian Szary: the king saw him with three spears in his body, holding in his spilled entrails — and supposedly this gave rise to the Jelita coat of arms with three spears.
level.plowce_1331.goal: The old king strikes a straggling column of the Order's knights, and the heir is led away from the field
level.plowce_1331.hint: The Order is strong as long as it marches as one army. First find where it has split. Keep the heir out of the fighting — he still has to rule.
level.plowce_1331.intro: 1331. The Teutonic Order, which has seized Gdańsk Pomerania, is sweeping through Kuyavia with fire. King Władysław the Elbow-high is over seventy, and his son Casimir is his only heir. The Order's army is larger than the Polish one.
level.plowce_1331.source: Jan Długosz, Annals, IX; Wigand of Marburg, Chronicle
level.plowce_1331.title: Płowce
level.poison.fact: The Borgias eliminated wealthy cardinals with the famous poison 'cantarella' to seize their assets. Cardinal Orsini became one of the victims of this practice of 'inheritance through poisoning'.
level.poison.goal: The Borgias poison a rival at a feast
level.poison.hint: Let Cesare first invite the cardinal to a friendly feast and lull his vigilance — and only to the trusting will he offer the cantarella. The poison will not work on the wary.
level.poison.intro: Cardinal Orsini is rich, and the Borgia need money. Cesare's hospitality is deadly.
level.poison.title: Cantarella
level.poison_death.fact: In August 1503, Alexander VI suddenly died of a fever. According to a persistent legend, the Pope and Cesare Borgia mistakenly drank wine they had poisoned for a wealthy cardinal. Cesare survived but lost everything. Historians, however, attribute his death to malaria.
level.poison_death.goal: The Pope drinks wine poisoned for another
level.poison_death.hint: Let Cesare first prepare poison for the cardinal — and by a fatal error, the poisoned wine at the feast will be drunk by the Pope himself. Without the son's plot, the feast is harmless.
level.poison_death.intro: The Borgia planned to eliminate a rich cardinal at a feast with poisoned wine. But fate had other plans.
level.poison_death.title: The Fatal Feast
level.poitiers.fact: On September 19, 1356, at Poitiers, the Black Prince defeated John II the Good: dismounted French knights advanced through a hedge under a hail of arrows, while an English cavalry flank attack decided the battle. The King, fighting with an axe alongside his fourteen-year-old son Philip ("Father, beware on the right! Father, beware on the left!"), surrendered. That evening, the Black Prince himself served him at table, refusing to sit with the King. A ransom of three million écus was set — France collected it for years; John, released on his word of honor, returned to captivity when his hostage son escaped, and died in London.
level.poitiers.goal: The French king is captured — and the victor serves him at dinner.
level.poitiers.hint: The hedge and archers behind it — the Prince's preparation, his strength. Retreating to Bordeaux means losing the king. The king attacks the strong and is defeated, and then the Prince himself serves the captive dishes at dinner.
level.poitiers.intro: The Black Prince, with a six-thousand-strong detachment, retreats towards Bordeaux, laden with spoils; King John the Good, with an army three times larger, overtakes him near Poitiers. The English positioned themselves behind a hedge and a marsh.
level.poitiers.source: J. Froissart, "Chronicles", I; Geoffrey le Baker
level.poitiers.title: Poitiers
level.polonium_1898.fact: In Paris Maria married the physicist Pierre Curie, and in 1898, in a cold shed on the rue Lhomond, they discovered two new elements. The first, announced in July 1898, she named polonium — "after the country of one of us". Radium was announced in December. In 1903 Skłodowska-Curie received the Nobel Prize in Physics, and in 1911 in Chemistry: she was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes. Her laboratory notebooks are still radioactive and are kept in lead boxes.
level.polonium_1898.goal: A Warsaw woman who studied in secret discovers a new element in Paris and names it after a country that is not on the map
level.polonium_1898.hint: She arrives in Paris already a student of the underground university. Radium was not announced first — the name of the first element was a political gesture.
level.polonium_1898.intro: 1891. Maria Skłodowska is twenty-four. In Warsaw, under imperial rule, university is closed to women, and she studies at the underground "Flying University", which moves from apartment to apartment. Now she is going to Paris, to the Sorbonne.
level.polonium_1898.source: M. and P. Curie, communication to the Academy of Sciences, July 1898
level.polonium_1898.title: Polonium
level.poltava.fact: On June 27, 1709, Peter I's army decisively defeated Charles XII's Swedes near Poltava. This victory turned the tide of the Great Northern War and transformed Russia into a great European power.
level.poltava.goal: Peter utterly defeats the Swedish king.
level.poltava.hint: Let Peter first assemble and train a regular army — and only a ready army will defeat the Swede Charles at Poltava. The traitor Mazepa is not the target.
level.poltava.intro: Charles XII invaded Russia, and Hetman Mazepa betrayed Peter and led the Cossacks to the Swede. The fate of the war is being decided.
level.poltava.source: Report on the Battle of Poltava
level.poltava.title: Poltava
level.pompey_death.fact: On September 28, 48 BC, Pompey landed in Egypt, hoping for asylum. By order of the courtiers of the young Ptolemy XIII (Pothinus and Achillas), he was stabbed to death directly in his boat, in front of his wife. The arriving Caesar, according to tradition, turned away and wept upon receiving his rival's head — and turned his wrath upon Ptolemy.
level.pompey_death.goal: Ptolemy's court murders Pompey — and Caesar mourns his fallen rival
level.pompey_death.hint: Keep Caesar away from the harbor — he will spare his rival. Ptolemy's court will kill the fugitive; later, Caesar will be presented with the head, but he will not reward the killers.
level.pompey_death.intro: Defeated at Pharsalus, Pompey flees to Egypt for refuge. Caesar is ready to forgive his rival — but Ptolemy's court has its own plans.
level.pompey_death.title: The Death of Pompey
level.poniatowski_1764.fact: Poniatowski was Catherine's lover in 1755–1758. On 7 September 1764 he was elected king while Russian troops stood near Warsaw; Catherine wrote that she had "made" him king. In 1767–1768 the Russian ambassador Nikolai Repnin arrested and exiled to Kaluga Bishops Sołtyk and Załuski and Hetman Rzewuski, who had opposed him, and forced the Sejm to pass laws under Russia's guarantee. Stanisław August was an intelligent, educated king and patron of the arts — and he reigned over a country that less and less governed itself.
level.poniatowski_1764.goal: The empress's former lover becomes King of Poland — and discovers that her ambassador will rule in his place
level.poniatowski_1764.hint: First the romance, then the crown. He dreamed of marrying the empress, but it never happened. A king by patronage signs what he is dictated.
level.poniatowski_1764.intro: 1755, St Petersburg. A young Polish aristocrat, Stanisław Poniatowski, serves as secretary to the British ambassador and falls in love with Grand Duchess Catherine. Nine years later she is empress, and Poland is electing a king.
level.poniatowski_1764.source: Memoirs of Stanisław August; letters of Catherine II
level.poniatowski_1764.title: A King by Patronage
level.popiel_piast.fact: Prince Popiel was cruel: legend has it that he poisoned his uncles at a feast and left their bodies unburied. When two wanderers came to the prince's feast for the first haircut of his son, they were driven from the courtyard. The wanderers knocked at the cottage of the poor wheelwright Piast and his wife Rzepicha — they too were celebrating, the first haircut of their son Siemowit, but there was only food enough for one table. Piast welcomed the guests like family — and then a miracle happened: the keg of mead and the piece of pork in his cottage kept growing and growing, until there was enough to feed even the prince's guests. The wanderers cut Siemowit's hair and foretold that he would be prince. And punishment overtook Popiel: from the bodies of the poisoned uncles came swarms of mice, which drove the prince into a tower above Lake Gopło and devoured him. The people chose Siemowit as their prince — and with him began the Piast dynasty, which ruled Poland for more than four hundred years.
level.popiel_piast.goal: A cruel prince drives wanderers from his feast, a poor wheelwright takes them in — and his son becomes prince, while Popiel is eaten by mice
level.popiel_piast.hint: The wanderers come to the prince first — they go to the wheelwright only after being driven away. Piast is no conspirator: it was hospitality, not rebellion, that made his family princes. And Popiel will be dealt with without human hands.
level.popiel_piast.intro: In Gniezno rules Prince Popiel — cruel and, rumour has it, the poisoner of his uncles. He is holding a feast: the young prince is having his hair cut for the first time, the ritual of postrzyżyny, after which a boy becomes a man. Two wanderers come to the town. In the outer settlement, the wheelwright Piast and his wife Rzepka are also holding a haircutting — for their son Siemowit — but the poor have food for only one table.
level.popiel_piast.source: Gallus Anonymus, The Deeds of the Princes of the Poles, I, 1–3; Wincenty Kadłubek, Chronicle
level.popiel_piast.title: Popiel and the Mice
level.porphyry.fact: On January 16, 1547, Grand Prince Ivan IV was crowned Tsar in the Dormition Cathedral of the Kremlin, the first to assume the title 'Tsar of All Rus'. Thus, the Russian Tsardom was born.
level.porphyry.goal: The Sovereign of All Rus receives the royal crown
level.porphyry.hint: First, crown Justinian himself — and only then will the reigning emperor elevate Theodora to co-empress. Germanus is not worthy of the crown.
level.porphyry.intro: 527 AD. The heir Justinian ascends the throne. He desires the unprecedented — to crown his wife as full co-empress.
level.porphyry.source: The Rite of Ivan IV's Coronation, 1547
level.porphyry.title: Coronation as Tsar
level.porta_pia.fact: On 2 September 1870 Napoleon III capitulated at Sedan and the French garrison left Rome. On 20 September Italian artillery pounded the wall by the Porta Pia for three hours; when the breach was passable Pius IX ordered a white flag raised so that no blood would be shed for nothing — losses came to about seventy men. The plebiscite of 2 October returned 133,681 votes for union with Italy against 1,507. Rome became the capital in 1871; the pope declared himself a prisoner of the Vatican and never stepped outside its walls — the rupture lasted until the Lateran Treaty of 1929. The twentieth of September became a national holiday, and the street driven through the breach is called Via XX Settembre.
level.porta_pia.goal: The French leave, Italian artillery breaches the wall at Porta Pia — and Rome votes to become the capital, while the pope shuts himself inside the Vatican
level.porta_pia.hint: Sedan first: without the French garrison the pope is no longer a force. Then the breach at Porta Pia: a strong general beats a weakened one. The plebiscite is held by the king and his victorious general — the pope never recognised it and took no part. Negotiating with the pope: he refused even to listen.
level.porta_pia.intro: Italy is united, but Rome belongs to the pope and is guarded by a French garrison. Pius IX has declared himself infallible and will not yield an inch. And in France a war with Prussia is beginning.
level.porta_pia.source: D. Mack Smith, Italy: A Modern History; General Cadorna's dispatches
level.porta_pia.title: Porta Pia
level.poselenia.fact: Alexander I had been nursing the idea of settling the army on the land since 1810, and from 1816 entrusted it to Alexei Arakcheev. By 1825 some 375 thousand people were living in the military settlements — nearly a third of the army. Peasants were turned into military settlers: identical houses, regulation haircuts, life by timetable, children enrolled as cantonists at the age of seven, ploughing to the drum and the rod for an untidy yard. The model was Arakcheev's own Gruzino, where guests were taken to see it. In the summer of 1819 the Chuguev Uhlan Regiment mutinied: about two thousand men were arrested, a court martial sentenced 275 of them to run the gauntlet, and twenty-five died under the sticks; Arakcheev conducted the inquiry in person. The tsar is credited with saying that the settlements would exist whatever the cost, 'even if the road from Petersburg to Chudovo has to be paved with corpses'. The settlements outlived both Alexander and Nicholas — they were abolished only in 1857.
level.poselenia.goal: Ploughing to the drum drives the settled regiment into mutiny — and the inquiry is run by the very man they mutinied against
level.poselenia.hint: First the plan: the sovereign entrusts it to the count — and the count is strong. Vested with that trust, he lays out the peasant's day by the hour. The settler thus timetabled rises against the hated count — and gets the gauntlet. The petition to resign is a trap: nothing is entrusted to a man who has gone.
level.poselenia.intro: The emperor wants the army to feed itself: the soldier ploughs, the peasant drills, the treasury pays nothing. Carrying it out is entrusted to a man who takes orders literally and does not know the word 'roughly'. By 1825 a third of the Russian army lives this way.
level.poselenia.source: K. Yachmenikhin, 'Military Settlements in Russia'; reports on the Chuguev case of 1819
level.poselenia.title: The Military Settlements
level.potemkin.fact: Grigory Potemkin, a favorite and, according to rumors, the secret husband of Catherine II, oversaw the annexation of Crimea (1783) and the development of Novorossiya. The annexation of Crimea is a fact; the 'secret marriage' is a rumor; and 'Potemkin villages' are a legend about ostentatious display.
level.potemkin.goal: The all-powerful favorite brings Crimea to the empire.
level.potemkin.hint: Let Catherine first elevate Potemkin to the foremost dignitaries — and only vested with trust will he annex Crimea. The former favorite Orlov will not expand the realm.
level.potemkin.intro: Catherine had many favorites — but only one became a statesman. Grigory Orlov is already in the past.
level.potemkin.title: Potemkin and Crimea
level.prince.fact: Renouncing his cardinalate, Cesare Borgia conquered Romagna with fire and sword, forging his own principality. Niccolò Machiavelli presented his ruthlessness and perfidy as the model of an ideal ruler in his treatise 'The Prince'.
level.prince.goal: Cesare carves out a state for himself in Romagna
level.prince.hint: Let the Pope first equip his son with an army from the Church treasury — and only the equipped Cesare will conquer Romagna. The Pope himself does not take lands.
level.prince.intro: Cesare dreams of carving out a state for himself in Romagna. But without an army, the dream is empty — and the treasury is with his father, the Pope.
level.prince.title: The Prince
level.princes.fact: In June 1483, preacher Ralph Shaw declared at St. Paul's Cross that Edward IV's marriage was invalid and his children bastards; two days later, the Duke of Buckingham offered the crown to Richard of Gloucester, who 'yielded to entreaties' at Baynard's Castle. The boys — Edward V and his brother Richard — were last seen in the windows of the Tower that summer. Thomas More wrote that they were smothered with pillows on Richard III's orders; in 1674, two child skeletons were found under the stairs of the White Tower, now interred in Westminster Abbey. Whether Richard was guilty is still debated; Buckingham rebelled against him three months later and was beheaded, and two years later Richard died at Bosworth — you have already played how.
level.princes.goal: The uncle declares his nephews bastards, takes the crown — and the boys are never seen again.
level.princes.hint: A sermon at St. Paul's Cross — a powerful speech by the uncle against the boy — renders the heir illegitimate. Then Buckingham proclaims the uncle king. The boy cannot be crowned. And the crowned uncle leaves the condemned nephews in the Tower — forever.
level.princes.intro: Edward IV died, leaving a twelve-year-old son and his brother Richard of Gloucester as regent. Richard housed his nephews in the Tower 'until the coronation,' and his friend Buckingham found a preacher willing to declare the children illegitimate.
level.princes.source: Dominic Mancini, 'The Usurpation of Richard III'; T. More, 'The History of King Richard III'
level.princes.title: The Princes in the Tower
level.proscriptions.fact: Victorious in 82 BC, Sulla forced the Senate to appoint him dictator without term limits and posted proscription lists in the Forum: a bounty was paid for the head of anyone listed, and their property was auctioned off. Marcus Crassus amassed a fortune from these auctions, buying up homes for a pittance — and was the only one Sulla reprimanded for it. The eighteen-year-old Gaius Julius Caesar also appeared on the lists: nephew of Marius' wife, married to Cinna's daughter, and refusing to divorce her. His relatives begged for his pardon, and Sulla, yielding, uttered a phrase recorded by Suetonius: 'In this boy, there are many Mariuses.'
level.proscriptions.goal: The dictator posts the lists – and one boy survives
level.proscriptions.hint: Without proclamation as dictator, the lists are merely paper. One whose name is on the list cannot be spared: decide beforehand whose name will appear there.
level.proscriptions.intro: The civil war is won, and Sulla returns victorious. He wants to slaughter his enemies not in secret, but by law — and the lists in the Forum turn murder into a procedure. On one of the lists is an eighteen-year-old boy, Marius's relative by marriage.
level.proscriptions.title: The Lists
level.prussian_homage.fact: On 10 April 1525, in the Main Market Square of Kraków, Albrecht knelt before Sigismund the Old and received Prussia as a fief, as a hereditary duchy. Thus appeared the first Protestant state in Europe — and the former Teutonic Order became a Polish vassal. The irony of history: in 1657 Albrecht's descendants freed themselves from vassalage, and a century later Prussia took part in the partitions of Poland. Jan Matejko painted "The Prussian Homage" in 1882, when Poland was not on the map.
level.prussian_homage.goal: The last Grand Master of the Teutonic Order dissolves the Order and, in a Kraków square, swears allegiance to the Polish king as a vassal
level.prussian_homage.hint: The Grand Master of a monastic order cannot become anyone's vassal — first he will have to stop being Grand Master. And finishing him off on the battlefield means years more of war.
level.prussian_homage.intro: 1525. The last war with the Order has ended in a truce. Grand Master Albrecht Hohenzollern — nephew of the Polish king Sigismund the Old — has visited Luther, who advised him to marry and turn the Order into a secular duchy.
level.prussian_homage.title: The Prussian Homage
level.psie_pole.fact: Gallus Anonymus, a contemporary of the events, relates that Bolesław forbade the people of Głogów to surrender, and when the truce ended the emperor had the hostages, the townspeople's children, tied to the siege engines — but the defenders beat off the assault all the same. The siege failed, and Henry's army, worn down by guerrilla warfare, withdrew. The battle of Psie Pole ("Dogs' Field") near Wrocław on 24 August 1109 is first mentioned by Wincenty Kadłubek a century later: supposedly the field was so named for the dogs that dragged away the corpses — this is more likely a legend, as Gallus is silent about a great battle. He does, however, quote a mocking song sung about the Germans: "Poland cannot be taken with gold."
level.psie_pole.goal: The townspeople of Głogów do not surrender even when the emperor ties their children to the siege engines — and the duke strikes the weakened army
level.psie_pole.hint: While the emperor is at full strength, he cannot be beaten in the field. The town will hold only if it knows the duke's will — without it, it will surrender. And no peace: the emperor left empty-handed.
level.psie_pole.intro: 1109. Emperor Henry V marches on Poland to put Bolesław Wrymouth's exiled brother, Zbigniew, on the throne. First in his path stands Głogów on the Oder. The townspeople begged a five-day truce and gave hostages, promising to surrender if the duke did not come.
level.psie_pole.source: Gallus Anonymus, III, 5–15; Wincenty Kadłubek, Chronicle, III
level.psie_pole.title: Głogów and Psie Pole
level.pugachev.fact: In 1773–1775, the Cossack Yemelyan Pugachev, posing as the 'miraculously saved' Peter III, led the largest rebellion in Russian history. Alexander Suvorov was called upon to suppress it.
level.pugachev.goal: Suvorov captures the impostor, who called himself Peter III.
level.pugachev.hint: Let the impostor first raise a rebellion, calling himself tsar — and only the one who has rebelled will Suvorov capture and condemn. Until he rebels, there is no one to catch.
level.pugachev.intro: Don Cossack Pugachev declared himself the miraculously saved Peter III and raised half of Russia. Suvorov has been sent against him.
level.pugachev.title: Pugachev's Rebellion
level.pushkin.fact: Pushkin saw sixteen-year-old Natalia Goncharova at a Moscow ball in the winter of 1828–1829 and married her in 1831. On November 4 (16), 1836, he received an anonymous 'diploma of the Order of Cuckolds' and challenged Dantes; Dantes married Natalia's sister Catherine, the duel was postponed, but the courtship continued, and in January, Pushkin sent an insulting letter to Dantes' adoptive father, Baron Heeckeren. On January 27 (February 8), 1837, at the Black River, Dantes shot first; the poet, wounded in the stomach, shot while lying down and lightly wounded his opponent. He died two days later at Moika, 12; Dantes was demoted and exiled; he lived to be eighty-three as a senator of France. Lermontov was sent to the Caucasus for 'Death of the Poet.'
level.pushkin.goal: The poet falls in love at a ball, receives a lampoon — and in the snow by the Black River, duels with a cavalry guard
level.pushkin.hint: First, the ball — love. The cavalry guard sends the enamored poet a diploma — insulted and an enemy. The insulted poet duels with the cavalry guard — Black River. To go to Mikhailovskoye — to leave the plot.
level.pushkin.intro: Russia's foremost poet is married to St. Petersburg's foremost beauty. Cavalry guard Dantes, the adopted son of the Dutch envoy, openly courts her. An anonymous 'diploma of the Order of Cuckolds' circulates through the city.
level.pushkin.source: P. Shchyogolev, 'The Duel and Death of Pushkin'; Pushkin's letters
level.pushkin.title: Black River
level.pyrrhus.fact: In 280 BC, at Heraclea, Pyrrhus defeated Consul Laevinus — elephants routed the Roman cavalry — but lost so many veterans that, according to Plutarch, he said: 'Another such victory, and we are undone.' Hence 'Pyrrhic victory.' Gaius Fabricius, sent to him for prisoners, rejected gold and elephants; and when Pyrrhus's physician offered the Romans to poison the king, Fabricius sent the physician's letter to Pyrrhus himself. Pyrrhus released the prisoners without ransom and said that it would be easier to divert the sun from its course than Fabricius from his honesty. Five years later, he left Italy, having lost two-thirds of his army.
level.pyrrhus.goal: A king wins a battle in such a way that he loses the war — and cannot buy Roman honesty
level.pyrrhus.hint: Elephants strike the legions — but after the victory, the king counts his losses and realizes he won't survive another. And a senator cannot be bought with gold: he even sends the poisoner-physician back to the king.
level.pyrrhus.intro: Tarentum called for help against Rome the best general of Greece — Pyrrhus, King of Epirus, with twenty elephants, which no one in Italy had ever seen. Opposing him are Consul Laevinus with his legions and the old senator Fabricius, known for his poverty.
level.pyrrhus.title: Pyrrhic Victory
level.quebec.fact: On the night of September 13, 1759, Wolfe led 4400 soldiers up a steep path to the Plains of Abraham above Quebec. Montcalm, instead of waiting for reinforcements, attacked; the British line fired two volleys from forty paces — the French fled. Wolfe was wounded three times and died upon hearing 'they run': 'Now God be praised, I will die in peace.' Montcalm, mortally wounded during the retreat, said: 'So much the better — I shall not live to see the surrender of Quebec.' The battle lasted a quarter of an hour and gave Canada to Britain; the painting 'The Death of General Wolfe' is known to every Canadian schoolchild.
level.quebec.goal: A night ascent up the cliff decides Canada's fate, and both generals die on the same day.
level.quebec.hint: Bombarding is not attrition; the city will endure. To ascend the path to the plains at night — that is the decisive move. The battle — and both commanders are mortally wounded: victor and vanquished depart together.
level.quebec.intro: Quebec stands on a cliff above the St. Lawrence River, and Montcalm behind its walls can wait for winter. Wolfe bombards the city for three months to no avail. On the night of September 12, he finds a goat path up the cliff.
level.quebec.source: F. Parkman, 'Montcalm and Wolfe'; J. Knox's diary
level.quebec.title: The Plains of Abraham
level.raleigh.fact: Walter Raleigh was convicted of treason in 1603, but James I spared his life in the Tower, where he spent thirteen years writing 'The History of the World'. In 1616, he was released to search for gold on the Orinoco with the condition not to provoke the Spanish; his men attacked the Spanish fort of Santo Tomé, Raleigh's son died, and no gold was found. The Spanish ambassador Gondomar demanded his execution, and the king, valuing the Spanish alliance, ordered the old sentence to be carried out. On October 29, 1618, Raleigh tested the axe blade with his finger: 'This is a sharp medicine, but a sure cure for all diseases.' His widow kept his embalmed head for a quarter of a century.
level.raleigh.goal: A fifteen-year-old sentence is carried out at the demand of the Spanish ambassador.
level.raleigh.hint: On the Orinoco, he will attack the Spanish and lose. Then the powerful Spanish ambassador will demand his head — the king will yield. The sentence has long been passed: only execution remains. No one will pardon him.
level.raleigh.intro: Walter Raleigh — Elizabeth's favorite, poet, privateer, and founder of Virginia — has been imprisoned in the Tower for thirteen years under a sentence from James I. He secured his freedom by promising to find the gold of El Dorado on the Orinoco and not to provoke the Spanish.
level.raleigh.source: J. Aubrey, 'Brief Lives'; records of the 1603 trial
level.raleigh.title: Raleigh's Head
level.rasputin.fact: Grigori Rasputin, a peasant from the Tobolsk village of Pokrovskoye, from 1907 alleviated the hemophilia attacks of Tsarevich Alexei — in October 1912 in Spala, when doctors expected death, he telegraphed from Siberia 'The little one will not die,' and the bleeding stopped. Empress Alexandra believed him implicitly; during the war, ministerial appointments went through him, and the Duma openly spoke of 'dark forces.' On the night of December 17 (30), 1916, Prince Felix Yusupov lured him to his palace on the Moika; cyanide-laced cakes and wine had no effect, Yusupov shot him, Purishkevich added more shots, and the body was thrown from a bridge into a hole in the ice of the Malaya Nevka. An autopsy showed water in his lungs. Two and a half months later, the monarchy was no more.
level.rasputin.goal: A peasant, healing the Tsarevich, rules the empire — until he is poisoned, shot, and drowned under the ice
level.rasputin.hint: First, the heir bleeds out — the elder casts a spell and becomes a saint for the court, with authority. The Prince treats the saint to cyanide-laced cakes — he doesn't take them, but now they are enemies. Then the ice hole: the Prince kills the elder. Sending him to Pokrovskoye — the plot will leave with him.
level.rasputin.intro: Heir Alexei suffers from hemophilia; doctors are powerless, but the Siberian peasant Grigori Rasputin stops the bleeding with prayer — and becomes 'Our Friend' for the Empress, who appoints ministers. Prince Yusupov decides to save the monarchy by assassination.
level.rasputin.source: F. Yusupov, «The End of Rasputin»; E. Radzinsky, «Rasputin»
level.rasputin.title: The Elder
level.reconquest.fact: With a small army, Belisarius crushed the Vandal kingdom in Africa (533–534) and reconquered Italy, including Rome, from the Ostrogoths. Justinian's dream of restoring the Roman Empire was almost realized.
level.reconquest.hint: Let Belisarius first crush the Vandals and take Carthage — and only then will the conqueror of Africa reclaim Italy. The glory must be his, not Mundus's.
level.reconquest.intro: Justinian dreams of restoring the West to Rome. Belisarius is ready — but other generals also yearn for glory.
level.reconquest.title: Reconquest of the West
level.reform.fact: Catherine II corresponded with Voltaire and Diderot, convened the Legislative Commission (1767), and wrote the 'Instruction.' Her reign is known as 'enlightened absolutism,' though serfdom only intensified.
level.reform.goal: The Empress gives the empire new laws.
level.reform.hint: Let the empress first be imbued with ideas through correspondence with Diderot — and only then will she issue the enlightened Nakaz. Dignitary Potemkin will not replace the philosopher.
level.reform.intro: Catherine corresponds with Enlightenment philosophers and fancies herself their pupil on the throne.
level.reform.title: The Enlightened Sovereign
level.reform_act.fact: The Reform Bill of 1832 disenfranchised 56 'rotten boroughs' and granted representation to industrial towns, doubling the electorate. The Lords twice rejected it; during the 'May Days' of 1832, Grey resigned, Wellington failed to form a government, and the country was gripped by rallies and rumors of bank runs ('To stop the Duke, go for gold!'). William IV, who hated the reform, gave Grey a written promise to create as many peers as necessary — and the Lords passed the bill without a vote. Not a single peer had to be created. Thus England avoided the revolution that France experienced that same year.
level.reform_act.goal: The threat of a hundred new peers breaks the House of Lords without a single new peer.
level.reform_act.hint: A majority in the Commons is Grey's strength, and he has influence as Prime Minister: the King will negotiate with him and promise peers. Wellington's speech against Grey will achieve nothing. And when the government resigns, the Lords will yield themselves.
level.reform_act.intro: In England of 1830, a rotten borough of two houses sent two representatives to Parliament, while Manchester sent none. Earl Grey introduced a reform bill. The House of Lords, led by Wellington, rejected it, and riots began across the country.
level.reform_act.source: Diary of C. Greville; J. Butler, 'The Passing of the Great Reform Bill'
level.reform_act.title: The Reform Bill
level.regulus_word.fact: In 255 BC, Marcus Atilius Regulus was defeated at Bagradas by the Spartan mercenary Xanthippus; the consul was taken prisoner. A few years later, the Carthaginians sent him to Rome to request peace and an exchange of prisoners, having taken an oath to return if the embassy failed. Regulus persuaded the Senate to reject the terms — and returned to Carthage, where, according to Roman tradition, he was tortured: his eyelids were cut off and he was exposed to the sun, then placed in a barrel with nails. Polybius, the most sober historian of that war, is silent about this death — likely, the legend was born later to justify Roman cruelty towards Carthaginian prisoners. But Rome made the image of a man who returned to die for his word paramount.
level.regulus_word.goal: A prisoner, sent to ask for peace, dissuades Rome from peace — and returns to captivity to die
level.regulus_word.hint: First, defeat — only then will a prisoner be sent as an envoy. In the Senate, he will persuade them to refuse and swear to return. To remain in Rome means breaking his word: that path is not open to him.
level.regulus_word.intro: Consul Regulus landed in Africa and was already at the gates of Carthage when the Carthaginians hired the Spartan Xanthippus. He reorganized the army — and the Roman army ceased to exist, and the consul was taken prisoner.
level.regulus_word.title: Regulus's Word
level.restoration.fact: On September 3, 1651, Cromwell defeated Charles II at Worcester. For six weeks, the prince made his way to the coast: he spent a day hidden in an oak tree at Boscobel while soldiers searched below, traveled disguised as a servant, and reached France. After Cromwell's death, General George Monck led an army from Scotland, convened Parliament, which in May 1660 invited the king back. Charles entered London on his thirtieth birthday; Monck became a duke. Oak Apple Day was celebrated until the 19th century, and 'The Royal Oak' is the second most popular pub name in England.
level.restoration.goal: The defeated prince hides in an oak, flees — and returns as king by the will of a general.
level.restoration.hint: The one defeated at Worcester will not be executed if he hides in an oak tree. Years later, a powerful ally — a general — proclaims him king. His father's execution block is not his fate.
level.restoration.intro: The son of the executed king led the Scots into England — and was defeated by Cromwell at Worcester. A thousand pounds were offered for his head, and he was twenty-one years old and two meters tall. Nine years later, General Monck would decide who would rule.
level.restoration.title: The Royal Oak
level.romanos_blinded.fact: Romanos IV, freed by Alp Arslan, learned en route that he had been deposed on October 24, 1071; Michael VII and Caesar John Doukas ruled in the capital. Romanos gathered troops in Cappadocia and was twice defeated — near Docia and in the spring of 1072 near Adana, where Andronikos Doukas commanded the imperial army. He surrendered under a written oath from three bishops — of Chalcedon, Heraclea, and Colonia — that he would not be harmed, and took monastic vows. Caesar John ordered him blinded; on June 29, 1072, an unskilled executioner did so in Kotyaion, and Romanos died of infection several weeks later on the island of Prote. Michael Psellos wrote him a congratulatory letter: God, he said, took his eyes because He deemed him worthy of the highest light. Alp Arslan, upon learning this, said that the oath of the Romans was worthless — and died that same year.
level.romanos_blinded.goal: The Sultan released the Emperor — his own people defeated him, gave the word of three bishops, and blinded him contrary to their word.
level.romanos_blinded.hint: First, the field near Adana: the strong Doukas defeats the one returned from captivity. The defeated is promised life under the oath of bishops — he surrenders and takes monastic vows. And then the perjurer blinds the monk. The Sultan is not a savior in this story: do not let him rescue the defeated.
level.romanos_blinded.intro: Alp Arslan released Romanos with peace and gifts — but while he was on his way home, in the capital the Doukas clan proclaimed his stepson emperor. They write to Romanos: lay down your crown. He does not. Against him, they send Andronikos Doukas — the one who led the rearguard away from the field of Manzikert.
level.romanos_blinded.title: The Oath of the Three Bishops
level.romanov.fact: On February 21, 1613, the Zemsky Sobor elected Mikhail Fyodorovich Romanov as Tsar; Cossacks and noblemen agreed on him as a compromise — 'young, not yet fully wise, and will be amenable to us,' one of the boyars reportedly said. Meanwhile, a Polish-Lithuanian detachment searched for the chosen one in the Kostroma forests; Ivan Susanin, a peasant from the village of Domnino, according to a 1619 charter, 'enduring immeasurable tortures,' did not reveal the Tsar's location and was 'tortured to death' — legend added that he led the Poles into a swamp. On March 14, the Sobor's embassy arrived at the Ipatiev Monastery; his mother, Nun Martha, refused for six hours — 'people have lost their courage, betrayed their sovereigns' — then blessed her son with the Fyodorovskaya Icon. The dynasty ruled for three hundred four years and ended in 1917 in a house also called Ipatiev.
level.romanov.goal: The Sobor chooses a boy, a peasant leads the Poles into a swamp, his mother blesses him — and the dynasty begins.
level.romanov.hint: A powerful voivode at the Zemsky Sobor chooses Romanov — elected. A Polish detachment searches for the chosen one in the Kostroma forest — Susanin leads them into a swamp, the boy is safe. Only now, the Sobor's embassy to Ipatiev Monastery: the mother releases the chosen and unharmed one — a right to the crown. The coronation at the end. Do not take the prince's gold — a bribed voivode will not choose.
level.romanov.intro: Moscow is liberated, but there is no Tsar. The Zemsky Sobor – for the first time, all estates – chooses between princes, the Swedish prince, and the Polish prince. There is also sixteen-year-old Mikhail Romanov, the grandnephew of Ivan the Terrible's first wife; he is hiding with his mother near Kostroma, while Polish detachments scour the forests.
level.romanov.source: «Confirmed Charter on the Election of Mikhail Fyodorovich to the Moscow State»; S. Platonov
level.romanov.title: The First Romanov
level.romulus_augustulus.fact: In 476, the Germanic federates demanded a third of Italy's lands; the magister Orestes refused, and he was killed in Pavia. His son, the boy-emperor Romulus, diminutively called Augustulus, was deposed by Odoacer — but not executed: he was granted an allowance of six thousand solidi and a villa in Campania, and his further fate is unknown. Odoacer sent the insignia of imperial power to Constantinople with a message that the West no longer needed a separate emperor. Thus ended the Western Roman Empire — with a boy named after both the first king of Rome and the first emperor.
level.romulus_augustulus.goal: The West no longer needs an emperor.
level.romulus_augustulus.hint: First, the demand for land and a refusal, then — the end of the one who refused: as long as the magister lives, the boy will not be touched. And only then are the insignia of power sent to the East.
level.romulus_augustulus.intro: The empire is ruled by a boy, for whom his father-magister decides everything. Italy's army has long consisted of Germans, and they desire not wages, but land.
level.romulus_augustulus.title: The Last
level.rubicon.fact: On the night of January 10, 49 BC, Caesar, with the XIII Legion, crossed the border river Rubicon, thereby violating the law and initiating civil war against the Senate and Pompey. According to Suetonius, he uttered 'Alea iacta est' — 'The die is cast'.
level.rubicon.goal: Caesar crosses the Rubicon — and Pompey flees Rome
level.rubicon.hint: Secure an ally in the Forum, and meet your rival at the river. But if the Senate condemns the general with an ultimatum – he will no longer lead his army.
level.rubicon.intro: The Senate decreed: Caesar must disband his legions and return to Rome as a private citizen. Beyond the Rubicon River lies Italy, and to enter it with an army is an act of rebellion.
level.rubicon.title: The Die Is Cast
level.sabines.coach.1: Three panels, left to right. Press and hold a panel to move it. Rome needs wives — start with the festival.
level.sabines.coach.2: Place Romulus and Hersilia in the frame: the rule will activate itself.
level.sabines.coach.3: It is done—she is with him. The fathers will not forgive this: what came next?
level.sabines.coach.4: Only she can part two armies, who has both a father and a husband there.
level.sabines.fact: According to tradition, Romulus invited the neighboring Sabines to the festival of Consualia, and at a prearranged signal, the Romans carried off their unmarried daughters. War was inevitable, but when the armies met, the abducted women stood between their fathers and husbands — Titus Tatius and Romulus began to rule together. Livy emphasizes: the Romans swore they took them as lawful wives, not concubines — from this scene originated the wedding custom of carrying the bride over the threshold.
level.sabines.goal: Rome procures wives — and reconciles with their fathers through their own hands.
level.sabines.hint: Make them fall in love – before the war: in the heat of battle, there is no time for festivities. And only she who has one husband and another father can stand between the lines.
