level.varna_1444.fact: On 10 November 1444 at Varna on the Black Sea coast, Władysław, against John Hunyadi's advice to hold the line, attacked the Janissaries at the sultan's headquarters with five hundred knights and was killed; according to tradition, Murad sent his head to Bursa in a jar of honey. It is said that the sultan had the charter of the broken peace raised on a spear like a banner. The king's body was never found — and so legends long circulated that he had survived; one of them made him the Portuguese knight Henrique Alemão on Madeira. Nine years later Constantinople fell.
level.varna_1444.goal: The young king swears peace to the sultan, breaks the oath — and dies attacking the sultan's tent
level.varna_1444.hint: You can only break an oath you have sworn. Hunyadi holds the line — but he is not the one who decides the campaign. The battle's fate was decided by the king's impulse.
level.varna_1444.intro: 1444. Władysław III, King of Poland and Hungary, is twenty years old. In the summer, at Szeged, he swears a ten-year peace to Sultan Murad II. But the pope and Venice promise a fleet, the cardinal-legate Cesarini says an oath to infidels is not binding, and the crusade goes on.
level.varna_1444.source: Jan Długosz, Annals, XII; Callimachus, History of King Władysław
level.varna_1444.title: Varna
level.vendee.fact: In March 1793, the Vendée rebelled against conscription and persecution of the church; peasants elected the peddler Jacques Cathelineau as their leader. The Catholic Royal Army took cities—Saumur, Angers—but on June 29, near Nantes, Cathelineau was mortally wounded, and the rebellion receded. In 1794, General Turreau led twelve 'infernal columns' through the Vendée with orders to burn everything and kill everyone: an estimated one hundred to two hundred thousand people died, including women and children—sometimes called the first modern genocide. The Vendée has not forgiven the Republic for this to this day.
level.vendee.goal: The peasant army takes cities, is broken at Nantes—and the Republic burns the region.
level.vendee.hint: The Sacred Heart on his chest—peasants follow the peddler, that's his influence; negotiating with the strong Republic won't work. At the walls of Nantes, its strength defeats him. The broken are finished off by infernal columns—along with the entire region.
level.vendee.intro: The Republic announced a levy of three hundred thousand—and the peasants of the west, whose churches were closed and king executed, took up pitchforks. Their leader is the peddler Cathelineau, 'the Saint of Anjou,' with the embroidered Sacred Heart of Jesus on his chest.
level.vendee.source: R. Secher, 'A French Genocide'; memoirs of Madame de La Rochejaquelein
level.vendee.title: The Vendée
level.verdi.fact: Verdi staged Nabucco, with its chorus of Hebrew captives Va, pensiero, at La Scala in 1842; the audience demanded an encore of the chorus although encores were forbidden by the Austrian censors, who had gone through the libretto line by line. Italians heard themselves in a song about a lost homeland, and the melody became the unofficial anthem of the Risorgimento. Later, by 1859, Viva VERDI began appearing on the walls of Italian cities — the censors could not ban a composer's surname, and it read as Viva Vittorio Emanuele Re D'Italia, long live Victor Emmanuel, King of Italy. In 1861 Verdi himself, at Cavour's insistence, became a deputy in the first Italian parliament, though he disliked politics. At his funeral in 1901 eighty thousand people sang Va, pensiero in the streets of Milan.
level.verdi.goal: Censors cut the words — and the chorus of captives becomes an anthem, while the composer's name turns into a slogan
level.verdi.hint: The censor's scissors first: the words are struck out — the music remains. The censored composer gives the hall its chorus, and the hall falls in love. The beloved composer and the king — and V.E.R.D.I. appears on the walls. Writing for Vienna: a man who has been bought writes no anthem.
level.verdi.intro: Lombardy is under Austria and the word fatherland is struck out of librettos. A young composer who has just lost his wife and both children swears never to write music again — and then picks up a libretto about the Babylonian captivity.
level.verdi.source: M. Phillips-Matz, Verdi: A Biography; La Scala chronicles
level.verdi.title: Viva V.E.R.D.I.
level.verginia.fact: In 449 BC, the decemvir Appius Claudius, seeking Virginia, orchestrated a trial where his client declared the girl his runaway slave — and then Claudius himself awarded her to the plaintiff. Her father, centurion Virginius, asked to take his daughter aside, seized a knife from a butcher's stall, and stabbed her: 'Only thus, my daughter, can I make you free.' He fled to the army, the army withdrew to the Aventine, and the decemvirs fell; Appius committed suicide in prison. The story deliberately echoes Lucretia — and Livy emphasizes this: for the second time in Rome, tyrants fall because of a woman who could not be touched.
level.verginia.goal: A father kills his daughter to save her honor — and the decemvirs fall
level.verginia.hint: Dishonor is brought by a false claim. Here, the father's knife replaces a vow of vengeance: it gives weight to the accusation. And only then — a speech in the forum against the one who started it all.
level.verginia.intro: Rome is ruled by ten decemvirs, who wrote laws and refused to step down. The chief among them, Appius Claudius, set his eyes on Virginia, the daughter of a centurion — and ordered his client to declare her a slave.
level.verginia.title: The Butcher's Knife
level.vespers.fact: On March 30, 1282, Easter Monday, near the Church of the Holy Spirit in Palermo, a French sergeant, Drouet, began to search a Sicilian woman under the pretext of looking for weapons; the crowd killed him, the bells rang for vespers, and by morning no Frenchmen remained alive in the city — about two thousand. Within two weeks, the revolt engulfed the island; foreigners were identified by their accent, forced to pronounce 'ciciri' — 'chickpea.' Charles of Anjou, according to tradition, said: 'Lord, if it is Your will to cast me down, let me at least fall gradually.' In August, Peter III of Aragon, married to the daughter of Manfred of Hohenstaufen, landed in Trapani and was crowned in Palermo; the War of the Sicilian Vespers lasted twenty years. Verdi wrote an opera about it.
level.vespers.goal: At vespers in Palermo, a massacre erupts, the French are slaughtered in two weeks — and the crown of Sicily goes to Aragon.
level.vespers.hint: First, Procida's conspiracy with Aragon — they are in league. The conspirator incites Palermo at vespers — the French are defeated and expelled, the conspirator has influence. The influential conspirator proclaims the Aragonese king. Complaining to the Pope is useless — a yielding conspirator won't raise a rebellion.
level.vespers.intro: Sicily is ruled by the Frenchman Charles of Anjou, brother of Saint Louis; his officials plunder, his soldiers grow insolent. The exile Giovanni da Procida secretly travels between Constantinople, Aragon, and Palermo, preparing an uprising.
level.vespers.source: S. Runciman, 'The Sicilian Vespers'; Chronicle of Bartholomew of Neocastro
level.vespers.title: The Sicilian Vespers
level.vesuvius.fact: On August 24, 79 AD, Pliny the Elder, commanding the fleet at Misenum, was about to set sail out of scientific curiosity, but received a note from Rectina, cut off at the foot of the volcano — and turned the excursion into a rescue mission, ordering the quadriremes to be launched. He landed at Stabiae, where he died of asphyxiation on the shore. His eighteen-year-old nephew remained home with his rhetoric lessons — and later, at Tacitus's request, wrote two letters that became the most detailed description of the eruption in antiquity. Eruptions with a column of ash reaching the stratosphere are now called Plinian.
level.vesuvius.goal: The fleet sails to rescue, the admiral remains forever, and yet the chronicle is written.
level.vesuvius.hint: The ships sail not out of curiosity, but at a plea for help — first, a note. Do not take your nephew with you: he who steps onto the deck will record nothing, and it is he who must record it.
level.vesuvius.intro: Over the bay rose a cloud in the shape of a pine. Pliny, commanding the fleet at Misenum, was about to go observe — and then a note arrived from the other shore. Beside him was his nephew, also Pliny, seventeen years old.
level.vesuvius.source: Pliny the Younger, Letters, VI, 16 and VI, 20
level.vesuvius.title: Vesuvius
level.veto_1652.fact: On 9 March 1652 the envoy from Upytė, Władysław Siciński, lodged a protest against extending the Sejm and left; Marshal Andrzej Maksymilian Fredro acknowledged that without everyone's consent the Sejm could not continue. It was said that Siciński had been bribed by the Lithuanian magnate Janusz Radziwiłł. It was the first Sejm broken up by a single vote — the liberum veto. In the following hundred-odd years nearly half of all Sejms ended this way, and the state almost lost the ability to make decisions. According to legend, Siciński's body did not decay after his death, and for a long time the "accursed" man was displayed in the church in Upytė.
level.veto_1652.goal: One envoy shouts "Nie pozwalam!" — and the entire Sejm of the Commonwealth is dissolved without a single decision
level.veto_1652.hint: You can only break up a Sejm whose term has expired and which has to be extended unanimously. And the "Nie pozwalam" isn't shouted for nothing — there is money behind it. If the king talks the envoy round, nothing will happen — but it did.
level.veto_1652.intro: 1652. In the Commonwealth, decisions of the Sejm are taken unanimously: every nobleman is equal to every other. Until now dissenters have been persuaded — or shouted down. The Sejm in Warsaw has been sitting for six weeks, and its term is running out.
level.veto_1652.source: Diary of the Sejm of 1652; W. Konopczyński, Liberum Veto
level.veto_1652.title: Liberum Veto
level.victoria_albert.fact: Lord Melbourne, premier and mentor, spent up to six hours a day with the young Queen; when in 1839 she refused to replace her Whig ladies-in-waiting with Tories, Peel's government failed to form – the 'Bedchamber Crisis.' In October 1839, Victoria, seeing Albert of Saxe-Coburg on the Windsor staircase, wrote: 'It was a painful pleasure to look at him,' – and five days later, she herself proposed to him, as etiquette required for a monarch. The wedding on February 10, 1840, introduced the fashion for white wedding dresses. Nine children, the Christmas tree, the Crystal Palace – and forty years of widow's mourning after his death in 1861.
level.victoria_albert.goal: The Queen, tutored by the old premier, proposes to the prince herself
level.victoria_albert.hint: First, friendship with Melbourne – he makes a queen out of a girl. Then love at Windsor: she makes the proposal. And the wedding in St. James's Chapel. The Bedchamber Crisis is not about this.
level.victoria_albert.intro: The eighteen-year-old Queen learns to rule from Prime Minister Melbourne – he is like a father to her. And from Coburg arrives cousin Albert, and by etiquette, only she can make the proposal.
level.victoria_albert.source: Queen Victoria's Diaries; L. Strachey, 'Queen Victoria'
level.victoria_albert.title: Victoria and Albert
level.vienna_1683.fact: In August Jerzy Kulczycki, who knew Turkish, passed through the besiegers' camp and back in Turkish clothes, carrying letters. On 12 September 1683 Sobieski led the combined army down from the hills of the Kahlenberg; the charge of about eighteen thousand horsemen, among them several thousand winged hussars, is considered the largest cavalry charge in history. The vizier fled, abandoning his camp; in December he was strangled in Belgrade on the sultan's orders. Sobieski wrote to the pope: "Venimus, vidimus, Deus vicit" — "We came, we saw, God conquered." Legend credits Kulczycki with the first Viennese coffee house, using captured beans; in fact the first was opened by the Armenian Johannes Diodato in 1685.
level.vienna_1683.goal: A spy carries word through the Turkish camp, King John III leads an army to the rescue — and the winged hussars charge down the hill and save Vienna
level.vienna_1683.hint: The king won't come until he knows. The emperor has left Vienna, and a sortie is beyond him. The charge from the hill decides it.
level.vienna_1683.intro: Summer 1683. Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa with a huge Ottoman army is besieging Vienna, the capital of the Habsburg empire. Emperor Leopold I has left for Passau. The city is holding on with its last strength. The Polish king John III Sobieski has promised to come to its aid — but for that someone must get through the Turkish camp.
level.vienna_1683.source: John III Sobieski, letters to Marysieńka (1683); John Stoye, The Siege of Vienna (1964)
level.vienna_1683.title: Vienna
level.vienna_congress.fact: The Congress of Vienna sat from September 1814 to June 1815. Talleyrand came to represent defeated France and put forward the principle of legitimacy — the inviolability of lawful dynasties: it suited every monarch and at the same time protected the Bourbons newly restored in France. Within six weeks France had joined the committee of powers deciding the fate of Europe. The quarrel over Poland and Saxony — Alexander I demanded Poland, promising Prussia the whole of Saxony — brought matters to the brink of war, and on 3 January 1815 France, Austria and Britain signed a secret defensive alliance against Russia and Prussia. Returning from Elba, Napoleon found a copy of the treaty in the Tuileries and sent it to Alexander, hoping to set the allies at each other's throats; the tsar showed the paper to Metternich and threw it into the fire, saying this was no time for quarrels. The Prince de Ligne summed the congress up: "The congress dances, but it does not move." Talleyrand outlived every regime he served: after the congress he saw two more changes of power, was ambassador in London until 1834 and died in 1838.
level.vienna_congress.goal: Defeated France walks into the circle of the victors — and six months later signs a secret alliance against two of them
level.vienna_congress.hint: First the green table: a single word wins the diplomat his seat, while the tsar shows his appetite. The tsar's appetite frightens the Austrian. The man who has taken his seat and the frightened one sign what no one expected. The ballroom is a trap: whoever is dancing is not at the table.
level.vienna_congress.intro: Vienna in the autumn of 1814: four victorious powers are dividing Europe, and the representative of a shattered France has no place at their table. He arrives without an army, without money and without a vote — but with one word that every monarch needs at once.
level.vienna_congress.source: C.-M. Talleyrand, 'Memoirs'; H. Nicolson, 'The Congress of Vienna'
level.vienna_congress.title: The Congress Dances
level.walewska_1807.fact: According to Walewska's memoirs, Polish patriots persuaded her that her favour towards the emperor was a duty to her homeland. On 7 July 1807, by the Peace of Tilsit, Napoleon created the Duchy of Warsaw — with a constitution and an army, but not a kingdom; Prince Józef Poniatowski became minister of war. In 1810 Walewska gave birth to a son, Alexandre, later French foreign minister. That same year the emperor married Marie Louise of Austria. Walewska visited him on Elba.
level.walewska_1807.goal: Patriots persuade a young countess to become Napoleon's lover for Poland's sake — and the emperor creates the Duchy of Warsaw
level.walewska_1807.hint: The countess did not seek this love herself — she was asked. The emperor did not marry her: his wife was chosen from the Habsburgs. And the duchy was won not for love, but through it.
level.walewska_1807.intro: January 1807, Warsaw. Napoleon has crushed Prussia, and the Poles hope he will restore their state. At a ball the emperor notices eighteen-year-old Countess Maria Walewska, wife of an elderly chamberlain.
level.walewska_1807.source: Memoirs of M. Walewska; Peace of Tilsit, 1807
level.walewska_1807.title: Madame Walewska
level.wallace.fact: On September 11, 1297, at Stirling Bridge, Wallace allowed half of the English army to cross the narrow bridge – and then annihilated it on the other bank. A year later at Falkirk, Edward I personally defeated him: Scottish schiltrons of spears could not withstand Welsh archers. Wallace hid for seven years, was betrayed in 1305, tried in Westminster as a traitor (he responded that he had never sworn allegiance to Edward) and executed in Smithfield: hanged, drawn, and quartered; his head was displayed on London Bridge. The 1995 film is true in spirit and almost nothing in detail.
level.wallace.goal: The rebel defeats the English at the bridge, loses to the king in the field – and dies on the block
level.wallace.hint: At the bridge, the rebel becomes a force through cunning – and defeats Surrey. But against the King himself with his archers, he is weak: Falkirk is a rout, and the defeated will be outlawed. The condemned will be executed by the King.
level.wallace.intro: Edward I conquered Wales and turned his attention to Scotland. Against him rose not a lord, but a minor knight, William Wallace – with peasants and spears. The English army of the Earl of Surrey marches towards Stirling, where a single narrow bridge crosses the River Forth.
level.wallace.source: 'The Chronicle of Lanercost'; Guido of Warwick; Blind Harry, 'Wallace'
level.wallace.title: Braveheart
level.wanda.fact: After Prince Krak died, his daughter Wanda came to rule in Kraków — so beautiful and wise that her fame reached the German lands. Prince Rytygier sent matchmakers, and when he was refused, he came with an army to take both the princess and her land by force. Wanda herself rode out at the head of her warriors to meet the enemy. But when Rytygier's soldiers saw her, they lowered their weapons and refused to fight her. Abandoned by his army, Rytygier in despair threw himself on his own sword. And Wanda, as another version of the tale goes, so that no one would ever shed blood over her again, offered herself to the gods and threw herself into the Vistula. Over her grave the people raised a mound — it still stands near Kraków today.
level.wanda.goal: A princess refuses a foreign suitor and rides out to face his army — and the army refuses to fight her
level.wanda.hint: A wedding is not for Wanda, and in the field her army is weaker. Her weapon is herself: first the refusal, then to ride out and face the foreign army.
level.wanda.intro: After the death of Kraków's founder, Prince Krak, his daughter Wanda took the throne — so beautiful and wise that her fame reached the German lands. Rytygier, prince of the Alemanni, sent matchmakers. And when he was refused, he brought an army.
level.wanda.source: Wincenty Kadłubek, Chronicle, I, 7; Jan Długosz, Annals, I
level.wanda.title: Wanda, Who Would Not Wed a German
level.warsaw_confederation.fact: On 28 January 1573 the Warsaw Confederation proclaimed: "we who differ in religion will keep the peace among ourselves" — for the first time in Europe, freedom of worship for the nobility was enshrined in law; only one of the bishops signed the act. In May Henry of Valois was elected king. When, in Notre-Dame Cathedral, he hesitated to swear to the religious peace, the Polish envoy told him: "Si non iurabis, non regnabis" — "If you do not swear, you will not reign." The act of the Confederation is listed in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.
level.warsaw_confederation.goal: The nobility swears not to wage war over faith and forces the new king, brother of the man behind the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre, to swear to this peace
level.warsaw_confederation.hint: First peace between the faiths — then the election, or they will elect someone who will break it. The primate will try to talk the marshal into backing down; don't give in.
level.warsaw_confederation.intro: 1573. The last Jagiellon is dead, and for the first time the king will be elected by the whole nobility. Among Catholics, Lutherans, Calvinists and Orthodox, it is frightening to recall that half a year ago in Paris, on St Bartholomew's night, Catholics slaughtered thousands of Protestants. The leading candidate is the French prince Henry of Valois, brother of the king who arranged that night.
level.warsaw_confederation.source: Act of the Warsaw Confederation (1573); Henrician Articles
level.warsaw_confederation.title: The Warsaw Confederation
level.warsaw_mermaid.fact: Two mermaid sisters swam in from the sea: one stayed by the shores of Denmark, while the other swam up the Vistula to a small fishing village. At night the fishermen would find their nets tangled and their fish set free, and they resolved to catch the mischief-maker. But when they heard her song over the river, their hands dropped — so beautifully did she sing. Then a sly, rich merchant caught the mermaid and locked her in a wooden shed, meaning to cart her around the fairs and charge money to see her. That night a young fisherman named Wars heard her weeping and, with his friends, set her free. The grateful mermaid swore to protect their town whenever danger threatened it. That is why the Warsaw Mermaid holds a sword and a shield — she guards Warsaw to this day.
level.warsaw_mermaid.goal: A greedy merchant catches a mermaid, a poor fisherman frees her — and the mermaid takes up a sword to defend the city
level.warsaw_mermaid.hint: For the mermaid to be saved, she must first be caught. Only someone who took no money will free her. And she gives her oath to her rescuer.
level.warsaw_mermaid.intro: On the bank of the Vistula stands a small fishing village. At night the fishermen hear wondrous singing over the river — and see that someone is tearing their nets. One day a wealthy merchant passing through hears the song too.
level.warsaw_mermaid.source: Warsaw city legends; Artur Oppman (Or-Ot), Warsaw Legends (1925)
level.warsaw_mermaid.title: The Warsaw Mermaid
level.wat_tyler.fact: On June 15, 1381, at a meeting in Smithfield, Lord Mayor of London William Walworth struck Wat Tyler with a dagger – for the insolence with which he spoke to the King. The crowd drew their bows; and then fourteen-year-old Richard II rode out to them alone with the words: 'I am your King, I will be your leader, follow me' – and led the rebels into the fields, where they were met by the militia. All promises – the abolition of serfdom, pardons – he later revoked: 'You were and remain villains.' But the poll tax was no longer collected, and serfdom in England quietly died out over the next hundred years.
level.wat_tyler.goal: The leader is killed during negotiations, and the crowd is led away by the boy-king
level.wat_tyler.hint: The rebels are strong – the King cannot attack them. At the meeting, the mayor will kill the leader. And then the boy has one option: ride out to the leaderless crowd and declare himself their leader.
level.wat_tyler.intro: The third poll tax in four years roused Kent and Essex. Wat Tyler's peasants entered London, burned the Duke's palace, and beheaded the Archbishop. King Richard II is fourteen years old, and he has agreed to meet them in Smithfield.
level.wat_tyler.title: I Will Be Your Leader
level.waterloo.fact: On June 18, 1815, at Waterloo, Napoleon's army was defeated by the forces of the Duke of Wellington and Prussian Field Marshal Blücher. The Emperor abdicated a second time and was exiled to the island of Saint Helena, where he died in 1821.
level.waterloo.goal: The Coalition deposes the Emperor — and he is sent into exile
level.waterloo.hint: Let the coalition first break the emperor on the field of Waterloo — and only then shall the broken one be exiled to Saint Helena. The undefeated cannot be sent overseas.
level.waterloo.intro: June 1815. Napoleon, returned from Elba, stakes everything on a single battle at Waterloo against Wellington.
level.waterloo.title: Waterloo
level.waterloo_1815.fact: On June 18, 1815, Wellington held the ridge of Mont Saint Jean all day against the attacks of Ney and the Old Guard, and by evening, Blücher, who had kept his promise to arrive, appeared on the French right flank. Wellington called it 'the nearest run thing you ever saw in your life' — 'a damned nice thing'. Napoleon abdicated four days later and died on Saint Helena. Wellington wept upon learning of the losses; Blücher suggested naming the battle 'Belle Alliance', but the victor named it after the village where he had spent the night. 'Wellington' boots, 'Waterloo' station, and the ABBA song — all from there.
level.waterloo_1815.goal: The ridge holds all day, the Prussians arrive by evening — and the Emperor loses forever.
level.waterloo_1815.hint: Occupy the ridge in advance — preparation; attack first — lose. The Prussians are allies: only with them does Wellington have strength against a strong Napoleon. And then the battle — three in one frame.
level.waterloo_1815.intro: Napoleon returned from Elba, and he has a hundred days. Wellington stands on the ridge near the village of Waterloo with an army of English, Dutch, and Germans, while Blücher's Prussians, defeated two days ago, are somewhere twenty kilometers away. It is raining.
level.waterloo_1815.source: Wellington's Dispatch of June 19, 1815; E. Creasy, 'The Fifteen Decisive Battles of the World'
level.waterloo_1815.title: Waterloo
level.wawel_dragon.fact: A dragon made its lair in a cave beneath Wawel Hill. At first it devoured the cattle, then it began demanding people, and Kraków lived in fear. Prince Krak promised his daughter's hand to whoever rid the city of the monster — and knights in gleaming armour went to the cave one after another, but none returned. Then a poor shoemaker named Skuba took a ram, stuffed its hide with sulphur and pitch, sewed it up and left it by the cave. The dragon swallowed it whole — and a fire blazed up in its belly. The monster rushed to the Vistula and drank, and drank, and drank, until it burst. Skuba won the princess as his bride, and the cave — the Smocza Jama, the Dragon's Den — can still be seen beneath Wawel; at its entrance stands a dragon that breathes real fire.
level.wawel_dragon.goal: Knights perish in the dragon's cave, but a simple shoemaker tosses it a ram full of sulphur — and the dragon drinks the Vistula until it bursts
level.wawel_dragon.hint: The dragon can't be beaten by force — it eats knights. Cunning is needed, and cunning has to be prepared first. The reward goes to the one who won.
level.wawel_dragon.intro: A dragon has settled beneath Wawel Hill. It devours cattle, and then people, and Prince Krak promises a generous reward to whoever rids the city of the monster. Knights in armour go to the cave one after another.
level.wawel_dragon.source: Wincenty Kadłubek, Chronicle, I, 5; Marcin Bielski, Polish Chronicle (16th century)
level.wawel_dragon.title: The Wawel Dragon
level.wierzynek_1364.fact: On 12 May 1364 Casimir founded a university in Kraków — the future Jagiellonian University, the second in Central Europe after Prague. In September the Congress of Kraków brought together Emperor Charles IV, Louis of Hungary, Peter of Cyprus, Valdemar of Denmark and German princes; Casimir reconciled Charles with Louis. According to Długosz, the guests were entertained by the wealthy Kraków merchant Wierzynek — and the Wierzynek restaurant on the Main Market Square still dates itself from 1364. Of Casimir, Długosz would say: "he found Poland wooden and left it brick."
level.wierzynek_1364.goal: The king founds a university, and at a feast hosted by a Kraków merchant he reconciles the emperor with the King of Hungary
level.wierzynek_1364.hint: The king founded the university in spring, before the congress. It is easier to reconcile guests at the table than on the battlefield — but first you need a table. And don't let the guests come to blows before they sit down.
level.wierzynek_1364.intro: 1364. Casimir the Great, the last of the Piasts, has turned a ruined country into a power to be reckoned with. Emperor Charles IV and King Louis of Hungary are quarrelling: the emperor insulted Louis's mother — Casimir's sister. Kings are converging on Kraków.
level.wierzynek_1364.source: Jan Długosz, Annals, IX; Jan of Czarnków, Chronicle
level.wierzynek_1364.title: The Feast at Wierzynek's
level.wilberforce.fact: In 1787, under an oak in Holwood, William Pitt said to his friend: 'Wilberforce, why don't you take on the slave trade?' Wilberforce introduced an abolition bill almost every year from 1791; he was opposed by Liverpool MP Banastre Tarleton, a hero of the American War, and the planter lobby. On March 25, 1807, the Act for the Abolition of the Slave Trade passed by 283 votes to 16 — the House stood and applauded. Slavery itself in the colonies was abolished in 1833; Wilberforce learned of it three days before his death. The anti-slavery campaign invented the sugar boycott, petitions with hundreds of thousands of signatures, and the badge 'Am I not a Man and a Brother?' — the entire toolkit of modern activism.
level.wilberforce.goal: Twenty years of speeches — and the House rises to applaud the ban on the slave trade
level.wilberforce.hint: Friendship with the Prime Minister is a pillar. A weighty speech condemns the slave trader. And then the bill will pass — but only if the MP hasn't been bought by Liverpool money.
level.wilberforce.intro: Britain transports forty thousand slaves across the Atlantic each year, and Liverpool thrives on it. Young MP Wilberforce, under an oak on the estate of his friend — Prime Minister Pitt — decides to dedicate his life to abolishing the trade. Against him stand Tarleton and all the money of Liverpool.
level.wilberforce.source: R. and S. Wilberforce, 'The Life of William Wilberforce'; W. Hague, 'Wilberforce'
level.wilberforce.title: The Holwood Oak
level.witte.fact: Sergei Witte, minister of finance from 1892 to 1903, brought in the liquor monopoly and the gold rouble of 1897 and pressed on with the Trans-Siberian; to shorten the route he ran the Chinese Eastern Railway through Manchuria. He thought the Far Eastern adventure ruinous and argued with the Bezobrazov circle, who were pursuing timber concessions on the river Yalu; in August 1903 Nicholas II removed him from the ministry, giving him the honorary chair of the Committee of Ministers. Six months later the war with Japan began, and after Tsushima in May 1905 there was no one left to send for peace — so Witte went. The talks were held at Portsmouth in America under the mediation of President Theodore Roosevelt; on 23 August (5 September) 1905 the peace was signed: Russia gave up the southern half of Sakhalin, the Liaodong peninsula and the South Manchurian Railway, but did not pay a single rouble of indemnity. Witte received the title of count — and the nickname 'Count Half-Sakhalin'. That autumn he drew up the Manifesto of 17 October and became the first chairman of a Council of Ministers in Russian history, and in April 1906 he was dismissed; Roosevelt received the Nobel Peace Prize for the mediation.
level.witte.goal: The dismissed minister is sent to fetch a peace — and brings back a peace without indemnity, a count's title and an insulting nickname
level.witte.hint: First the rails: the minister is strong, and the sovereign is looking to the Far East. Carried away by the East, the sovereign moves the strong minister into an honorary chair. And then the dismissed man travels to Portsmouth, to the mediator. The timber concession is a trap: a man who has been bought will not be let near the peace table.
level.witte.intro: The minister of finance gave the empire a gold rouble and the longest railway in the world — and straightened it through somebody else's Manchuria. He also argued with those who were pushing Russia towards a war over timber concessions on the Yalu. He was removed from office six months before that war, and after Tsushima there was no one left to send for peace.
level.witte.source: S. Witte, 'Memoirs'; the Treaty of Portsmouth, 1905
level.witte.title: Count Half-Sakhalin
level.wolsey.fact: Thomas Wolsey, the son of an Ipswich butcher, became a cardinal, Lord Chancellor, and papal legate – the de facto ruler of England under the young Henry VIII. He could not obtain a divorce from Catherine of Aragon from Pope Clement VII: the Pope was in the hands of Emperor Charles V, her nephew. In 1529, Wolsey was stripped of his offices and property; in 1530, he was accused of treason and taken to London. En route, at Leicester Abbey, he died, saying: 'If I had served God as diligently as I have done the King, He would not have given me over in my grey hairs.' Hampton Court Palace, which he built, was taken by the King.
level.wolsey.goal: The all-powerful minister fails to secure a divorce – and dies en route to the block
level.wolsey.hint: There's no negotiating with the Pope – the Emperor's power is behind him. The King, by decree, strips the cardinal of everything. He won't reach the Tower: he will die in an abbey on the way. There will be no need to execute him.
level.wolsey.intro: Cardinal Wolsey has ruled England for the King for twenty years. Now the King needs a divorce, but the Pope is a prisoner of the Emperor, the Queen's nephew. Wolsey goes to ask, knowing he will return with nothing.
level.wolsey.source: G. Cavendish, 'The Life of Cardinal Wolsey'
level.wolsey.title: If I Had Served God
level.wrath.fact: In November 1581, Ivan the Terrible, in a fit of rage, fatally wounded his eldest son and heir, Tsarevich Ivan, with his staff. Ilya Repin immortalized the scene. The heir's death doomed the dynasty to extinction.
level.wrath.goal: The Tsar, in a fit of fury, kills his own son.
level.wrath.hint: First the Oprichnina with Malyuta; the heir is then ruined by the Tsar himself in his chambers.
level.wrath.source: I. Repin, 'Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan'
level.wrath.title: The Wrath of the Terrible
level.wrzesnia_1901.fact: In the spring of 1901 the schoolchildren of Września refused to answer in German in religion lessons; they were punished with the rod. On 20 May the parents burst into the school; in the autumn a court in Gniezno sentenced dozens of adults to prison, the mother of one of the pupils to two and a half years. Newspapers all over Europe wrote about Września, and Henryk Sienkiewicz and Maria Konopnicka spoke out in defence of the children. In 1906–1907 a school strike involved, by various estimates, up to seventy-five thousand children in the Prussian part of Poland.
level.wrzesnia_1901.goal: Schoolchildren refuse to pray in German, they are flogged — and their mothers' protest echoes across Europe
level.wrzesnia_1901.hint: If the mother persuades her son to give in, nothing will happen — but it did. The parents' protest began with the rods.
level.wrzesnia_1901.intro: 1901, the town of Września in Greater Poland, part of Prussia. The Polish language is being squeezed out of the schools; now even religious instruction must be learned and answered in German, from German catechisms.
level.wrzesnia_1901.source: Records of the 1901 Gniezno trial; M. Konopnicka, Rota
level.wrzesnia_1901.title: The Children of Września
level.wyatt.fact: In February 1554, Thomas Wyatt the Younger led the Kentishmen to London against the Spanish marriage. Mary I spoke at Guildhall on February 1: 'I am wedded to the kingdom, and on my finger is my coronation ring' — and the Londoners locked the gates. Wyatt reached Ludgate, found it closed, and surrendered. He was executed on April 11; on the scaffold, he cleared Elizabeth of all suspicion. Lady Jane Grey and her husband were also executed — as too dangerous banners. The marriage to Philip took place in July; they had no children.
level.wyatt.goal: The Queen's speech locks the capital's gates against the rebellion — and the rebel goes to the block
level.wyatt.hint: Kent gives the rebel strength. But the Queen addresses the Londoners — and the city becomes her strength. At Ludgate, the gates are closed: the defeated rebel is outlawed, and the Queen executes him with authority.
level.wyatt.intro: Mary announced her marriage to Philip of Spain, and Kent rose up: Thomas Wyatt, with four thousand men, marches on London. The Council advises the Queen to flee. She rides to Guildhall to speak with the citizens.
level.wyatt.source: J. Foxe, 'Book of Martyrs'; 'The Chronicle of Queen Jane and Two Years of Queen Mary'
level.wyatt.title: Wyatt's Rebellion
level.yarmouk.fact: In August 636, on the Yarmouk River near the Golan Heights, the Arabs of Khalid ibn al-Walid fought for six days against the Byzantine army commanded by Vahan; on the decisive day, a sandstorm blew into the Byzantines' faces, Arab cavalry outflanked them, and the retreating forces were driven into ravines. Heraclius, who was in Antioch, traditionally said: 'Peace be with you, Syria — what a beautiful land falls to the enemy,' and withdrew beyond the Taurus Mountains. Within two years, Damascus, Jerusalem (Patriarch Sophronius personally surrendered the city to Caliph Umar), and Antioch fell; by 642 — Egypt. The Empire lost two-thirds of its territory and never recovered it; Arabic became the language of the Middle East.
level.yarmouk.goal: The Sword of Allah emerges from the desert where none expected, and the Empire loses Syria forever.
level.yarmouk.hint: First, the march through the desert — Khalid is strong. Yarmouk: strong Khalid defeats the Emperor's army. The defeated Emperor bids farewell to Syria. There's no need to buy off the Arabs — they didn't come for gold.
level.yarmouk.intro: Six years after the triumph over Persia, Arabs of a new faith emerge from the desert. Khalid ibn al-Walid, 'The Sword of Allah,' crosses the waterless desert with his army in six days and outflanks the Byzantines at the Yarmouk River.
level.yarmouk.source: al-Baladhuri, 'Book of the Conquest of Lands'; W. Kaegi, 'Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests'
level.yarmouk.title: Yarmouk
level.yorktown.fact: In December 1773, Bostonians, disguised as Native Americans, dumped 342 chests of tea into the harbor – a protest against taxation without representation. In 1781, de Grasse's French fleet defeated the British at Chesapeake and trapped Cornwallis in Yorktown; after a three-week siege, he surrendered to Washington on October 19 – according to legend, British bands played 'The World Turned Upside Down.' George III, upon learning, drafted an abdication but did not sign it. In 1783 in Paris, Britain recognized the independence of the United States. Two years later, the King received the first American ambassador – John Adams – and said that he was the last to consent to the separation, and would be the first to welcome friendship.
level.yorktown.goal: Britain loses America when the French fleet traps its army with their backs to the sea
level.yorktown.hint: Tea in the harbor — a challenge from the colonies, from it their influence. Strength comes with the French fleet in Chesapeake. Then the siege of Yorktown — and Cornwallis is defeated. The King does not yield until the end — but it no longer matters.
level.yorktown.intro: The Thirteen Colonies refuse to pay taxes to a Parliament where they have no representation. George III deems this a rebellion. Cornwallis drove Washington's army south, only to find himself on the Yorktown peninsula, with his back to the sea.
level.yorktown.source: G. Washington's Diary; E. Gibbon, letters 1781.
level.yorktown.title: The World Turned Upside Down
level.zama.fact: In 202 BC, at Zama, Scipio won over the Numidian king Masinissa and for the first time gained superiority in cavalry — Syphax, the second Numidian king, sided with Carthage and had by then been defeated and captured. Against the elephants, Scipio rearranged his maniples into corridors: the animals passed through the ranks, almost without touching them. Masinissa's cavalry, returning from the pursuit, struck the rear — and Hannibal, who had never lost a battle before, fled. Later, according to tradition, he placed Scipio third on the list of the greatest generals, and when asked where he would place himself had he won at Zama, he replied: 'Then — above Alexander.'
level.zama.goal: Hannibal flees the field: cavalry and corridors decide everything.
level.zama.hint: Hannibal has two trump cards – elephants and cavalry. Elephants are given way, and cavalry is bought: Carthage bought one king, the second is still free.
level.zama.intro: Scipio has brought the war to Africa, and Carthage has recalled Hannibal from Italy. For the first time, they will meet face to face, and two things will decide the matter: whose cavalry and what to do with the elephants. The Numidians have the cavalry, and there are two Numidian kings.
level.zama.title: Elephants at Zama
level.zara.fact: By the treaty of 1201, Venice built a fleet for 33,500 crusaders for 85,000 marks, but by the summer of 1202, only about 12,000 had gathered, and the army underpaid by 34,000. Doge Enrico Dandolo, blind and, according to chroniclers, over eighty, offered a deferment in exchange for help against Zara, and in September 1202, at San Marco, he himself took the cross — Villehardouin writes that it was sewn onto his cotton cap. Innocent III, through his legate Peter of Capua, forbade attacking Christians under pain of excommunication; the letter was hidden from the army. Zara fell on November 24, 1202, after five days of siege; the Pope excommunicated the entire army, then forgave the Franks — but not the Venetians, and Dandolo concealed this from the rank and file. On January 1, 1203, envoys of Prince Alexios arrived in Zara with promises of two hundred thousand marks, church union, and an army — and the fleet turned towards Constantinople.
level.zara.goal: The blind Doge sews on the cross, leads crusaders against a Christian city for a debt, receives excommunication — and the prince's offer
level.zara.hint: First, the cross at San Marco: the Doge is a crusader and a force. Only a crusader takes Zara — and not a bought one: the prince's promises come after. The Pope excommunicates one who has already taken the city. The legate must not be listened to: a Doge who yields to the Pope will sail nowhere.
level.zara.intro: The crusaders gathered in Venice, but there are three times fewer than agreed, and they owe the republic thirty-four thousand marks. The blind Doge Dandolo knows how to settle the debt: Zara lies on the way — a Christian city that has fallen to the Hungarian king. Pope Innocent threatens excommunication to anyone who raises a sword against Christians.
level.zara.source: Geoffrey of Villehardouin, "The Conquest of Constantinople," §§ 56–108; Registers of Innocent III, V, 160–161
level.zara.title: Zara

ui.menu_sub:
Assemble the story from panels —
and discover what truly happened.
ui.onb.1.body: A level is three comic panels. Read them left to right: first the cause, then the consequence.
ui.onb.1.title: Three panels
ui.onb.2.body: Above is how the story must end. How you get there is up to you.
ui.onb.2.title: The goal
ui.onb.3.body: These are your characters. One can appear in several panels — and some are better left out.
ui.onb.3.title: The cast
ui.onb.4.body: Caesar meets Ptolemy on the battlefield, and Cleopatra's rival is gone. The first panel decides everything after it.
ui.onb.4.title: The cause
ui.onb.5.body: The Forum wins Cleopatra the backing of Rome; the throne room gives her the crown. The same figures in another order, and the story falls apart.
ui.onb.5.title: Order decides
ui.onb.6.body: The level comes together: you learn how it really happened, with the source it came from.
ui.onb.6.title: The truth is the prize
ui.paywall_sub: Unlock this chapter or subscribe to all content
ui.reset_msg:
All completed levels will be locked again.
This action cannot be undone.
ui.swap_hint: Press and hold a panel, then drag it onto another — panels swap places
ui.tip.1: Press and hold a panel and drag it onto another — order sometimes decides everything.
ui.tip.2: Extra characters are decoys. Not everyone needs a place.
ui.tip.3: Panel order is cause and effect: friendship, then the dagger!
ui.tip.4: The same character does different things in different scenes.
ui.tip.5: Yellow highlight: right characters, wrong order!
ui.tip.6: Each level is a real historical episode. Solve it to learn what truly happened!
ui.tip.7: One detail changes everything: a feast turns fatal with a dash of poison.
ui.tip.8: Ask yourself: what are three ways to mess this up?
ui.unlock_body: First chapter is free. A one-time purchase unlocks all chapters, including future ones.
ui.wrong_inert: Completely wrong — neither place nor characters
ui.wrong_order: The right scenes — but not in this order: press and hold a panel to move it
ui.wrong_slots: The right people, but the wrong parts: reposition them in the frame.
ui.wrong_unused: This scene isn't part of the story
